There is no known reliable record of McCain saying he couldn’t support repeal specifically “because of the economy.”

claim: "There's been a 1,700 percent increase in asylum claims over the last 10 years."
rationale: The claim is unsupported as stated because it gives no country, dataset, or exact 10‑year period; major datasets (UNHCR, Eurostat, national agencies) do not show a consistent 1,700% rise in asylum claims across large jurisdictions over typical 10‑year spans. While some countries or small subgroups have seen very large percentage changes in short periods, a sustained 1,700% increase over a decade for asylum claims broadly is highly unlikely and not corroborated by standard statistics.

claim: "CDC announces that students may be kept from parents overnight as Ohio sets up COVID-19 FEMA camps."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the CDC announced students may be held from parents overnight nor that Ohio established ‘COVID-19 FEMA camps’ for students. CDC issued public-health guidance on isolation/quarantine, but it does not create or operate detention camps, and Ohio did not set up FEMA-run camps to sequester students. This claim mixes conspiracy terminology with incorrect attribution of a CDC policy.

claim: "The unemployment rate for folks who've never gone to college is almost double what it is for those who have."
rationale: This claim is misleading as stated. Bureau of Labor Statistics data show unemployment is higher for people with less education, but the gap depends on how groups are defined and on the year — people with only a high school diploma or some college often have only modestly higher unemployment than college graduates, and only the <high-school group sometimes has roughly double the rate of those with a bachelor's. The statement omits a timeframe and precise definitions, so it overgeneralizes.

claim: "Over 80 percent of the people want the shot to vote" on whether to approve same-sex marriage, according to polls.
rationale: There is no clear evidence from major public-opinion polls that over 80% of people want a public vote (referendum) to decide approval of same-sex marriage. Polls on this topic typically show much lower and variable proportions (often around half to the low‑60s depending on wording, country and time), and support figures above 80% are not documented. The claim appears to overstate or misinterpret available polling results.

claim: Obama "suggested bombing Pakistan."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Obama suggested bombing Pakistan as a policy or publicly called for bombing the country. While his administration authorized targeted drone strikes against militant targets inside Pakistan and ordered the 2011 raid that killed Osama bin Laden in Abbottabad, those actions are not equivalent to advocating bombing Pakistan as a whole and have been mischaracterized in some attacks on his record.

claim: "Wisconsin lost more jobs over the past 12 months than any other state."
rationale: The claim gives no specific 12‑month period and therefore can’t be verified as stated. Historical state payroll data (e.g., BLS monthly state nonfarm payrolls) shows which state lost the most jobs changes over time, and major downturns typically saw larger absolute losses in much larger states than Wisconsin. Without a precise date range and data source, the assertion that Wisconsin lost more jobs than any other state is unsupported.

claim: The Dow Jones Industrial Average "jumped 1000 points in last 5 weeks, Record fastest 1000 point move in history."
rationale: The claim is misleading and likely false. The Dow has recorded 1,000+ point moves in much shorter time spans (including single trading days) during the 2020 market volatility and at other times, so a 1,000‑point rise over five weeks would not be the fastest such move in history. Without a specific date range or definition of “fastest” (calendar days, trading days, intraday), the assertion that this was a record is unsupported.

claim: "Science says that being single will kill you faster than obesity."
rationale: The claim overstates and mischaracterizes the research. Some studies and meta-analyses show social isolation or loneliness is associated with higher mortality risk—sometimes described as comparable to major risk factors—but that is not the same as saying being single (unmarried) will “kill you faster” than obesity. Single status is heterogeneous and confounded by socioeconomic, behavioral, and health factors, and obesity remains a well-established independent mortality risk.

claim: "We actually have this critical race theory moved into all our schools in Virginia."
rationale: The claim that Critical Race Theory (CRT) has been "moved into all our schools in Virginia" is false as a broad, factual statement. CRT is primarily an academic legal theory rather than a mandated K–12 curriculum, there is no evidence of a statewide requirement that every Virginia school teach CRT, and Virginia has had public debate and legal restrictions around teaching divisive concepts rather than a uniform CRT rollout. Individual districts or schools may include lessons on race or systemic racism, but that is not the same as a statewide adoption of CRT in all schools.

claim: On allowing abortion in cases of rape or incest, "I have never said that or advocated that."
rationale: This claim is not verifiable as written because it lacks the identity of who said "I have never said that or advocated that." Without a named speaker and timeframe, one cannot confirm their entire public record. Because verification requires checking that person's statements and votes, and many public figures have at times expressed support for rape/incest exceptions, the blanket denial is treated as unreliable.

claim: Says Jeb Bush "said he would take his pants off and moon everybody ... Nobody reports that."
rationale: There is no credible record or contemporaneous news reporting that Jeb Bush publicly said he would ‘take his pants off and moon everybody.’ Such an attention-grabbing remark by a major political figure would have been widely reported and documented; its absence in reliable sources indicates the claim is false or a misattribution. Without a verifiable source, the quote should not be treated as genuine.

claim: It is a myth that Florida's education legislation was "negotiated in secret."
rationale: Contemporary reporting and legislative records indicate that key Florida education bills were largely shaped through closed-door discussions among legislative leaders, the governor's office, and select stakeholders rather than through broad public negotiation. While some hearings and committee votes were public, the core drafting and amendment process for major provisions occurred in private, so labeling the claim that negotiations were secret as a "myth" is inaccurate.

claim: Says Oregon’s highest income tax bracket included anyone making more than $250,000 in 2012 before the state expanded its upper bracket to include "anyone making more than $125,000."
rationale: The claim is misleading. In 2012 Oregon’s top marginal rate already applied at $125,000 for single filers (and at $250,000 for married filing jointly), so it was not the case that only those making more than $250,000 were in the highest bracket before any expansion. The statement conflates filing-status thresholds and misstates how the bracket change operated.

claim: Says Sen. Thad Cochran "voted to spend hundreds of millions of dollars on ... the Bridge to Nowhere in Alaska instead of shifting the money to repair a bridge damaged by Hurricane Katrina."
rationale: This specific claim overstates the record. The notorious Alaska “Bridge to Nowhere” (Gravina Island Bridge) was primarily championed by Alaska lawmakers and was an earmark of roughly $223 million in the 2005 transportation bill; I do not have clear evidence that Sen. Thad Cochran personally cast a vote that explicitly directed those funds instead of reallocating them to a particular Katrina-damaged bridge. Cochran did vote on broader transportation and emergency-spending measures around that period, but tying him to a distinct, documented vote to fund the Alaska bridge instead of repairing a named Katrina bridge is not supported by clear, specific evidence.

claim: After merging with Tim Hortons of Canada, Burger King is "not moving. … Our headquarters will remain in Miami" and "(we) will continue to pay all of our federal, state and local U.S. taxes."
rationale: At the time of the 2014 merger creating Restaurant Brands International, Burger King executives publicly stated that Burger King’s operational headquarters would remain in Miami and that the company would continue to pay U.S. federal, state and local taxes. Those were explicit pledges made during the merger announcement. However, the legal parent was domiciled in Canada, which affected the company’s overall tax structure and drew controversy.

claim: Says to Hillary Clinton, "You heard what I said about (the Trans-Pacific Partnership trade deal), and all of a sudden you were against it."
rationale: The claim implies Hillary Clinton flipped to oppose the Trans‑Pacific Partnership only after hearing the speaker (implying Trump). In reality Clinton announced her opposition in October 2015 after sustained pressure from primary challengers (notably Bernie Sanders) and labor/progressive groups; while Trump had also criticized TPP, there is no clear evidence his remarks directly caused her change. The claim therefore overstates and misattributes causation.

claim: "Kyle Rittenhouse used his COVID-19 stimulus check to purchase the AR-15 he used in the fatal Kenosha shooting."
rationale: There is no evidence that Kyle Rittenhouse used a COVID-19 stimulus payment to buy the rifle used in the Kenosha shooting. Rittenhouse was 17 at the time and ineligible for an individual CARES Act stimulus check, and multiple news outlets and fact-checkers investigated and found no proof the firearm was purchased with stimulus funds. The claim appears to be a false attribution of the source of funds.

claim: The Republican replacement for Obamacare does not give massive tax cuts to wealthy Americans.
rationale: Analyses of Republican replacement proposals (notably the 2017 American Health Care Act) found they repealed ACA taxes that mainly affected high earners (e.g., the 3.8% net investment income tax and the 0.9% Medicare surtax) and shifted benefits such that higher-income households received larger net tax reductions. The Congressional Budget Office and independent groups concluded the package produced disproportionate tax gains for wealthier households rather than eliminating substantial tax breaks for them.

claim: Since Sept. 11, 2001, "270,000 Americans were killed by gunfire at home."
rationale: The claim is not supported by official U.S. mortality data. CDC/NCHS firearm-death statistics show total firearm deaths since Sept 11, 2001 number well into the hundreds of thousands and the phrase “killed by gunfire at home” is ambiguous; there is no authoritative source that matches the precise figure of 270,000 for that stated phrasing and period.

claim: "Republicans in Congress are plotting to take away Medicare, Medicaid and Social Security."
rationale: The claim overstates and mischaracterizes available evidence. While some Republican members and proposals have called for cuts, restructuring, block grants, or partial privatization of Medicare, Medicaid, or changes to Social Security benefits, there is no credible evidence that Republicans in Congress are unified in a plan to abolish or "take away" all three programs outright. Party leaders and mainstream GOP platforms typically argue for reforms to reduce costs rather than complete elimination.

claim: Judge Ketanji Brown Jackson "gave child porn offenders sentences below the guidelines and below what the prosecutors were requesting," showing she is "soft on child pornography offenders."
rationale: Records and contemporary fact-checking show Judge Ketanji Brown Jackson did impose some below-guideline sentences in certain child‑pornography cases, but not universally, and departures often had case-specific explanations (cooperation, offense role, mental health, legal issues). The claim's jump from isolated below‑guideline sentences to the broad conclusion that she is "soft on child pornography offenders" is an opinion and not supported as an objective fact.

claim: "Tonight in Ohio, more people came out to vote for Barack Obama in an unopposed race than voted for (Mitt) Romney and (Rick) Santorum combined."
rationale: This claim is likely false: in Ohio primaries with a contested Republican race (e.g., 2012), the combined vote for leading Republican candidates typically exceeded the vote total for an unopposed incumbent Democrat. A contested GOP primary in Ohio drew substantial turnout, whereas an unopposed Obama primary normally produced much lower raw vote totals. Without a specific date the claim appears to contradict typical historical turnout patterns and reported Ohio primary results from that cycle.

claim: "Australia Closing Borders in a few hours for 6-months"
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official announcement that Australia is instituting an immediate border closure for six months. Australian border policy changes are publicly announced by federal ministers and widely reported in mainstream news; no such announcement has been made. While Australia did close or heavily restrict borders during the COVID-19 pandemic, that historical precedent does not support the present claim.

claim: Says Madison and Milwaukee County both carry sanctuary status for illegal immigrants and released undocumented immigrants who have committed multiple crimes including sexual assault of a child
rationale: The claim mixes vague language and broad assertions that are not supported by public records. While Madison has local policies limiting municipal cooperation with federal immigration enforcement (often described as “welcoming” or partial sanctuary), and some Milwaukee-area jurisdictions have limited-cooperation policies, neither is a blanket legal sanctuary that prevents arrest or prosecution for serious crimes. There is no verified evidence that both jurisdictions systematically released multiple undocumented immigrants who had committed multiple crimes including sexual assault of a child as a general policy.

claim: "When Fidel Castro came into office, you know what he did? He had a massive literacy program."
rationale: True. After coming to power following the 1959 Cuban Revolution, Castro's government launched the nationwide 1961 National Literacy Campaign, mobilizing hundreds of thousands of teachers and volunteers and sharply reducing illiteracy. The program is widely documented as a major, early social initiative of his administration.

claim: "On issue after issue that really were hard to explain or understand, you voted present . . . And anytime anyone raises that, there's always some kind of explanation."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it names no person, time period, or specific votes; assessing whether someone repeatedly voted "present" on hard-to-explain issues requires checking public roll-call records. Without those specifics or supporting evidence, the assertion is unsubstantiated and cannot be confirmed as factual.

claim: "The president gave the (auto) companies to the UAW."
rationale: There is no evidence any U.S. president "gave" auto companies to the UAW. While the federal government intervened in the 2008–09 auto crisis (bailouts and bankruptcy restructurings) and the UAW obtained concessions, board representation and a retiree VEBA that received company stock, the companies were not transferred wholesale to the union nor nationalized by a president. The claim overstates and mischaracterizes those interventions and settlements.

claim: Says "CNN host Fareed Zakaria calls for jihad rape of white women."
rationale: There is no credible evidence, transcript, or reporting that Fareed Zakaria—an established CNN host and journalist—called for "jihad rape of white women." The accusation appears to be a defamatory social-media hoax or a doctored/misattributed quote and is inconsistent with his public record and past statements. Given the severity of the claim and absence of reliable sourcing, it should be treated as false.

claim: "More black babies are aborted in NYC than born."
rationale: This claim is not supported by official New York City vital-statistics reporting and has been repeatedly debunked. NYC abortion records are reported by the mother’s race and cannot be straightforwardly compared to live births without careful definition, and available yearly data show that live births to Black mothers in NYC equal or exceed abortions among Black women rather than being outnumbered by them. The claim conflates different measures and omits a year or data source, producing a misleading conclusion.

claim: Image of expansive pit shows a lithium mine.
rationale: There is insufficient evidence to identify the photographed pit as a lithium mine from the image alone. Many open pits and evaporation ponds look similar and can be used for copper, phosphate, sand, salt, or other minerals; some lithium is produced from brine ponds rather than large open pits. Without provenance, geolocation, or expert analysis, the claim cannot be verified and is more plausibly treated as false.

claim: Says Patrick Henry said, "The Constitution is not a document for the government to restrain the people: it is an instrument for the people to restrain the government."
rationale: There is no primary-source evidence that Patrick Henry ever used this exact wording; the sentence does not appear in his collected speeches or correspondence and seems to emerge in later secondary sources. The line is a succinct modern paraphrase of a republican idea and has been widely misattributed to Henry without documentary support.

claim: Says Ted Cruz "never denied" his father was photographed with Lee Harvey Oswald.
rationale: There is no clear record of Ted Cruz himself stating the exact claim that he “never denied” his father was photographed with Lee Harvey Oswald. Contemporary news coverage and responses from the Cruz campaign disputed and questioned the identification of the man in the photo rather than containing a straightforward admission framed as “never denied.” Given ambiguous sourcing and no direct quotation, the assertion as phrased is likely false or a mischaracterization.

claim: Brookhaven homeowners pay hundreds of dollars less in property taxes compared with owners of the same-value homes in unincorporated DeKalb County.
rationale: I cannot confirm the blanket claim that Brookhaven homeowners uniformly pay "hundreds of dollars less" than owners of same-value homes in unincorporated DeKalb County. Property-tax bills depend on specific millage rates, overlapping city and county levies, homestead exemptions, bond levies and the tax year; in some years Brookhaven residents might pay less, in others they could pay the same or more. Without a specific year and calculation the statement is too general to be treated as a fact.

claim: "There's no negative advertising in my campaign at all."
rationale: The absolute statement that there is “no negative advertising in my campaign at all” is implausible and unverifiable without a comprehensive audit. Political campaigns and allied independent groups commonly run attack or contrast ads, and even subtle comparisons can be classified as negative, so claiming zero negative advertising is unlikely to be accurate unless proven.

claim: Says Joe Cunningham voted for $5 million in taxpayer funds to go into his and other politicians’ campaigns to pay for personal expenses and TV ads.
rationale: There is no evidence that Rep. Joe Cunningham voted to direct $5 million in taxpayer funds into his or other politicians’ campaigns for personal expenses and TV ads. Federal campaign finance law prohibits using public or campaign funds for personal expenses, and no major federal bill enacted during his term authorized a $5 million earmark for politicians’ campaign personal spending. The claim appears to conflate or invent a funding action that did not occur in the congressional record.

claim: Says that except for Donald Trump, "every other major party nominee" for the past 40 years has released their tax returns.
rationale: The statement is an overbroad generalization that depends on ambiguous definitions (what counts as the "past 40 years," who counts as a "major party nominee," and whether partial/restricted disclosures count as "released"). While most recent major-party nominees have disclosed at least some tax information, there have been variations in how complete those disclosures were, so the claim that every other nominee without exception released their returns is unsupported. Trump’s refusal was notable, but the blanket "every other" formulation is likely incorrect without tighter definitions and a nominee-by-nominee check.

claim: "We’re now spending 42 percent of our economy on government."
rationale: The claim is presented as a current, unqualified fact but is ambiguous and therefore misleading. Depending on the country, the exact measure (federal vs. total government spending) and the year, government spending as a share of GDP has varied; in the U.S. total government spending (federal + state + local) has been in the mid-30s to low-40s percent range and only briefly approached or exceeded ~42% during pandemic stimulus years. Without specifying which measure and what time point, the blanket statement "we're now spending 42 percent of our economy on government" is not reliably true.

claim: Says the U.S. Department of Justice has "seen in the past" that police department "consent decrees don’t work, that there’s very little change, that oftentimes immediately after a consent decree goes into effect, crime actually goes up."
rationale: This claim overstates and mischaracterizes DOJ practice and findings. The Department of Justice has long used consent decrees as a remediation tool and DOJ publications and independent research show mixed to positive effects on police policies and misconduct; there is no DOJ-wide conclusion that consent decrees “don’t work” or that crime routinely rises immediately afterward, and empirical evidence on crime effects is inconclusive and context-dependent.

claim: U.S. Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz "has blamed the Republicans for the creation of Hamas."
rationale: There is no reliable record that Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz said the Republican Party "created" Hamas. Hamas was founded in Gaza in 1987 as an offshoot of the Muslim Brotherhood, and attributing its creation to U.S. Republicans is historically inaccurate and appears to be a misattribution or rhetorical distortion rather than a documented quote by Wasserman Schultz.

claim: "The amount of money that we put into running our own state legislature is nearly as much as we put into the University of Rhode Island."
rationale: State legislative operating budgets are typically a small fraction of public university budgets or state appropriations for universities. The University of Rhode Island has annual operating expenses and state support measured in the tens to hundreds of millions, while the cost of running a state legislature (staff, member pay, facilities, operating costs) is generally much smaller, so it is unlikely the two amounts are nearly equal. Without a very specific fiscal year and definitional scope the comparison is misleading.

claim: "I did not support the war in Iraq … The record shows that I’m right."
rationale: The claim as presented is unverified and likely false because no speaker or specific record is named. Many public figures who later said they did not support the Iraq War in fact voted for 2002 authorizations or otherwise backed military action, and those roll-call votes and statements are the authoritative record. Without identifying who “I” is and which document or vote is meant, the assertion that “the record shows that I’m right” cannot be confirmed and is often contradicted by available records.

claim: The Buffalo protester pushed to the ground "had been previously arrested 300 times. 82 times for incitement. Riots is what he does for a living."
rationale: Independent fact-checks and contemporary news reporting found no evidence that the Buffalo protester pushed to the ground had been arrested 300 times or 82 times for incitement. Records and reporting showed only limited history of past activism and no substantiation for the specific large arrest counts, and the claim appears to have originated as social-media speculation. Therefore the numeric arrest allegations are false.

claim: Sen. Sherrod Brown "has chosen to side with Washington bureaucrats and fringe extremists in the attacks on our natural resources."
rationale: The statement is an unsupported, partisan assertion rather than a specific verifiable fact. Sherrod Brown, a Democratic U.S. senator from Ohio, has a public record of supporting environmental protections and regulatory oversight, and there is no documented evidence that he has broadly allied with 'Washington bureaucrats and fringe extremists' to attack natural resources. The claim uses vague, charged labels and provides no concrete incidents or votes to substantiate it.

claim: Says Mitt Romney flip-flopped on an assault weapons ban.
rationale: The claim is misleading because Romney’s record shows shifts on specific gun policies but not a clear, single, documented public reversal on an explicit federal ‘assault weapons ban’ phrasing. He backed certain gun restrictions while governor of Massachusetts and has later opposed some federal bans, so whether that counts as a “flip‑flop” depends on timing and policy details. Without a precise quote or timeframe the blanket claim is not reliably true.

claim: U.S. military involvement in Libya "allowed thousands of surface-to-air missiles to fall into the hands of radical Islamists."
rationale: This statement overstates the evidence. After the 2011 Libya conflict there were documented losses and illicit spreading of shoulder‑fired air defenses (MANPADS) and other weapons, and U.S./NATO forces did not secure all stockpiles, but independent investigations and UN reports do not support a verified figure of “thousands” of surface‑to‑air missiles being delivered to radical Islamist groups and the responsibility was shared among many actors and chaotic post‑collapse looting. The claim thus combines an inflated numeric assertion and a simplistic attribution to U.S. military action that is not supported by reliable public evidence.

claim: Says the Hawaii governor "can’t find anything that says (President Barack Obama) was born in Hawaii."
rationale: This claim is false. Hawaii's Department of Health had a Certification of Live Birth on file for Barack Obama that was made public in 2008, and a scanned long-form birth certificate was released by the state in 2011, showing he was born in Honolulu. While there was media attention and some politically charged statements about records, the official state records did show his Hawaiian birth.

claim: Says Julie Parrish is "one of Sarah Palin’s mama grizzlies."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Julie Parrish was identified or officially endorsed by Sarah Palin or SarahPAC as one of Palin's 'Mama Grizzlies.' The 'Mama Grizzly' label was publicly applied to a specific set of high‑profile Palin‑backed candidates around 2010, and Parrish (an Oregon state legislator) was not listed or widely described in that group.

claim: "The unemployment rate among (the) non-college-educated is well into the double digits in America. It's 4 percent or 5 percent for people who have college degrees."
rationale: This claim overstates typical U.S. unemployment for the non-college-educated. Bureau of Labor Statistics data show unemployment rates vary by educational attainment, but for the broad group without a college degree the rate is usually in the low-to-mid single digits (not “well into the double digits”), while college graduates commonly have lower unemployment—often in the roughly 2–5% range. Only during the COVID-19 peak in 2020 did many less-educated groups briefly hit double-digit unemployment.

claim: "The average student will be spending $1,700 to $1,800 more during the life of their loan because of this surcharge."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it lacks key context (which surcharge, which loans, which students) and no supporting evidence is provided. Average extra cost from any surcharge depends on loan size, interest rate, repayment term, and borrower behavior, so a blanket $1,700–$1,800 figure is not generally demonstrable without specific modeling or sources.

claim: "Teenage births cost Texas taxpayers $1.1 billion in health care, foster care and lost tax revenue in 2010 alone."
rationale: Contemporary public-health and policy analyses estimated that teen childbearing imposed roughly $1.1 billion in taxpayer costs in Texas for 2010. Those calculations combined projected public expenditures (Medicaid/health care, foster care and related services) and lost tax revenue from lower earnings among teen mothers to arrive at the total. The claim accurately paraphrases that widely-cited estimate.

claim: The United States is "about to have the smallest Army since before WWII, the smallest Navy since WWI and the smallest Air Force ever."
rationale: The statement is misleading and not accurate as presented. Historical personnel and force-level data show the Army, Navy and Air Force have fluctuated over decades and whether a branch is the "smallest" depends on the metric (personnel, ships, aircraft) and the exact year referenced; under common measures the claim’s blanket comparisons are incorrect. Fact-checks of similar claims have found parts misleading or false.

claim: "About 80 percent of (the manufacturing and agriculture) tax credit goes to claimants who are making $1 million or more."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and unsupported by public analyses: there is no widely-cited evidence that roughly 80% of a generic “manufacturing and agriculture” tax credit is captured by claimants with $1 million+ income. Distribution of tax-credit benefits varies widely by specific program and many manufacturing and agricultural credits are claimed by smaller businesses and farms as well as large firms, so a blanket 80% figure is unlikely. Without a named program, time period, or jurisdiction the assertion cannot be substantiated.

claim: "(GM and Chrysler) repaid their loans."
rationale: Both GM and Chrysler received large federal bailout loans and went through bankruptcy/restructuring, but they did not fully repay the government the amounts originally lent. The Treasury recovered only a portion of its investments (selling GM shares and accepting restructurings for Chrysler), and taxpayers experienced a net loss on the auto bailout overall.

claim: Fox News changed its accreditation to "entertainment."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Fox News formally ‘changed its accreditation’ to an “entertainment” classification. Accreditation categories are assigned by host institutions (e.g., White House, Congressional press galleries), and while isolated website mislabels or social-media claims have occasionally shown outlets listed as “entertainment,” that is not the same as Fox News itself changing accreditation. Major news organizations and credentialing bodies continue to treat Fox News as a news organization.

claim: The Senate GOP plan does not raise taxes for Americans earning less than $70,000.
rationale: This claim is misleading/false because past Senate GOP tax proposals have been shown by nonpartisan analysts to produce tax increases for some households earning under $70,000 once changes like elimination of deductions, phase‑outs, state interactions, or expiration of temporary cuts are counted. Effects vary by filing status, state, and whether the figure refers to individual or household income, so a blanket assertion that no one under $70,000 would see a tax increase is inaccurate.

claim: "The recidivism rate is nearly 29 percent and has been climbing steadily since detainees began being released from Guantanamo."
rationale: The 29% figure is misleading: the Department of Defense at times reported a similar number only when combining both “confirmed” and broader “suspected” returns to the fight, not a stable confirmed recidivism rate. Independent analyses and DoD updates show rates that vary by definition and year, and the proportion has fluctuated rather than showing a clear, steady climb since releases began.

claim: Says Bill Clinton opposes President Barack Obama's plan to raise taxes on wealthy Americans.
rationale: The claim that Bill Clinton opposes President Obama’s plan to raise taxes on wealthy Americans is inaccurate in general. Publicly, Clinton has supported measures to raise taxes on high-income households (for example endorsing allowing Bush-era tax cuts to expire for those above about $250,000) and did not mount a public campaign opposing Obama’s proposals to tax the wealthy. Without a specific date or proposal, the broad claim of Clinton opposition is misleading.

claim: Veterans should vote Republican "because the damn Democrats blocked the VA Healthcare bill again."
rationale: The statement is a generalized, unverified attribution that Democrats “blocked the VA Healthcare bill again” without naming a specific bill or vote; legislative outcomes depend on particular bills, amendments, and roll-call records. Public voting records show VA-related measures have been passed and opposed by members of both parties at different times, so it’s misleading to claim Democrats singularly and repeatedly blocked a VA healthcare bill without evidence.

claim: "Dems have removed any mention of ‘God’ from their Platform."
rationale: The claim is incorrect as stated — Democrats did not formally "remove" mentions of God from a party platform. In 2020 the Democratic National Committee chose not to adopt a new full platform (opting instead for a unity resolution and task-force proposals), so there was no single late-year platform document from which to excise references; earlier Democratic platforms did include references to God. Fact-checkers reported the claim as misleading and lacking necessary context about which document and year are meant.

claim: The "Back the Blue" Act that Gov. Kim Reynolds signs means you can't wear the American flag. "So throw out those towels and swimsuits ... or you’re a criminal!"
rationale: The claim is false: the Iowa "Back the Blue" law signed by Gov. Kim Reynolds increases penalties related to assaults on or obstruction of law enforcement and addresses certain protest-related conduct, but it does not criminalize wearing or displaying the American flag on clothing, towels, or swimsuits. Fact-checks and the bill’s text show the law targets crimes against officers and protest activities rather than banning U.S. flag apparel.

claim: "Snitker has been virtually ignored by the major media."
rationale: The claim is implausible given that Brian Snitker (the Atlanta Braves manager commonly referenced) has been covered repeatedly by major national and sports outlets, especially during the Braves’ playoff runs and managerial milestones. Saying he was “virtually ignored” contradicts the existence of numerous game reports, profiles, and interviews in mainstream media. The claim is also vague about time period and which outlets count as “major.”

claim: What Republicans call the "death tax" is the estate tax "on the ultra wealthy" which, in 2016, was paid by only "two out of every 1,000 people."
rationale: Republicans commonly call the federal estate tax the “death tax,” and in 2016 the federal estate tax applied only to estates above a high exemption (about $5.45 million per person), i.e. very wealthy estates. IRS/Tax Policy Center estimates and Form 706 filings show only about 0.2% of decedents’ estates (roughly two per 1,000 deaths) owed federal estate tax in 2016. The phrasing ‘‘on the ultra wealthy’’ matches the high exemption threshold that limits liability to a very small share of estates.

claim: "94 percent of winning candidates in 2010 had more money than their opponents."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated as written and lacks necessary context (which offices, raised vs. spent, including outside/independent expenditures). While campaign cash strongly correlates with winning and many 2010 winners outraised opponents, I could not confirm a universal 94% figure across all contests for 2010; reported percentages differ by chamber and by whether outside spending is counted. Because the statement is precise but unsupported and ambiguous, it is likely incorrect as a blanket claim.

claim: "One in 19 Americans today get SSDI or SSI. That's one in 19 Americans (who) are disabled."
rationale: The claim mixes program enrollment and a disability prevalence claim and is misleading. Combined monthly counts of SSDI and SSI recipients are in the mid‑teens of millions depending on year and counting methodology, but simple addition double‑counts some concurrent beneficiaries and SSI includes aged/blind recipients who aren’t all disabled; likewise many disabled Americans do not receive SSDI/SSI. Thus it’s incorrect to state flatly that “one in 19 Americans are disabled” based on SSDI/SSI enrollment.

claim: A study found an "82% miscarriage rate" among women between 30 days and 20 weeks pregnant who got an mRNA COVID-19 vaccine.
rationale: The 82% figure is a misinterpretation of limited or passive-reporting data and is not supported by higher-quality studies. Large surveillance and prospective vaccine-safety analyses (including CDC v-safe and a NEJM report of mRNA vaccines in pregnancy) found miscarriage/spontaneous-abortion rates in line with expected background risks, far below 82%.

claim: Before the coronavirus pandemic, the United States had "the greatest economy in the history of our country."
rationale: The claim is a subjective value judgment rather than an objectively verifiable fact. Although immediately before the COVID-19 pandemic the U.S. had record nominal GDP, very low unemployment and a high stock market, calling it "the greatest economy in the history of our country" depends on which metrics (real GDP per capita, inequality, labor force participation, productivity, etc.) and timeframes are used, so it cannot be stated as an unequivocal fact.

claim: "Facts have now come out to show conclusively" that the 2020 presidential election wasn’t legitimate.
rationale: Multiple independent audits, recounts, state certifications, and hundreds of court rulings found no credible evidence of widespread fraud that would change the 2020 outcome. Federal and state election officials, including the DOJ and CISA, concluded there was no evidence of widespread fraud; no court accepted a case proving the election was illegitimate.

claim: "If you put the $47 billion in revenue (raised over 10 years by the Buffett rule) into infrastructure you could create 611,000 infrastructure jobs."
rationale: The claim conflates a money-to-jobs conversion that depends on key assumptions. $47 billion over 10 years divided by commonly-cited infrastructure multipliers (roughly ~13,000 job‑years per $1 billion) yields about 611,000 job‑years, not 611,000 permanent, year‑round jobs; different studies produce very different job counts. The Buffett Rule revenue estimate itself and whether jobs are counted as direct, indirect, or induced (and over what time period) are disputed, so the straight statement is misleading.

claim: "In six years, (U.S. Rep. Gary) Peters introduced zero bills that became law."
rationale: I cannot confirm the ambiguous phrase “in six years,” but it is unlikely to be true that Rep. Gary Peters introduced absolutely zero bills that later became law over any six‑year span of his congressional career. Congressional sponsorship records (e.g., Congress.gov) typically show at least some bills sponsored or co‑sponsored by Peters that were enacted; the claim is unverified as stated and implausible without a specified timeframe.

claim: "When I was Mayor of South Pasadena, we actually reduced the property taxes we collected."
rationale: The claim is presented without any identifying details (who, when) and is not verifiable as stated. In California municipalities like South Pasadena, property tax levies and assessed values are governed largely by county administration and state rules (e.g., Proposition 13), and a mayor alone typically cannot unilaterally reduce the property taxes collected by the county. Without specific dates, council actions, or documentation showing a measurable reduction in taxes collected during the named mayoralty, the claim cannot be substantiated.

claim: Says the Koch brothers want to "protect tax cuts for companies that ship our jobs overseas."
rationale: The Koch brothers and their network have broadly advocated for lower corporate taxes and free‑market policies, which critics say can benefit companies that offshore jobs, but there is no clear, direct evidence they explicitly stated a goal to "protect tax cuts for companies that ship our jobs overseas." The claim frames a critic’s interpretation as an expressed intent by the Kochs; that stronger, specific assertion is not substantiated by public statements or policy documents attributed to them. Thus the phrasing overstates what is verifiable about their stated goals.

claim: Says Gov. Chris Christie’s "poll ratings have been going up."
rationale: The statement is too vague to be verified as written — it provides no timeframe, poll source, or population. Chris Christie’s approval ratings have risen at certain points (notably after Hurricane Sandy in 2012) and fallen at others (notably after the Bridgegate scandal and at various points during his presidential bid), so a blanket claim that his “poll ratings have been going up” is not generally true without context. Given the mixed historical trend, the claim as stated is unreliable.

claim: Says President Barack Obama has launched "twice as many strikes (on) countries that are predominantly Muslim" than President George W. Bush.
rationale: The claim is imprecise and not supported by consistent data. While the Obama administration significantly increased and expanded U.S. strike activity (notably drone strikes) into more predominantly Muslim countries than the Bush administration, different metrics (number of strikes, countries affected, or casualties) produce different counts and do not reliably show a simple “twice as many strikes.” Because the statement lacks definitions and is contradicted by nuanced counts and reporting, it is misleading as stated.

claim: Says Justice Elena Kagan recused herself in "many cases where she had little role" as solicitor general, simply because of the appearance of a conflict of interest.
rationale: When Justice Kagan joined the Supreme Court she filed a list of recusals covering dozens of matters stemming from her prior role as Solicitor General; several involved cases where the SG's office had a role but she had limited personal involvement. She and court ethics observers explained the recusals were meant to avoid even the appearance of a conflict of interest, not necessarily because she had personally litigated each matter.

claim: "Fox News barely covered (the Duggar family) scandal until Megyn Kelly was able to secure this interview."
rationale: This is inaccurate: when the Josh Duggar molestation allegations resurfaced in May–June 2015, Fox News and FoxNews.com ran reports and segments about the story before Megyn Kelly’s high-profile interview. Kelly’s sit-down was a prominent, later piece of coverage, but it did not mark the beginning of Fox News’ reporting on the scandal.

claim: A Virginia principal "expelled two kids for wearing a crucifix around their necks  saying, ‘there is no place for religion at school.’"
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reputable news reporting that a Virginia principal expelled two students for wearing crucifixes while declaring "there is no place for religion at school." Public schools are generally prohibited by the First Amendment from disciplining students solely for wearing religious symbols, and similar viral claims have repeatedly been debunked or shown to be mischaracterizations of dress-code or safety enforcement. Given the lack of corroborating reporting and the legal implausibility, the specific claim is false.

claim: Says he and Mitt Romney "always said that we agree with the 2014 deadline" for leaving Afghanistan.
rationale: The claim is unverified and likely false because it presents a specific quoted joint position without identifying the speaker or sourcing the statement. Public records of Mitt Romney's 2012-era statements about Afghanistan show varied emphasis on conditions and timelines rather than a single, consistently repeated joint claim that they "always said" they agreed with a 2014 withdrawal deadline. Without a cited source or named speaker, the precise quotation and its attribution cannot be confirmed.

claim: Says "If you compare the Portland Metro area to the CDC’s statewide cavity rates ... the Portland Metro area would actually rank as having the 15th lowest cavity rate in the U.S."
rationale: The claim asserts a precise national ranking for the Portland Metro area against CDC statewide cavity rates, but the CDC publishes dental decay statistics at the state level and does not provide a directly comparable "Portland Metro" state-equivalent rank. Without citing a specific metric, age group, year, or local survey that was converted to a state-equivalent rate, the asserted placement as "15th lowest" is unsupported. Therefore the claim is not reliable as stated.

claim: "Irish superstar Saoirse Ronan dies after on-set accident in St. Lucia."
rationale: There are no credible reports or announcements that Saoirse Ronan died in an on-set accident in St. Lucia; major news outlets and industry trade publications would have widely reported such an event. Public appearances, statements from representatives, and the absence of reliable coverage indicate this claim is a rumor and not true.

claim: Says a gun bill before the Senate would make it a federal felony to "leave town for more than seven days, and leave someone else at home with your firearms."
rationale: This is false. No recent federal gun bill makes it a felony merely to leave town for more than seven days and leave your firearms with someone else; federal proposals in circulation have addressed background checks, safe storage, transfers to prohibited persons, or ghost guns, but they do not criminalize routine temporary custodial arrangements in a homeowner’s absence. The claim appears to misread or exaggerate language about unlawful transfers or storage that may appear in some proposals or state laws.

claim: Facebook is changing its hate speech policy to ban "Let’s go Brandon."
rationale: There is no evidence Meta (Facebook) announced a change to its hate speech policy specifically banning the phrase “Let’s go Brandon.” Meta’s hate-speech rules target protected characteristics and calls for violence or dehumanization, while “Let’s go Brandon” is a political slogan aimed at an individual/political figure and has been repeatedly debunked as a claimed policy ban by fact-checkers. Enforcement of platform rules can remove specific posts for other reasons, but a targeted policy banning that phrase was not announced.

claim: Says a photo of a young girl crying alongside an ISIS member is a Christian being forced into sexual slavery as a child bride.
rationale: The specific claim that the pictured child is a Christian being forced into sexual slavery as a child bride is not supported by verifiable evidence and has been commonly miscaptioned in viral posts. Independent reporting and fact-checkers have shown such images are often used out of context and the victim’s religion, age, and circumstances are not reliably established from the photo alone. Because the identity and context are unverified, the claim is misleading and treated as false.

claim: Says "Cost of Mueller’s investigation: $3,200,000; Benghazi "investigation": $7,000,000; Trump’s golfing trips: $83,000,000; New debt from Republican tax bill: $1,500,000,000,000."
rationale: The claim mixes several figures and is inaccurate or misleading. DOJ accounting shows the Mueller Special Counsel office spent on the order of tens of millions (about $30–35 million), not $3.2 million; the total costs attributed to multiple Benghazi investigations are disputed and depend on what’s included (the commonly quoted $7 million figure is misleading or incomplete); estimates of taxpayer costs for Trump’s golf-related travel vary by method and timeframe and are not a definitive $83 million; only the “$1.5 trillion” figure for the Republican tax bill is roughly consistent with official 10‑year deficit estimates. Because multiple items are wrong or lacking context, the overall claim is false.

claim: "New Jersey's governor cut $1.6 billion from public education while handing out $2.1 billion in corporate tax breaks, more than the entire previous decade."
rationale: The claim bundles several contested figures and an unclear time frame. While New Jersey governors (notably Chris Christie) did reduce direct school aid in some years and approved large business tax incentives, independent accounting shows the $1.6 billion “cut” and the characterization of $2.1 billion in corporate tax breaks being “more than the entire previous decade” are imprecise or dependent on specific accounting choices and time windows; available reporting does not support the exact consolidated claim as stated. Because the numbers, definitions (cuts vs. shifts; credits vs. enacted breaks), and comparison period are ambiguous, the claim is not reliably true as presented.

claim: Says Austin Mayor Steve Adler’s transportation plans linked to Proposition 1 on the ballot remove "27+ miles of traffic lanes around the city," replacing "them with lanes dedicated to usage by bicycles" and buses.
rationale: This statement mischaracterizes the plans. Austin under Mayor Steve Adler endorsed creation of dedicated bike lanes and bus/rapid transit corridors and at one point set targets of roughly 27 miles of new bikeways, but that figure referred to new/protected bikeway mileage or targeted bike network additions—not the wholesale removal of more than 27 miles of general-purpose traffic lanes citywide. Proposed changes were limited corridor road-diets and reallocations in specific locations rather than removal of traffic lanes around the entire city as claimed.

claim: "If Joe Manchin had his way, Judge Gorsuch never would have been able to get a vote."
rationale: The statement overstates Manchin’s power. A single senator cannot unilaterally prevent a Supreme Court nominee from getting a floor vote; Republicans held the Senate majority in 2017 and invoked the “nuclear option” to lower the cloture threshold so Gorsuch could be confirmed. Even if Manchin opposed Gorsuch, he alone could not have stopped the process once the GOP changed the rules and had the votes to proceed.

claim: Says "Obama’s deadliest cover-up (in an explosion that killed 29 miners) has been uncovered" by internal government documents.
rationale: The claim that internal government documents have uncovered an "Obama" cover-up around an explosion that killed 29 miners is unsupported. The April 2010 Upper Big Branch mine disaster did lead to MSHA and NTSB investigations and criminal proceedings against the mining company and its executives, but mainstream investigations and court records attribute failures to the company and regulator shortcomings, not to a deliberate presidential cover-up by the Obama administration. No credible evidence has emerged showing the administration orchestrated or concealed culpability.

claim: "Clerks in Milwaukee and Dane Counties colluded to (add) nearly 250,000 individuals to the ‘Indefinitely Confined’ voter list."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that clerks in Milwaukee and Dane Counties colluded to add nearly 250,000 people to an 'indefinitely confined' list. Official statements and investigations by Wisconsin election authorities and independent fact-checkers found no coordinated scheme; many voters self-identified as indefinitely confined during the COVID pandemic and clerks provided assistance but did not fraudulently add huge numbers. The claimed figure and allegation of collusion are not supported by the available records and reporting.

claim: "Here in Wisconsin, we've put in previous budgets more money into mental health services than any governor has in the last 25 years."
rationale: The claim is a strong comparative statement about 25 years of Wisconsin budgets that requires detailed budget-by-budget, program-by-program and inflation-adjusted accounting to verify; I do not have such comprehensive numbers and public records indicate multiple governors and budgets made significant mental-health investments. Because the assertion is unverified and depends on definitional choices (total vs. annual increase, which programs counted, inflation adjustments), I judge it false as stated.

claim: "Clinton's former pastor convicted of child molestation."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated: there is no credible reporting or public record identifying a pastor described simply as “Clinton’s former pastor” who was convicted of child molestation. Major figures and clergy publicly associated with Bill or Hillary Clinton have not been reported convicted of such crimes, and the assertion appears to conflate or invent details without a named person or source.

claim: A Mack Trucks employee told Joe Biden, "You can’t drive anything besides the country into the ground."
rationale: I could not find corroborating reports or verified video showing a Mack Trucks employee telling Joe Biden the quoted line. Public coverage of Biden plant visits does not support that exact exchange; such wordings have circulated as paraphrases or memes rather than documented quotes. Because the claim rests on a precise quotation without a reliable source, it should be treated as false until verified.

claim: Says Brett Kavanaugh’s mother presided over foreclosure case against Christine Blasey Ford’s parents, which fueled motivation for sexual assault accusation.
rationale: Contemporary fact-checking and court-record reviews found no evidence that Brett Kavanaugh’s mother presided over a foreclosure case involving Christine Blasey Ford’s parents. Additionally, there is no documented evidence linking any such court action to Ford’s decision to accuse Kavanaugh; the claim appears to conflate names and events.

claim: Says Obama replaced the American flag on the tail of his plane with his campaign logo.
rationale: This claim is false. Official presidential aircraft (Air Force One and other government planes) are required to display the U.S. flag and the lettering 'United States of America' and were not replaced by a campaign logo; campaign-chartered planes can display campaign branding but that is different from the presidential aircraft. No credible evidence supports that Obama replaced the American flag on the tail of an official presidential plane with his campaign logo.

claim: There is a Republican "plan to end Medicare."
rationale: False. There is no mainstream, explicit Republican plan to completely abolish Medicare; however, many Republican policymakers and budgets have proposed reforms (premium‑support/voucher models, raising the eligibility age, block grants, or shifting more care to private plans) that critics describe as effectively ending Medicare’s current guaranteed, traditional benefit. Those proposals would change or reduce the federal guarantee but are not identical to an explicit party-wide plan to terminate the program.

claim: Says condoms "used to be tax-exempt here in Texas."
rationale: Texas has generally taxed condoms as tangible personal property and there is no widely documented statewide period when condoms were a broad sales-tax-exempt item. Claims of past exemption likely confuse free distributions by public-health programs, charitable/resale exemptions, or local pilot programs with a formal statewide sales-tax exemption.

claim: Says President Barack Obama’s "own economists say the stimulus cost $278K per job ‘created.’ "
rationale: This claim misrepresents and misparses economic analyses. The $278,000 figure stems from dividing large aggregate stimulus outlays by a narrow or mis-specified employment metric (e.g., a short-term point estimate or wrong denominator), not from a statement by Obama’s economists that each job created cost $278K. White House economists and independent analysts described costs in terms of job-years or estimated jobs saved/created with much lower implied per-job-year costs and never endorsed a $278K-per-job claim as stated.

claim: The racial and ethnic makeup of the Gwinnett County Sheriff’s Office mirrors the community it serves.
rationale: This is false because Gwinnett County is a highly diverse, majority-minority community, while the Gwinnett County Sheriff’s Office has historically had a higher proportion of white personnel and lower proportional representation of Hispanic and Asian residents. Local reporting and public personnel data have noted these disparities rather than a close mirror of community demographics. Without the agency's most recent detailed staffing breakdown, exact gaps can't be quantified here, but available information indicates a mismatch.

claim: "Wisconsin’s economy is in the best shape it’s been since 2000."
rationale: The statement is unverified and too vague: "best shape" is undefined and different economic indicators give mixed pictures. Wisconsin has had very low unemployment in recent years but slower real wage growth and mixed per-capita GDP performance since 2000, so claiming an across-the-board best condition is unsupported without specifying metrics and dates. Because the claim lacks definitional and temporal precision, it cannot be affirmed as a factual statement.

claim: "Taxpayers are paying a fortune for the use of Air Force One on the campaign trail" by President Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton.
rationale: The claim is misleading. Air Force One is the presidential aircraft and is available only to the sitting president (so Barack Obama, as an incumbent, could and did use it for travel that sometimes overlapped campaign-related events and those costs are paid by the government, sometimes with limited reimbursements). Hillary Clinton, as a private candidate, did not have access to Air Force One, so grouping both together is false and the phrase “paying a fortune” is subjective and unsupported without specific cost accounting.

claim: "‘MAGA bomber’ identified as former CNN employee who donated to heavily to Hillary Clinton."
rationale: This is false. The 2018 "MAGA bomber" was identified as Cesar Sayoc, who was not a former CNN employee and was publicly known for pro‑Trump social media; reporting and public records showed his donations were to Republican candidates, not large contributions to Hillary Clinton. The claim appears to conflate or invent ties that fact‑checking and official records do not support.

claim: "California lawmakers are planning to push free abortion pills on all students across the state as part of a ‘super progressive’ new policy."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that California lawmakers are planning to mandate distributing free abortion pills to all students statewide. Recent state proposals have focused on expanding abortion access, funding clinics, and increasing availability via pharmacies and telehealth, but not on compulsory, universal distribution to K–12 or college students. The claim conflates access-expanding measures with a blanket policy to 'push' pills on all students.

claim: The average Georgia family makes $6,000 less than the average family did 10 years ago when inflation is factored in.
rationale: The claim is unverified and likely incorrect as stated because it gives no precise 10-year window or definition of “average” (mean vs. median) and income time-series for Georgia do not uniformly show a $6,000 real decline across plausible ten‑year spans. Real income changes depend on the chosen base year and inflation index; official sources (Census/ACS and BLS CPI) are needed to compute an accurate inflation‑adjusted change for a specified period. Without that specificity the assertion cannot be confirmed.

claim: Abigail Spanberger and other Democrats "voted to spend public funds on their political campaigns; up to $5 million..."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated as written: there is no record that Rep. Abigail Spanberger and other Democrats voted to allocate public taxpayer funds for individual political campaigns up to $5 million. Federal public campaign financing is tightly regulated and limited (and largely not used for House campaigns), and votes that involve party or committee spending or legal-defense funds are not the same as authorizing public taxpayer dollars for candidates’ campaigns. Without a specific bill or vote cited, this reads like a mischaracterization or conflation of different funding mechanisms.

claim: Says the State Department has "had half a year" to respond to a Benghazi document request, yet "I have not gotten a single, solitary scrap of paper."
rationale: The claim lacks necessary context (who made the request, exact dates, and which documents were sought) and cannot be verified as stated. Public records show the State Department and other agencies produced multiple Benghazi-related documents over time via congressional inquiries and FOIA releases, so the blanket assertion of receiving “not a single, solitary scrap of paper” after “half a year” is not reliably supported. Without precise details the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: Says Georgia’s secretary of state won’t let the people recounting ballots check the signatures for fraud.
rationale: This claim is false as stated. Georgia law and the Secretary of State require election officials to perform signature verification on absentee ballots and oversee that process; the office does not forbid official signature checks. What is restricted is private individuals or unauthorized contractors handling ballots or conducting independent forensic signature matching — recounts are governed by state procedures and handled by trained election staff.

claim: "Too many" tattoos "on visible body parts" keep some applicants out of the military.
rationale: U.S. military branches have formal tattoo policies that limit tattoos in visible locations (face, neck, hands, etc.) and on overall coverage; applicants whose visible tattoos exceed those limits can be disqualified or must obtain a waiver. Recruiters have reported turning away or delaying enlistment for applicants with too many visible tattoos, so the claim that visible tattoos can keep some applicants out is accurate.

claim: Voters in Maricopa County, Ariz., were forced to vote using Sharpie pens that aren’t read by voting machines.
rationale: This claim is false. Maricopa County provided Sharpie pens at many polling places but voters were not forced to use them, and the county's optical scanner equipment and the vendor confirmed that ballots marked with Sharpie ink are read correctly and are not invalidated. Election officials demonstrated and audits showed Sharpie marks did not prevent ballots from being counted, though initial confusion about handed-out pens created some local reports.

claim: Says of President Donald Trump’s actions on the coronavirus: "No. 1, he fired the pandemic team two years ago. No. 2, he's been defunding the Centers for Disease Control."
rationale: The claim conflates a partly accurate event with a misleading assertion. The NSC’s global health/pandemic unit was disbanded in 2018 during an NSC reorganization (often described as elimination of the pandemic team), so saying it was ended around that time is broadly correct but calling it that Trump 'fired the pandemic team' is imprecise. The assertion that 'he's been defunding the CDC' is misleading: the Trump administration proposed budget cuts to the CDC in multiple budgets, but Congress did not enact wholesale defunding and CDC appropriations were not consistently reduced.

claim: Says there is a "traditional 60-vote threshold for confirming Supreme Court nominees."
rationale: There is no constitutional or long-standing Senate rule that Supreme Court nominees must receive 60 votes. The 60-vote figure refers to the Senate cloture threshold historically needed to end debate/overcome a filibuster, but filibusters of Supreme Court nominations were not consistently applied and in 2017 the Senate changed its rules to allow confirmation by a simple majority. Saying there is a "traditional 60-vote threshold" for Supreme Court confirmations is therefore misleading and incorrect.

claim: Says Stacey Evans "voted for (school) vouchers...in the beginning."
rationale: There is no clear public record showing Stacey Evans cast a vote in favor of broad school voucher legislation; reporting and her public statements emphasize support for public schools and opposition to vouchers. The claim is vague about timing and the specific bill, and available legislative records and news coverage do not substantiate an early vote for vouchers by Evans.

claim: "Most of your serial killers, most of your people who commit domestic violence, they start off by abusing animals."
rationale: This statement overstates the evidence. Research shows a correlation between childhood animal cruelty and some later interpersonal violence and many high‑profile offenders had histories of animal abuse, but empirical studies do not support that a majority of serial killers or a majority of domestic violence perpetrators universally “start off” by abusing animals. The so‑called Macdonald triad and related claims have been criticized for inconsistent findings, selection and recall bias, and lack of clear predictive power.

claim: "A black woman in New York City is 12 times more likely to die in childbirth than a white woman."
rationale: The headline statement is misleading. Nationally, non‑Hispanic Black women in the U.S. are around 2.5–3 times more likely to die of pregnancy‑related causes than non‑Hispanic white women; while some narrow NYC reports or single‑year/small‑sample analyses have shown much larger ratios, a general, city‑wide 12× risk is not a consistently supported or routinely reported statistic. The claim omits timeframe and exact measure (pregnancy‑related deaths, maternal mortality ratio, or in‑hospital deaths), which can greatly change the number.

claim: "Many Nevadans relied on Uber for work, but after accepting $70,000 from taxi companies, Catherine Cortez Masto went after Uber ... (driving) them out of town."
rationale: This claim is unsubstantiated. Publicly available information does not show Catherine Cortez Masto took a $70,000 payment from taxi companies, nor that she single‑handedly drove Uber out of Nevada — Uber has operated in the state and rideshare policy disputes involved multiple local regulators and lawmakers. While there were industry fights over regulation, the specific allegation about a $70,000 payoff and her forcing Uber out is not supported by reliable evidence.

claim: Says Rick Scott’s per-pupil education spending is "about $200 less" than what it was under Charlie Crist during the recession.
rationale: The claim is misleading because per‑pupil spending comparisons depend on which year, whether one counts only state dollars versus total (state+local+federal) and whether figures are inflation‑adjusted. Independent fact‑checks and state budget data show the difference is not a straightforward “about $200 less” across common measures — in some measures Scott‑era per‑pupil spending is similar or higher once stimulus aid, local contributions and inflation are accounted for. Without specifying the exact measure and year the “$200” figure cannot be confirmed.

claim: Says Florida's economy "is largely propped up on low-wage work."
rationale: Florida's workforce is heavily concentrated in tourism, hospitality, retail, agriculture and other service sectors that typically pay lower wages and employ many seasonal and part‑time workers, and the state's median income/wages have tended to be below the national median. Although higher‑paying industries (finance, real estate, aerospace, healthcare) exist and contribute substantially to GDP, a large share of jobs and recent employment growth are in lower‑wage occupations, supporting the claim in a jobs/employment sense.

claim: President Barack Obama is "ending Medicare as we know it."
rationale: The claim is false as a literal statement: President Obama did not abolish or terminate Medicare. The Affordable Care Act and other Obama-era policies made changes aimed at reducing cost growth and cutting certain payments (for example to some providers and Medicare Advantage plans) while preserving Medicare’s guaranteed benefits and core program structure. Opponents’ rhetoric that he was "ending Medicare as we know it" was an exaggeration of those payment and cost-control reforms.

claim: "People have actually broken down the transcripts for oral arguments and (Antonin Scalia) told more jokes and got more laughs than any of the other justices."
rationale: There is no widely accepted, comprehensive empirical study of all Supreme Court oral-argument transcripts showing Antonin Scalia uniquely told more jokes or elicited more laughs than every other justice. While commentators and limited-timeframe analyses have noted Scalia’s frequent humor and audience reactions, those are anecdotal or confined to specific years and methods, not definitive proof that he ranked highest across the Court’s history. The claim overstates available evidence and lacks the necessary definition of timeframe and measurement.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Paul Ryan’s budget proposal "eliminates Medicare" in 10 years.
rationale: Ryan’s budget proposals did not literally abolish Medicare within ten years; they proposed replacing traditional Medicare’s guaranteed benefit with a premium-support (voucher-like) system beginning around 2022, changing how benefits are financed and delivered rather than immediately terminating the program. Critics accurately said the plan would end Medicare as an entitlement/guaranteed traditional benefit, but the program itself and federal payments for seniors would continue under a different structure.

claim: "We know how to stop AIDS: persuade men not to have sex with men."
rationale: The claim is false because HIV/AIDS transmission is not limited to men having sex with men (MSM); it also occurs via heterosexual sex, injection drug use, mother-to-child transmission, and contaminated blood. Public-health evidence shows effective prevention requires a range of measures (condom use, PrEP, antiretroviral treatment as prevention, needle-exchange, blood screening, and PMTCT) rather than attempting to 'persuade' or stigmatize a group. Moreover, efforts that criminalize or stigmatize MSM worsen access to testing and care and are unethical and ineffective.

claim: After they bought GST Steel, "Mitt Romney and his partners loaded it with debt, closed the Kansas City plant and walked away with a healthy profit, leaving hundreds of employees out of work with their pensions in jeopardy."
rationale: Contemporary reporting and later fact-checks show that Bain (of which Romney was a partner) participated in the leveraged purchase of GST Steel, the company was burdened with debt, the Kansas City plant was later closed and many workers lost jobs, and investor payouts/recapitalizations preceded the firm's collapse leaving pension obligations imperiled. While precise details about Romney's personal role in day-to-day decisions and the exact dollar amount he personally gained are debated, the core elements of the claim are supported by available evidence.

claim: Quotes show Democrats supported riots "when BLM was BURNING down cities and killing people in the streets!"
rationale: The claim misrepresents the record. While some protests in 2020 included arson, looting, and instances of violence, independent analyses found the vast majority of Black Lives Matter-related demonstrations were peaceful, and Democratic elected officials typically condemned violence even as they supported protests against police brutality. There is no credible evidence of widespread Democratic endorsement of "burning down cities" or of BLM as an organized campaign systematically "killing people in the streets."

claim: "Attention hunters: Voting in North Dakota could cost you your out-of-state hunting licenses."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Simply voting in North Dakota would not automatically cause someone to lose out-of-state hunting licenses; voting can be one piece of evidence of a change in residency, but states determine hunting-license residency using multiple factors and procedures rather than an automatic revocation for casting a ballot. Any loss of nonresident privileges would depend on the other state's residency rules and a factual finding that the person has become a resident of North Dakota.

claim: "We have more people working in the state of New Jersey today than we've ever had in our history."
rationale: The claim is presented as an absolute, but it lacks a date and a clear definition of “people working” (payroll jobs vs employed residents vs labor force). Verifying it requires current BLS or New Jersey Department of Labor time‑series data; without that timestamped data I cannot confirm the absolute historical record and therefore must treat the claim as unverified/likely false. Historical employment peaks have varied by metric and season, so an undated blanket statement is not reliably true.

claim: "Drunk" Nancy Pelosi "was removed from the House floor for cursing at Republicans."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Nancy Pelosi was intoxicated and removed from the House floor for cursing at Republicans. House floor actions are publicly recorded and widely reported, and no reputable news or official record documents such an event; viral posts making this claim appear to misrepresent or doctor footage. The claim appears to be based on miscaptioned or manipulated video or satire rather than factual reporting.

claim: UW-Madison "spent down reserves" as it was told to do two years ago and, facing new state budget cuts, has "no more reserves to spend down."
rationale: This is misleading. While UW System leaders in recent years encouraged campuses to use available fund balances to mitigate budget pressures and UW–Madison did draw on some reserves, the campus still reports significant fund balances and also holds many legally or functionally restricted reserves that cannot be spent on general operating cuts. Saying it has “no more reserves to spend down” overstates the situation and conflates different types of reserves and restrictions.

claim: Speaking of an HIV outbreak in Indiana during his time as governor, says "we immediately deployed health resources."
rationale: This is misleading. During the 2015 Scott County HIV outbreak in Indiana, then‑Governor Mike Pence's administration did eventually deploy public‑health resources (testing, treatment support, and later authorization of a temporary syringe‑exchange), but those steps came only after weeks, public pressure, and CDC involvement rather than being taken 'immediately.' Independent timelines and reporting show an initial reluctance to authorize harm‑reduction measures and a delayed emergency response.

claim: Virginia voters are being turned away from polling locations because they were told they already requested absentee ballots when they haven’t.
rationale: The claim is broad and asserts a systematic practice but there is no evidence that Virginia election officials are widely turning voters away on the basis they supposedly requested absentee ballots when they had not. Virginia law and guidance allow in-person or provisional voting for people whose records are unclear, and news reporting and state officials have identified only isolated errors rather than an organized effort to deny ballots. Without specific time, locations, or corroborated incident counts the claim overstates known facts.

claim: "At his father's bank, Alexi made tens of millions in risky loans to convicted mobsters. Then, the bank collapsed."
rationale: The claim conflates and exaggerates known facts. Alexi Giannoulias worked at his family's Broadway Bank and the bank was seized by regulators in 2010, and he was criticized for some loans to borrowers who later faced legal trouble, but there is no reliable evidence that he personally made “tens of millions” in loans specifically to convicted mobsters or that such loans alone caused the collapse. Public reporting shows some risky lending and problem borrowers, but not the precise criminal-lender narrative asserted here.

claim: Says President Donald Trump "is still yet to say anything as the president of the United States about bounties on American troops."
rationale: This claim is false because President Trump publicly addressed the reports about alleged bounties on U.S. troops. In late June/early July 2020 he made several statements acknowledging the reports, saying he had been briefed (and at other times saying he had not been briefed) and later claimed he raised the issue with President Putin. Therefore it is incorrect to say he "is still yet to say anything" on the matter.

claim: "An estimated 8 million children worldwide live in orphanages or residential institutions. Shockingly, 80 percent of these children are not orphans."
rationale: Major international assessments and NGO reports have estimated roughly 8 million children living in residential institutions worldwide and have repeatedly found that the large majority of those children have at least one living parent. The frequently cited figure that about 80% are not true orphans (i.e., have one or both parents alive) is consistent with multiple UNICEF, Better Care Network, and NGO studies, though exact percentages vary by country and study.

claim: "Today, the five largest financial institutions are 38 percent bigger than they were back in 2008, when they were too big to fail."
rationale: The claim is too vague to verify as stated — it gives no date for “today,” no country or list of which five institutions, and no metric (assets, market cap, deposits). While some analyses of the largest U.S. banks showed roughly ~30–40% asset growth relative to 2008 at certain points in the 2010s, that specific 38% figure is not universally accurate without specifying timeframe, jurisdiction, and measurement. As written the statement is misleading and cannot be confirmed.

claim: "I was speaking out on pension reform almost 17 years ago."
rationale: The claim is untestable as stated because it provides no speaker identity or the date when it was made, so there is nothing to compare to public records. Without knowing who 'I' is and when 'almost 17 years ago' refers to, the statement cannot be verified and is treated as false under the instruction to prefer FALSE when uncertain.
