rationale: The claim is presented without specifying which state “we” refers to and is unlikely to be true as a blanket statement. Counts of pediatric or freestanding children’s hospitals are concentrated in a few large states (commonly California and Texas), and no universally recognized, up-to-date source supports an unspecified state having more children’s hospitals than every other state. Without specific, time-stamped data tying the speaker’s state to such a verified count, the claim cannot be accepted as true.

claim: Promotes a chart saying that Barack Obama has "increased the debt" by 16 percent, compared to George W. Bush, who increased it by 115 percent.
rationale: This claim is incorrect. Using standard measures and presidential start/end dates, Barack Obama presided over a much larger rise in federal debt than 16% (gross federal debt rose from roughly $10.6T in Jan 2009 to about $19.9T in Jan 2017, ~80–90% increase), while George W. Bush’s rise is substantially below 115% (depending on exact start/end and metric, roughly 70–85%). The viral chart’s percentages reflect a nonstandard choice of baseline or debt measure, not the commonly reported Treasury/CBO totals.

claim: "Trump’s tax reform plan was nothing more than a middle-class tax increase."
rationale: Independent analyses of the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) show that on average middle-income households received tax cuts in the years after enactment, while the law provided large permanent benefits to corporations and wealthier taxpayers. Some middle-class taxpayers—particularly in high‑tax states hit by the $10,000 SALT cap—and many households after 2025 (when most individual provisions expire) saw or could see higher taxes, but that does not make the overall plan “nothing more than a middle-class tax increase.”

claim: Quotes Donald Trump as saying in 2013, "A shutdown falls on the President’s lack of leadership. He can’t even control his own party and get people together in a room. A shutdown means the president is weak."
rationale: I find no reliable record that Donald Trump uttered that specific formulation in 2013; major contemporary news coverage of the 2013 government shutdown does not attribute this quote to him and the wording matches a paraphrase that appears to be misattributed. Given Trump’s public statements from that period are well-documented and this exact sentence does not appear in those records, the claim is unlikely to be true.

claim: The unemployment rate may be as high as "42 percent."
rationale: As a general claim this is false: typical official unemployment measures have not reached 42% in modern times. For example, U.S. official unemployment (U-3) peaked at 14.8% in April 2020 and broader U-6 peaked near the low-20s; even historical peaks outside the Great Depression are far below 42%. A 42% unemployment rate would only be plausible with an unusual definition, a very small subgroup, or a specific locality.

claim: Says more Austinites voted in the city’s 1973 election featuring a mayor’s race than in the city’s most recent mayoral election.
rationale: This is very unlikely to be true: Austin’s population and registered voter base are many times larger now than in 1973, so recent mayoral elections have had larger absolute vote totals. Without a very specific, anomalous 1973 turnout number, the raw count of votes in a 1973 mayoral contest would almost certainly be lower than in the city’s most recent mayoral election.

claim: "The higher the education level, the more likely they are to vote Democratic."
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization. In some contexts (recent U.S. national elections) voters with college and postgraduate degrees have trended more Democratic, but that pattern varies by country, election year, racial and age groups and was not always true historically. Therefore the blanket statement that higher education always increases likelihood of voting Democratic is false.

claim: Says he holds the record for "most appearances on 'Meet the Press'."
rationale: The claim as written is unverifiable because it does not identify who “he” is or specify a timeframe. Without a named individual and up-to-date records, one cannot confirm that any particular man holds the record for most appearances on Meet the Press. Because this key context is missing, the statement cannot be validated and is treated as false for lack of evidence.

claim: In the past decade in New York State "more than 30 current and former state officeholders have been convicted, sanctioned or accused of wrongdoing — more than any other state."
rationale: The statement is unverified and likely false because there is no authoritative, comparative dataset showing New York had over 30 current or former state officeholders convicted, sanctioned, or accused in the past decade and higher than every other state. The claim mixes categories (convicted, sanctioned, accused) that greatly expand possible counts and are sensitive to definitions and time window; other states (for example Illinois, New Jersey, Louisiana and California) have also had numerous high-profile prosecutions and ethics actions in the same period, so the superlative is unsupported without a clear source.

claim: "Florida Governor Rick Scott now listed as ‘critical’ after bizarre hurricane cleanup accident."
rationale: There are no credible reports from major news outlets that Rick Scott is critically injured after any hurricane-cleanup accident, and such a high-profile medical event would be widely reported. Additionally, the claim mislabels him as 'Florida Governor' (he has been a U.S. senator since 2019), which is a common feature of circulated misinformation.

claim: President Trump "hasn’t built any new (border) wall" during his time in office.
rationale: This is false. The Trump administration completed construction of hundreds of miles of border barriers during 2017–2021; although a substantial portion replaced older fencing, there were also stretches of new primary barriers built where none previously existed. Therefore the blanket statement that he "hasn’t built any new (border) wall" is incorrect.

claim: Says that the "28th Amendment" prohibits Congress from creating laws that apply to U.S. citizens but not to them, and vice-versa.
rationale: There is no ratified 28th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, so no such nationwide prohibition exists. Only 27 amendments have been adopted; proposals or internet claims about a "28th Amendment" do not have legal force unless properly ratified. The claim misstates constitutional law and appears to rely on an unratified or fictitious amendment.

claim: Says U.S. Sen. Ron Johnson "voted to cut $700m from Medicare."
rationale: The claim asserts a specific, standalone vote by Sen. Ron Johnson to “cut $700m from Medicare,” but there is no clear record of him casting a vote that directly and explicitly cut exactly $700 million from Medicare. Votes that affect Medicare typically occur as part of larger budget or reconciliation packages with much larger (often billions) impacts or as changes to payment formulas; without a specific bill/date the claim appears to mischaracterize or oversimplify a vote. Because the statement is precise and no direct match is known, it is likely false or misleading.

claim: "After every major conflict ... what happened was that we ultimately hollowed out the force, largely by doing deep, across-the-board cuts."
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization. While U.S. and other militaries often demobilized and cut forces after many major wars (e.g., after WWI, WWII, and Vietnam leading to reduced readiness in some cases), there are clear counterexamples—most notably the post-9/11 period and other occasions when budgets and force structure were expanded or selectively rebuilt rather than hollowed out by uniform, across-the-board cuts. Therefore the absolute phrasing “after every major conflict…we ultimately hollowed out the force” is inaccurate.

claim: Says Beto O’Rourke is "the only candidate to the U.S. Senate to call for" impeaching President Donald Trump.
rationale: The claim is inaccurate: Beto O’Rourke was not the only person running for the U.S. Senate to call for President Trump’s impeachment. In 2018–2019, multiple Democratic senators and Senate candidates publicly supported impeachment or an impeachment inquiry after the Mueller report and during the Ukraine-related controversy, so O’Rourke was not unique.

claim: Says President Barack Obama said that if he doesn’t turn the economy around after three years in office, he’ll be a one-term president.
rationale: There is no reliable record of President Obama uttering the precise line that if he didn’t turn the economy around after three years he would be a one-term president. He often said he would be judged on the economy and that reelection would depend on economic performance, but the specific three-year ultimatum appears to be a paraphrase or misquote rather than a documented direct statement. Given available speech records, the claim overstates and misattributes wording.

claim: "The Lancet peer-reviewed study confirms vaccine efficacy, not as 95% stated by the vaccine companies, but as: AstraZeneca 1.3%; Moderna 1.2%; J&J 1.2%; Pfizer 0.84%."
rationale: This claim is incorrect: no Lancet peer‑reviewed study reports vaccine efficacy values of ~0.84–1.3% for those products. Phase III trials and subsequent peer‑reviewed studies show mRNA vaccines (Pfizer/Moderna) had about 94–95% relative efficacy against symptomatic COVID in trials, with lower but substantial efficacy for AstraZeneca and J&J; the tiny percentages in the claim appear to be a misinterpretation or misreporting (e.g., confusing absolute risk reduction, event rates, or per‑person percentages) rather than published efficacy estimates.

claim: Says President Barack Obama "spent nearly a trillion dollars on make-work government jobs."
rationale: This is inaccurate. The largest single program often cited is the 2009 American Recovery and Reinvestment Act (~$787 billion), much of which were tax cuts, transfers, and infrastructure investments rather than payments solely for "make-work" government jobs, and only a portion funded public-sector hiring or job programs. Describing nearly $1 trillion as spent on "make-work government jobs" misstates the size, composition, and intent of the spending.

claim: Congressman Robert Hurt has a plan to cut education by 40 percent.
rationale: There is no reliable record that Rep. Robert Hurt publicly proposed a specific plan to cut “education” by 40 percent. While Hurt supported Republican budget proposals and votes that sought large reductions in federal discretionary spending (which could reduce some federal education programs), those measures do not equate to an explicit, standalone 40% cut to education as the claim states. The statement appears to be a mischaracterization or exaggeration of budget-vote impacts rather than a factual description of a named plan.

claim: "Fox News went from 97% reporting to 94% in Virginia. The fraud is so blatant it's not funny anymore."
rationale: The claim alleges Fox News reduced a "reporting" figure from 97% to 94% in Virginia and calls it blatant fraud, but offers no specific race, time, or evidence. Live reporting percentages can be revised downward for benign reasons (data corrections, changes in which precincts are counted or the denominator used) and a downward revision alone is not proof of fraud. No independent, verifiable evidence supports the assertion that Fox News intentionally manipulated Virginia reporting to commit fraud.

claim: The impeachment inquiry hearings "going on behind closed doors over which Congressman Schiff is presiding—they are consistent with the rules" of the U.S. House of Representatives.
rationale: House committees have long had authority under House rules to conduct investigations and take testimony in closed (executive) sessions, and committee chairs may run closed-door depositions once an inquiry is authorized by House leadership. While Republicans disputed beginning a formal impeachment inquiry without a full House floor vote, procedural rules and historical practice do allow committee-led closed hearings and depositions. Thus the claim that Schiff’s closed-door hearings were consistent with House rules is accurate.

claim: Says the Steele dossier "was—according to (James Comey's) June 2017 testimony—'salacious and unverified.' "
rationale: James Comey publicly described the Steele dossier as “salacious and unverified” in his 2017 congressional testimony. He used that characterization in testimony and public statements around the March–June 2017 hearings about the Russia investigation.

claim: At the State of the Union address, Democrats, "even on positive news … were like death and un-American. Un-American. Somebody said, ‘treasonous.’ I mean, yeah, I guess, why not? Can we call that treason? Why not?"
rationale: The statement is presented as a direct quote but lacks attribution and I cannot verify the exact wording as reported by reliable sources. While political figures (notably former President Trump) have criticized Democrats' reactions to State of the Union addresses using similar language, I could not confirm this precise phrasing and context, so the claim as stated is not verifiable as true.

claim: "Wages are on the rise — in fact we were the top small-business wage growth state in the nation."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it gives no state or timeframe and cites a superlative ranking that would require specific labor-market data. Wage and small-business wage growth rankings vary by data source and period (BLS, ADP, Census) and I find no clear, universally accepted source that supports this blanket statement. Without a specific state and period, the claim cannot be confirmed and is therefore treated as false.

claim: "The Biden Administration is recklessly releasing hundreds of illegal immigrants who have COVID into Texas communities."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that the Biden administration systematically or recklessly released hundreds of migrants known to be COVID-positive into Texas communities. Border authorities operated under public-health measures during the pandemic (including testing, isolation, expulsions under Title 42 at times, and coordination with local authorities), and specific state claims about mass releases were disputed by federal officials and reporting. The claim appears to conflate isolated incidents, political statements, and differing definitions of 'release' into a broad, unsupported assertion.

claim: "That’s 5,615 projected coal-powered plants in just 8 countries. The USA has 15 - building 0 more."
rationale: The claimed figure (5,615 projected coal plants in 8 countries) is inconsistent with publicly available aggregate data on global coal projects: global planned/under-construction coal capacity is commonly reported in gigawatts and would not correspond to thousands of separate full-scale coal-fired plants in only eight countries. While the vast majority of new coal capacity proposals are concentrated in a handful of countries (e.g., China, India, Indonesia, Vietnam, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Turkey, Philippines), the raw count of individual plants cited here is implausibly high and appears to conflate units, proposals, or megawatts with whole power plants. The US currently has effectively no major new commercial coal plants under construction, so the statement that the USA has 15 and is building zero more is misleading without clear definition of what those 15 represent.

claim: Quotes Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez as saying "I’m speaking with myself, number one, because I have a very good brain and I’ve said lots of things."
rationale: I find no reliable reporting or verifiable video showing Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez uttering that exact line; it appears in social-media memes and misattributions rather than documented interviews. The phrasing also resembles known parody/misattribution patterns, so absent a primary source the claim is likely false.

claim: Says "Eric Holder and his group came in and made" the Wisconsin Supreme Court race "highly partisan."
rationale: The claim assigns primary causal responsibility to Eric Holder and his unnamed "group" for making the Wisconsin Supreme Court race "highly partisan." While Holder has led national Democratic organizing efforts (e.g., the National Democratic Redistricting Committee) and national Democratic groups did spend on Wisconsin judicial contests, the race’s nationalization and partisanship involved many actors on both sides over years. Attributing the heightened partisanship solely to Holder and his group is an oversimplification and not supported as a factual causal claim.

claim: "The United States is the No. 1 country in the world for energy resources. … We are the king daddy dogs when it comes to energy."
rationale: The claim is an overbroad exaggeration. The United States is a top energy producer (leading in recent years in oil, natural gas and total primary energy production) but it does not hold the largest proven reserves of key fuels globally (countries like Venezuela, Saudi Arabia, Russia, and Iran have larger proven oil or gas reserves). Saying the U.S. is simply “No. 1 ... for energy resources” without specifying production versus reserves is therefore inaccurate.

claim: "CNN reports DemDebate had 2.3 million viewers. Trump rally had 6.7 million last night!"
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated and likely misleading. TV/audience numbers vary by date, metric (average vs peak viewers, Nielsen cable-only vs streaming/online totals) and source; CNN typically reports Nielsen figures but I cannot confirm a specific CNN report of exactly 2.3 million for a Democratic debate or that a Trump rally had exactly 6.7 million the same night. Comparing two numbers without specifying the date, measurement window, or whether online streams are included produces a misleading comparison.

claim: Photos prove the Denver light rail system has low ridership.
rationale: Photos are snapshots of a particular place and time and therefore cannot reliably demonstrate systemwide ridership levels. Ridership is measured by systematic counts and averaged across days, times, and lines; empty cars or platforms in photos can reflect off‑peak hours, service changes, or selective framing rather than overall low usage. Without comprehensive data, photos do not prove the claim.

claim: "The FBI just confirmed that it was ANTIFA, not Trump supporters, who breached the Capitol."
rationale: This is false. The FBI and the Department of Justice investigated the January 6 Capitol breach and have charged and prosecuted hundreds of people, many identified as Trump supporters and members of far‑right groups; the FBI has stated it had no evidence that Antifa organized the attack. Public video, social media postings by participants, and official charges overwhelmingly contradict a claim that Antifa, rather than Trump supporters, was responsible.

claim: European allies "pay us $2.5 billion a year to keep our forces there. It would cost us more money to bring the troops home than to keep them in Europe."
rationale: The claim is false. European NATO allies do not collectively pay the US $2.5 billion per year as a direct fee to keep US forces in Europe; direct host‑nation reimbursements and cost‑sharing arrangements are far smaller and NATO burden‑sharing refers to allies’ own defense spending rather than direct payments to the US. The second part—that it would cost more to bring troops home than to keep them in Europe—is unsupported: one‑time redeployment costs can be substantial but are not demonstrably larger than ongoing basing costs without specifying timeframe, scope, and accounting rules.

claim: "We now have more jobs in solar than we do in oil."
rationale: The claim as stated is too broad and is misleading. Globally (and in many countries) the oil and gas sector still employs more people than the solar industry, even though solar jobs have grown rapidly and can exceed employment in specific fossil-fuel subsectors or in particular regions. Without a clear time frame, country, or definition of ‘‘jobs’’ (direct vs. indirect), the blanket statement is not supported.

claim: "George Floyd’s ‘murder’ filmed before COVID-19."
rationale: The video of George Floyd’s death was recorded on May 25, 2020, which is after COVID-19 was already spreading globally and after the WHO declared a pandemic on March 11, 2020. Therefore it is false to say the murder was filmed before COVID-19; even measures like U.S. lockdowns occurred earlier in March 2020.

claim: "Have the suburbs been inundated with former residents of Atlanta housing projects? Absolutely not."
rationale: The claim asserts an absolute denial that suburbs were ‘inundated’ with former Atlanta public‑housing residents. Historical evidence from Atlanta’s HOPE VI and public‑housing demolition shows residents were relocated to a variety of destinations — some to suburbs, many to other parts of the city or region — but there is no support for a blanket claim of widespread suburban inundation. Because relocation patterns were mixed and the statement is an absolute, it is misleading to say ‘absolutely not.’

claim: Says marijuana is "legal in most states in this country."
rationale: The claim is misleading because legality varies by type and jurisdiction: a majority of U.S. states have legalized medical cannabis, but adult-use (recreational) marijuana is legal in fewer than half of states and cannabis remains illegal under federal law. Without specifying medical vs. recreational (and the country and date), saying it is "legal in most states" is inaccurate.

claim: "While (women) represent 47 percent of the overall work force, we only make up 23 percent of STEM-related occupations."
rationale: The first part (women ≈47% of the overall U.S. labor force) is roughly correct for recent years, but the stated 23% share in STEM occupations is an imprecise figure. U.S. government data (BLS/NCSES) generally place women's share of STEM occupations in the mid-to-high 20s percent (often ~25–29%), and the exact percentage depends on the year and how “STEM” is defined. Because the claim gives a single precise number without timeframe or definition, it is misleading.

claim: The FEMA health care workers replacing the noncompliant nurses and doctors are NOT required to get vaccinated via the CDC."
rationale: The CDC issues public-health guidance and recommendations but does not itself impose vaccination mandates on individuals. Vaccination requirements for FEMA personnel would come from their employer (FEMA/DHS) or federal employee/contractor vaccine policies, not a CDC-imposed legal requirement. Therefore the statement that they are not required to be vaccinated "via the CDC" is correct, though other mandates could still apply.

claim: "I can send every qualified person to a four-year college in their state for $150 billion."
rationale: The claim is implausible given basic enrollment and tuition math and because it omits key definitions (who is “qualified”, whether $150B is annual or total, and whether it covers only tuition). The U.S. has roughly 3.6–3.8 million high‑school graduates per year and average public in‑state four‑year tuition is on the order of $8–12k/year; covering four years of in‑state tuition for a cohort would approach or exceed $100–150 billion even before adding room/board, expanded campus capacity, aid administration, or adult/transfer students. Policymaker estimates for broad free‑college plans routinely range into multiple tens to hundreds of billions per year, so a flat $150 billion figure without qualifiers substantially understates likely costs.

claim: Says Oregonians for Food and Shelter "proudly features board members from Monsanto and Syngenta and the (Oregon) Farm Bureau also receives funding from biotech companies."
rationale: The claim bundles two assertions that are not clearly supported by public, time-stamped evidence. While agricultural advocacy groups commonly include or work with agribusiness employees and Farm Bureau affiliates may accept sponsorships from biotech firms, I could not confirm that Oregonians for Food and Shelter currently 'proudly features' Monsanto and Syngenta board members or that the Oregon Farm Bureau specifically receives direct funding from biotech companies as stated. The wording is imprecise and likely overstates or conflates typical industry relationships and sponsorships.

claim: "One out of every two kids who are graduating college right now can't find a job."
rationale: National labor statistics and graduate outcome surveys do not support a 50% unemployment rate for recent college graduates; measured unemployment for new degree-holders in the U.S. is typically in the low single digits to low teens depending on year and cohort, and most graduates are employed or in further education within months of graduation. Even broader measures like underemployment (working outside the field or in part-time roles) fall well below one-in-two overall, though rates vary by major and economic cycle.

claim: Says we could have saved ourselves the cost of building the Powell Butte water reservoir.
rationale: The statement is a speculative value judgment that cannot be verified as a factual claim. Whether the cost could have been avoided depends on unavailable context — such as alternatives considered, engineering requirements, regulatory mandates, and prior studies — and official project analyses for the Powell Butte reservoir have characterized it as necessary for storage and seismic resilience. Without evidence showing a feasible, equivalent-cost-free alternative, the blanket claim that the cost could have been saved is unsupported.

claim: "One would have to go back more than a century to find a scenario where a president’s nominee for the Supreme Court was confirmed by the opposition party in the Senate when the vacancy occurred during an election year."
rationale: This claim is incorrect. In 1956 (an election year) President Dwight D. Eisenhower, a Republican, nominated William J. Brennan Jr. and the Senate — then controlled by Democrats (the opposition party) — confirmed Brennan. That is a clear post‑century example contradicting the statement.

claim: "She’s voted for 60 tax increases, hurting the middle class and small businesses."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it does not identify who “she” is and provides no source for the count of 60 tax increases. Similar allegations have been repeatedly debunked by fact-checkers for relying on selective counting and loose definitions of what counts as a tax increase; without a clear subject, time frame, or methodology the precise figure and the asserted harm cannot be substantiated. Therefore the claim is misleading and cannot be treated as factual.

claim: Repeal of Obamacare would "take away health care for 10.3 million Americans" who have received coverage since Oct. 1, 2013.
rationale: The statement is misleading. The 10.3 million figure appears to refer to cumulative marketplace sign‑ups since the first open enrollment (or a particular cohort) rather than the number of people who would immediately lose coverage if the law were repealed; many of those enrollees no longer rely on ACA marketplace plans (they moved to other coverage, experienced churn, or gained employer/Medicaid coverage). Repeal would eliminate marketplace plans and subsidies and would risk coverage loss for current enrollees, but it would not automatically “take away” health care from a one‑time cumulative total of 10.3 million people.

claim: "Hillary Clinton killed in monster truck mishap."
rationale: The claim is false. Hillary Clinton, a high‑profile public figure, has not been reported killed in a monster truck mishap; such an event would have been widely and immediately reported by reputable news organizations and official sources, which has not occurred. No credible evidence supports this claim.

claim: "Why would our president close the embassy to the Vatican? Hopefully, it is not retribution for Catholic organizations opposing Obamacare."
rationale: There is no record that a U.S. president closed the U.S. Embassy to the Holy See; formal diplomatic relations have been continuous since they were established in 1984 and ambassadors remained in place. The idea that an embassy closure would be "retribution" for Catholic organizations opposing the Affordable Care Act is speculative and unsupported—disputes over the contraception mandate produced litigation and policy negotiations, not a closure of the embassy.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Steve Southerland "voted himself health care for life."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Rep. Steve Southerland cast a vote specifically to give himself "health care for life." Members of Congress participate in the Federal Employees Health Benefits program like other federal employees and may be eligible for retiree benefits under existing rules, but routine votes that affect federal employee benefits are often mischaracterized as granting "lifetime" care to individual members. Without a specific bill or provision cited, the claim is misleading and not supported by recordable, explicit action by Southerland to enact permanent personal lifetime coverage.

claim: Says David Perdue wants to abolish the U.S. Department of Education, which would cost Georgia schools $1 billion a year and eliminate millions in student loans.
rationale: This claim mixes a partial truth with inaccurate consequences. David Perdue has at times said he supports shrinking or eliminating the U.S. Department of Education, but abolishing the agency would not automatically erase federal student loans and the specific figure of “$1 billion a year” for Georgia schools is misleading — federal K–12 and higher-education funding streams are complex and typically exceed or vary from that single rounded number depending on which programs are counted. Eliminating the Department would shift administration of programs and obligations rather than instantly canceling loans or producing the precise stated fiscal impact.

claim: President Joe Biden will "control health care costs by slapping a 95% tax on prescription drugs."
rationale: This is false. There is no Biden administration policy or enacted law that would “slap a 95% tax on prescription drugs.” Biden-era actions (for example the Inflation Reduction Act and other proposals) focus on allowing Medicare drug-price negotiation, capping certain out‑of‑pocket costs, and limiting price increases — not imposing a 95% tax on drugs. Assertions about a 95% tax are mischaracterizations or misinformation about drug‑pricing proposals or penalties.

claim: Says Joe Biden stayed silent about violence at Black Lives Matter protests.
rationale: The claim that Joe Biden “stayed silent” is false in general. Biden repeatedly spoke about Black Lives Matter protests, condemning violence while also calling for peaceful protest and police accountability in speeches, interviews, and official statements during 2020 and thereafter. Although critics sometimes argued his responses could have been faster or stronger in specific moments, he did not remain silent overall.

claim: "#GradInsurance debacle is a DIRECT result of #ObamaCare. #MIZZOU has to break the law to do the right thing."
rationale: The statement asserts a direct causal link and an obligation to break the law without supporting evidence. While the Affordable Care Act includes employer-coverage rules that can complicate how universities offer student or graduate employee benefits, those provisions do not force an institution to violate the law; universities have legal options (offer compliant plans, reclassify roles, provide waivers or subsidies). There is no clear evidence that the specific “GradInsurance debacle” was solely or directly caused by Obamacare or that Mizzou must break the law to resolve it.

claim: Student loans from the federal government issued between 2007 and 2012 are on target "to produce $66 billion in profits for the United States government."
rationale: This figure matches Congressional Budget Office estimates using Federal Credit Reform Act accounting that the cohort of federal student loans disbursed roughly 2007–2012 was projected to yield about $66 billion in net positive subsidy (i.e., profits) to the government. However, that result depends on the accounting method used; under fair-value accounting the same loans are scored as a net cost. The claim as stated is accurate for the FCRA measure commonly cited by analysts.

claim: Says U.S. Sen. Ron Johnson "opposes faster broadband internet in small towns" and "got nearly $90,000 in campaign contributions from the telecom special interests."
rationale: The statement mixes two different claims and is misleading. Ron Johnson has opposed certain federal subsidies, regulatory interventions, and municipal broadband approaches while advocating private-sector solutions, but that is not the same as a blanket opposition to "faster broadband in small towns." The specific dollar figure about "nearly $90,000" from telecom special interests is unverifiable without a stated timeframe and appears to be presented without necessary context (contributions vary by cycle and source).

claim: Says Texas U.S. Rep. John Culberson "was caught using campaign cash on collectibles, including Civil War memorabilia and fossils."
rationale: Contemporary news reporting documented that Rep. John Culberson’s campaign disbursements included purchases of collectible items, with media accounts specifically citing Civil War–era memorabilia and purchases described as meteorites/fossils or other natural-history items. Those reports raised questions about the appropriateness of using campaign funds for such collectible purchases.

claim: That Donald Trump said in 1998 if he were to run for president he would run as a Republican because "They’re the dumbest group of voters in the country. They believe anything on Fox News. I could lie and they’d still eat it up. I bet my numbers would be terrific."
rationale: There is no credible contemporaneous source or reliable reporting that Donald Trump said this in 1998; major fact-checkers have found the quote circulating on satirical and misleading sites and could not verify an original source. While Fox News existed by 1998, the specific phrasing and attribution appear to be fabricated or a later misattribution rather than a documented Trump statement from that year.

claim: Says a car driving former University of Missouri System President Tim Wolfe "ran through the students, hit one of them" at the MU Homecoming Parade.
rationale: Contemporary news reports and video of the MU Homecoming Parade incident do not identify former University of Missouri System President Tim Wolfe as the driver, nor report that he ran through students or struck one. Wolfe was not reported to be operating a vehicle at that event; the claim appears to misattribute the driver and actions to him.

claim: "The stock market does better when you have a Democratic president in the White House."
rationale: Multiple empirical analyses of U.S. stock-market performance over the 20th and 21st centuries show that average returns (e.g., S&P 500 annualized returns) have been higher during Democratic presidencies than Republican ones. However, this is a correlation observed in historical data and does not prove causation — results depend on the chosen time period and are influenced by many non-presidential factors (Fed policy, business cycles, global events).

claim: Says President Donald Trump's "effort to roll back regulations means that Big Ag now gets to inspect its own pork" and "they decided to stop testing for E. coli."
rationale: This is a misleading oversimplification. The USDA's swine inspection 'modernization' rules allowed companies to perform some tasks previously done on the line, but federal inspectors and USDA oversight remain in place rather than fully handing inspection to industry. Likewise, FSIS did not stop testing for pathogenic E. coli strains (like E. coli O157:H7 and other STECs) — while some sampling or indicator-testing policies have been adjusted, testing and enforcement for dangerous E. coli pathogens continues.

claim: Says Ted Cruz’s father "was with Lee Harvey Oswald" before the assassination of President John F. Kennedy.
rationale: This claim is false. Multiple independent fact-checks and contemporary records find no credible evidence that Rafael (Ted) Cruz’s father was with Lee Harvey Oswald before JFK’s assassination; alleged photos and rumors have been debunked or shown to be misidentifications and the Cruz family and timelines do not support the assertion.

claim: This year’s state budget and my spending proposal for Fiscal Year 2016 represent an infusion of more than $1 billion in additional money for K-12 education.
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it lacks any identifying state, speaker, or clear baseline for what counts as “additional” K–12 money. Whether a state budget plus a separate FY2016 proposal together increase K–12 funding by more than $1 billion depends on the specific state, the baseline year, and whether one counts one-time, federal, or redirected funds. Because those critical details are missing, the claim as presented is unprovable and therefore judged false.

claim: Says Mitt Romney flip-flopped on gun control.
rationale: Romney’s public positions on gun policy have changed over time: earlier in his political career he backed some state-level gun-safety measures, while during his presidential runs he adopted more pro-gun-rights stances and opposed new federal restrictions. Multiple news and public-record accounts have documented these shifts, so saying he “flip-flopped” on gun control is a reasonable characterization.

claim: "Governor (Perry), you were a Democrat, having worked for Al Gore as his campaign manager..."
rationale: The claim is incorrect. No credible evidence shows Governor Rick Perry (or any widely known Governor named Perry) served as Al Gore’s campaign manager, and Rick Perry is a long-time Republican rather than a Gore campaign official. Gore’s campaigns were led by other Democratic operatives, not Perry.

claim: The debt ceiling deal will result in "the lowest level of annual domestic spending since Dwight Eisenhower was president."
rationale: The claim is incorrect as stated. Domestic spending in absolute and inflation-adjusted terms is far higher today than in the 1950s, and the recent debt‑ceiling agreement limited future growth of certain categories but did not roll total annual domestic spending back to Eisenhower‑era levels. Major entitlement programs and baseline spending remain much larger than in the 1950s, so the deal cannot plausibly produce the “lowest level” since Eisenhower.

claim: "45.6 million people watched (the State of the Union), the highest number in history. @FoxNews beat every other Network, for the first time ever, with 11.7 million people tuning in."
rationale: The claim is incorrect. Historical Nielsen totals show previous State of the Union addresses drew equal or larger audiences than 45.6 million, so it was not the highest in history; likewise, Fox News has previously been the top-rated network for some SOTU broadcasts, so the assertion that 11.7 million tuning in was the first time Fox beat every other network is false. The headline numbers can also differ depending on which platforms and measurement windows are included, which the claim does not specify.

claim: "The violent crime rate has risen, and the homicide rate has risen by more than 20 percent in just two years, really after 30 years of decline in violent crime."
rationale: This matches U.S. national trends: violent crime rates fell for roughly three decades from the early 1990s through the 2010s, but then rose around 2020–2021. FBI data and other national compilations show murders/homicides jumped sharply during that period — on the order of 20–30% when comparing 2019 to 2021 (and about a ~29% rise 2019→2020).

claim: Says taxpayer subsidy for the Oregon Convention Center hotel jumped $100 million in closed-door sessions
rationale: I cannot find verifiable evidence in available knowledge up to mid‑2024 that taxpayer subsidy for the Oregon Convention Center hotel increased by $100 million in closed‑door sessions. The claim is unsourced and contains specific numeric change and procedural detail (closed‑door sessions) that should be supported by public records or reputable reporting; absent that, the assertion cannot be confirmed. Because the statement is specific and currently uncorroborated, it is judged false pending reliable documentation.

claim: Says "in Katrina, they approved $60 billion within 10 days of the storm on a voice vote."
rationale: This claim is incorrect as stated. Congress did approve emergency Katrina aid very quickly but the first immediate package was only about $10.5 billion within days; larger supplemental totals approaching $50–60+ billion were worked out over subsequent weeks and were enacted through normal recorded votes and multiple bills rather than a single $60 billion voice vote within ten days. The specific claim that $60 billion was approved on a voice vote within 10 days is not supported by the legislative record.

claim: Says "some people in the Great State of North Carolina have been sent TWO BALLOTS. RIGGED ELECTION in waiting!"
rationale: Reports around North Carolina elections have documented isolated administrative errors where a small number of voters were sent duplicate mailings, but independent fact-checkers found no evidence of a widespread scheme or that those mailings enabled a ‘rigged’ outcome. State election procedures—ballot tracking, signature verification, cancellation of duplicates, and provisional/in-person voting safeguards—make systemic vote-stealing via occasional double mailings highly unlikely.

claim: "74 percent of Republicans support the Affordable Care Act."
rationale: Major national polls and public-opinion trackers over the past decade show that only a minority of self-identified Republicans favor the Affordable Care Act; typical Republican support has been well below 50% (often in the teens or low 30s depending on timing and question wording). A claim that 74% of Republicans support the ACA is inconsistent with widely reported polling and with long-standing Republican opposition to the law.

claim: "There were 36 states where Republicans who were in charge refused to implement a state (health insurance) exchange."
rationale: The claim misstates the politics and count. While around 36 states used the federal or partnership exchanges rather than fully state-run exchanges circa 2013–2014, not all of those decisions were made by Republican officials who 'refused' to implement a state exchange; some were technical, some states were led by Democrats, and the number changes with timing and definitions. Therefore the categorical statement that there were 36 states where Republicans in charge refused is inaccurate.

claim: Says Gerald Daugherty advocated lowering the penalty for crimes like strangulation in domestic violence cases because "they just ‘throw more people into the’" jail "‘system."
rationale: I cannot find independent, verifiable evidence that Gerald Daugherty publicly advocated lowering penalties for strangulation in domestic violence cases with the quoted language about ‘throw[ing] more people into the … system.’ The claim appears to be a specific quoted attribution that is not corroborated by available reporting or public statements known up to mid-2024, so it is likely a misquote or misattribution. Without a reliable source for that quote and policy position, the claim should be treated as false.

claim: Wisconsin is "clearly seeing a decline in COVID infections"
rationale: The statement is time‑dependent and gives no date or data source; COVID trends in Wisconsin have fluctuated over time with periods of both increases and declines. Without specifying a timeframe and metrics (cases, test positivity, hospitalizations, or wastewater), the claim that Wisconsin is "clearly seeing a decline" cannot be verified and is therefore treated as false.

claim: If Missouri Amendment 1 passes, the auditor's office "could take one district, St. Louis here, and merge it with a district in southwest Missouri, a Republican district, and they don't even have to touch."
rationale: The claim describes an auditor under “Amendment 1” being able to splice a St. Louis district onto a distant southwest Missouri district without touching intervening areas. Redistricting rules in Missouri and federal case law require districts to be contiguous and to follow other constitutional constraints, so a mapmaker cannot lawfully create wildly noncontiguous pairings. Even where a fallback official (such as the auditor) might be empowered to implement maps, they must still comply with those legal requirements and standard redistricting criteria.

claim: "The permission to engage was given before the word RPG was ever used."
rationale: The statement lacks any contextual details (who, when, where, and what 'RPG' means) and there is no provided evidence showing authorization timing. Timing claims require contemporaneous authoritative records or credible eyewitness/source attribution; absent that, the assertion is unverified and thus judged false. If specific actors, a date, or a transcript are supplied the claim could be re-evaluated.

claim: "There are no provisions in here that substantially affect or advantage the big Wall Street bankers."
rationale: The claim is an absolute denial about an unspecified text (‘here’) and cannot be verified as stated. In general, legislative or regulatory texts frequently contain provisions that can affect large financial institutions; absent the specific document and line-by-line review, asserting that there are no provisions that ‘substantially affect or advantage’ Wall Street bankers is implausible. Therefore I rate the blanket claim as false pending concrete citation.

claim: "If you’re a low-wage worker and you’re single and don’t have children, we’re literally taxing you into poverty."
rationale: The claim is a broad and literal assertion that taxation universally drives single, childless low-wage workers into poverty; this is not generally true. Taxes (especially payroll taxes) reduce take-home pay and childless workers receive fewer refundable credits, but whether someone falls below the poverty line depends on wage rate, hours worked, state taxes, and credits; many low-wage workers owe little or no federal income tax due to the standard deduction. In some cases taxes can push a borderline earner under the poverty threshold, but the statement as an absolute is inaccurate.

claim: "U.S. teenagers have now fallen behind their counterparts in Ireland, Poland and even Vietnam in math and science."
rationale: The claim is misleading because international test results vary by assessment, year, age group and subject. OECD PISA and IEA TIMSS results show the U.S. scores are below some countries (Poland and Ireland in some recent PISA cycles) and that Vietnam posts strong results on TIMSS and selected PISA rounds, but the pattern is not a uniform, current decline across all math and science measures for all U.S. teenagers. Without specifying the year, age group, or which test, the blanket statement is not supportable.

claim: Says a gun bill before the Senate "is proposing the universal registration of all firearms and their owners."
rationale: The claim is a broad assertion without identifying a specific bill and is inconsistent with how most recent Senate gun proposals are written. While some bills expand background checks or reporting for certain transfers or weapons, they do not typically establish a federal, universal registry of every firearm and owner; opponents often overstate provisions as ‘‘universal registration.’' Determination requires checking the specific bill text, but as stated the blanket claim is unsupported.

claim: Says Texas "high school graduation rates are at all-time highs."
rationale: The statement is too general and therefore not verifiably true as presented. While Texas four‑year high school graduation rates have trended upward and have hit record levels in some recent cohorts, whether they are "at all‑time highs" depends on the specific year and metric (e.g., four‑year cohort, adjusted cohorts, or subgroup rates), which the claim does not specify. Without a precise timeframe or metric the blanket present‑tense claim is not reliably supported.

claim: "Two million more people just dropped out of Obamacare. It is in a death spiral."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that ‘two million more people just dropped out’ of the ACA marketplaces in a single recent change; official enrollment data since the law’s implementation show year-to-year fluctuations far smaller or explained by normal churn, shifts to employer coverage, or Medicaid, not a sudden 2‑million exodus. Independent analysts and government reports have also rejected the characterization that the marketplaces are in a ‘death spiral,’ which would require widespread insurer exits and rapidly rising premiums driven by severe adverse selection — outcomes not observed broadly in recent years.

claim: Says professional football coach Rex Ryan "won championships in New York. The AFC, I think, twice."
rationale: Rex Ryan coached the New York Jets to the AFC Championship game twice (2009 and 2010 seasons) but lost both games, so he did not "win" the AFC championship twice. He has no AFC conference championships as a head coach.

claim: "Most of Ted Cruz’s money comes from Washington, from outside the state of Texas."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and likely false as stated: campaign finance records and public reporting show Ted Cruz raises substantial funds both from within Texas and from nationwide donors and PACs, but there is no clear evidence that a majority of his money specifically originates from Washington, D.C. or exclusively from outside Texas. At minimum, “money” and “from Washington” are ambiguous (campaign vs. personal vs. PAC funds; D.C. donors vs. out-of-state), so the blanket statement cannot be supported.

claim: President Barack Obama, Nancy Pelosi and Harry Reid support Rick Perry’s "decision to give in-state tuition to illegal immigrants."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Obama, Nancy Pelosi and Harry Reid formally endorsed a specific decision by Governor Rick Perry to grant in‑state tuition to undocumented students. While Democratic leaders including Obama, Pelosi and Reid have broadly supported measures like the DREAM Act and policies expanding access for undocumented students, that is not the same as publicly backing a particular action by Perry; in fact Democrats often opposed Perry politically. The claim conflates general Democratic support for immigrant-friendly policies with an endorsement of Perry’s conduct.

claim: "If we keep the minimum wage at the current level, then single-parent families earning the minimum wage at a full-time job will live in poverty in New Jersey."
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim but is false as written because whether a single-parent family is in poverty depends on household size and the exact minimum wage. At New Jersey’s recent minimum-wage levels (around $15/hour), a full-time worker (40 hrs/week × 52 weeks) earns roughly $30–32k/year, which exceeds federal poverty thresholds for a single parent with one or two children; larger households could be near or below poverty. Thus the blanket assertion that single-parent families earning minimum wage full‑time will live in poverty in NJ is incorrect without specifying family size or benefit offsets.

claim: Insurance companies have seen their profits soar by more than 400 percent since 2001.
rationale: The claim is too broad and unsupported as stated: insurance-sector profits vary widely by country, line of business, and time period, and there is no clear authoritative measure showing aggregate insurer profits rose by more than 400% from 2001 to the present. Depending on the subsector, specific years, and whether figures are inflation-adjusted or pre-tax vs. net income, results differ substantially, so the blanket >400% statement is misleading. Without a defined timeframe, geographic scope, and profit metric, the claim cannot be verified and is likely false as a universal fact.

claim: "We borrow $4 billion every single day, much of it from China."
rationale: The headline number ($4 billion/day) is a rough, context-dependent approximation of the U.S. annual deficit divided by days of the year and can be close to true in some years, but the second part is misleading: China holds roughly around $1 trillion of U.S. Treasuries (a minority share of total public debt), so it does not supply “much” of daily U.S. borrowing. Most Treasury financing comes from a mix of domestic investors, institutions and other foreign holders, not primarily China.

claim: Figures for September 2014’s job growth in Wisconsin mark the "largest private-sector job creation we've had in the month of September in more than a decade"
rationale: I cannot confirm that September 2014 was the largest September private‑sector job gain in over a decade for Wisconsin. State and BLS monthly employment series are needed to compare the September 2014 private‑sector gain against each September in the prior ten years, and I have no definitive figures showing it exceeds all those months. Without that direct comparison the claim is unverified and therefore judged false under uncertainty.

claim: The Wisconsin state Assembly chambers extend to the bathroom and the parlor, and rules allow members to vote for each other if the member is in the chambers.
rationale: This claim is incorrect. Wisconsin Assembly rules require members to be physically present on the floor to record votes and do not generically treat bathrooms or parlors as part of the official chamber nor permit one member to cast another member’s ballot. While some adjacent areas may be used for legislative business, there is no standing rule allowing votes to be cast from restrooms or allowing members to vote on behalf of absent colleagues.

claim: Early morning election results from Michigan and Wisconsin show voter fraud.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that early‑morning shifts in reported totals from Michigan or Wisconsin constitute voter fraud. Election officials, bipartisan canvasses, audits, and court reviews have repeatedly explained that late-reporting precincts, the staggered counting of absentee/mail ballots, and reporting practices commonly produce overnight swings without any indication of illegality. Claims of fraud based only on early‑morning result changes have been investigated and not substantiated.

claim: "People (are) paying more in taxes than they will for food, housing and clothing combined."
rationale: The claim as stated is a blanket generalization and is not supported by routine household spending/tax data. For typical households in countries like the United States, combined spending on housing and food alone is usually larger than total tax payments (federal, state, local), and clothing adds further to that total; while some high‑income individuals may pay more in taxes than they spend on these categories, that is not true for most people. Thus the universal claim is false without narrower context.

claim: "The average life expectancy for African Americans in Saint Louis and Saint Louis County varies by as much as 18 years compared to the white population, with nearly half of all African-American kids under the age of 18 living in poverty."
rationale: The claim mixes two related but differently scoped facts in a way that is misleading. While studies and local health reports have documented neighborhood life‑expectancy gaps in the St. Louis area approaching ~18 years between predominantly Black and white neighborhoods, the statement that nearly half of all African‑American children under 18 live in poverty across St. Louis City and St. Louis County combined is not supported as a blanket fact — very high child poverty exists in St. Louis City but countywide rates are substantially lower. Because the claim conflates city and county figures and presents a countywide ‘nearly half’ child‑poverty rate that overstates combined metrics, I rate it false.

claim: New York is "leading the nation with the lowest imprisonment rate of any large state"
rationale: This statement is misleading and not reliably true. Rankings of state imprisonment rates vary by year and by the metric used (prison-only vs. jail+prison+probation/parole), and other states—particularly New Jersey and Massachusetts—have frequently recorded equal or lower incarceration rates than New York; without a clear definition of “large state” and a specific time period the claim cannot be supported.

claim: Says the Ohio Consumers’ Council office employs 74 lawyers and that the funding them is wasteful duplication.
rationale: The claim that the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel office employs 74 lawyers is inaccurate. The Ohio Consumers’ Counsel (sometimes misnamed “Consumers’ Council”) is a small state agency with a modest legal staff and has not historically employed anything near 74 in‑house attorneys; its role is to represent residential utility consumers, not to duplicate other agencies’ functions, so labeling its funding as wasteful duplication ignores its statutory consumer‑advocate purpose.

claim: Says New Hampshire had the fourth-lowest unemployment rate in the country during Maggie Hassan’s time in the state Senate.
rationale: The claim asserts a precise nationwide rank ('fourth-lowest') for New Hampshire's unemployment during Maggie Hassan’s tenure in the state Senate, but unemployment rankings varied year-to-year and rose during the 2008–2009 recession. While New Hampshire has often been among the states with relatively low unemployment, I cannot confirm a consistent fourth-lowest rank across Hassan’s entire Senate tenure (2004–2010) and the statement is too specific without a cited year. Because the claim is both specific and ambiguous in time, it is not reliably supported.

claim: Supported in-state tuition in Arkansas for illegal immigrants "if you'd sat in our schools from the time you're 5 or 6 years old and you had become an A-plus student," among other things.
rationale: I could not verify that any Arkansas official or public figure said that exact quoted line or that the claim as stated is supported by reliable sourcing. While Arkansas has had debates over in-state tuition for undocumented students and some advocates have argued students raised in-state should qualify, the specific wording and attribution in the claim are not corroborated in available records. Without a named speaker or source, the assertion as presented is unproven.

claim: Says Ayn Rand said, "The question isn’t who is going to let me; it’s who is going to stop me."
rationale: The sentence is widely attributed to Ayn Rand, but no primary source (novel, essay, or recorded speech) containing that exact wording has been verified. Quote researchers and reference compendia report the line as a likely misattribution or a paraphrase of sentiments expressed by her characters rather than a direct Rand quotation.

claim: The debt is "nearly $6 trillion more than when President Obama was sworn into office."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate as a general present-tense claim. When Obama was sworn in (Jan 20, 2009) total federal debt was about $10.6 trillion and by the end of his presidency (Jan 20, 2017) it was about $19.9 trillion — an increase of roughly $9.3 trillion, not nearly $6 trillion. Without a specific date the claim is misleading because the increase varied over his time in office and thereafter.

claim: Insurance companies "have made a fortune with Obamacare."
rationale: The statement is an overgeneralization. While some large insurers and certain lines of business (e.g., Medicare Advantage, Medicaid expansion, and some companies in later years) have seen substantial profits after the ACA, many insurers lost money on the new ACA individual marketplaces—especially in early years—and performance has varied by company, state, and year. Saying insurers broadly “made a fortune” from Obamacare is misleading without specifying which firms, time period, or market segments.

claim: "Most of these killers tend to be 18, 19 years old."
rationale: The statement is vague and unsupported. Empirical data on perpetrators (whether homicide suspects, mass shooters, or school attackers) show a broad age range rather than a majority concentrated at exactly 18–19; while some high-profile cases involve perpetrators that age, that does not justify the blanket claim that 'most' are 18–19.

claim: Property taxes "are now 18% higher than when (Mark Sharpe) first took office."
rationale: The claim is unverified and likely false because it gives no jurisdiction or timeframe and I have no reliable data tying an 18% increase in property taxes to the moment Mark Sharpe took office. Verifying such a statement requires the specific locality, the date he assumed office, and comparison of the official tax rate/levy or average bill over that period; without those details the assertion cannot be confirmed.

claim: As Massachusetts governor, Mitt Romney used a line-item veto to cut "millions of dollars for firefighting equipment," including firefighters' "coats, pants, helmets and boots."
rationale: This claim exaggerates and misstates the record. Romney did use line-item vetoes as Massachusetts governor that affected some public-safety appropriations, but independent fact-checkers found the narrative that he deliberately cut “millions” earmarked specifically for firefighters’ coats, pants, helmets and boots is misleading — the vetoes were part of broader budget reductions, the amounts and items cited were not accurately characterized, and many items were changed or restored through the legislative process.

claim: "We've got 7.2 percent unemployment (in Ohio), but when you include the folks who have stopped looking for work, it's actually over 10 percent."
rationale: The claim gives no date or source, so it is not verifiable as stated. Ohio's headline unemployment (U‑3) has been 7.2% in certain months, and the broader measure that adds discouraged and marginally attached workers plus underemployment (U‑6) is typically 2–4 points higher and can exceed 10% in some periods, but whether it did at the time implied cannot be confirmed without a specific month. As presented as a definitive statement, it is therefore unsubstantiated.

claim: An email from Hillary Clinton to Donna Brazile Oct.17th, 2016 stated: "If that f-----’ bastard wins, we’re all going to hang from nooses! You better fix this s---!"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Hillary Clinton sent an email to Donna Brazile on Oct 17, 2016 with that violent, profane language. Extensive releases of Clinton campaign/Podesta emails (including Wikileaks dumps) and contemporary fact-checking and news reporting do not contain or corroborate this quote, which appears to be a fabricated viral claim.

claim: We live in "a time of historically low violent crime rates and historically high gun ownership rates nationally."
rationale: The statement overgeneralizes two different measures. Violent crime in the U.S. is well below its early-1990s peak but saw notable increases in homicides and some violent categories around 2020–2021, so it is not uniformly at an all-time low. Meanwhile the civilian stock of firearms is at or near record highs, but household or adult ownership rates have not consistently been at historical maxima and depend on the measure used, so saying both parts are unambiguously true is misleading.

claim: Says "Rep. Jim Weidner proposed a bill taking away health care for 80,000 of Oregon's children."
rationale: I could not find evidence that an Oregon legislator named Jim Weidner authored a bill to remove health care for 80,000 Oregon children. A proposal that would strip coverage from that many children would have drawn broad reporting and official records, and the claim appears to be a misattribution or exaggeration of other policy proposals affecting eligibility.

claim: The STAR Ohio fund "just received the highest possible credit rating one of these funds can receive."
rationale: The claim is unverified as stated because it omits which rating agency, what “highest possible” means for that agency, and when the rating was issued. STAR Ohio has historically received high ratings from some agencies, but without a specific agency and date the blanket statement that it "just received the highest possible credit rating one of these funds can receive" cannot be confirmed. Given the ambiguity and absence of supporting evidence, the claim is treated as false.

claim: "We work longer hours than any people in the industrialized world, including the Japanese."
rationale: International labor statistics do not support the absolute claim that “we” (typically the U.S.) work longer hours than any people in the industrialized world. While Americans work more hours than many Europeans, several industrialized countries (e.g., Mexico, South Korea, Turkey and others in some years) report higher average annual or weekly hours than the U.S.; Japan also is not the single-longest. The superlative “any people” is therefore incorrect based on available OECD/ILO comparisons.

claim: "Today and every day, an estimated 14,000 Americans will lose their health insurance coverage."
rationale: The claim that an estimated 14,000 Americans lose health insurance "today and every day" implies about 5.1 million people per year losing coverage. That annualized figure is higher than typical authoritative estimates of annual coverage loss or churn and no consistent, reputable source supports a constant 14,000-per-day figure across time. Variations in measurement period and definition (temporary gaps, Medicaid churn, employer terminations) make the blanket daily claim unsupported.

claim: "Wisconsin is not as obese as the national average is. The national average, 35.7 percent of the population is obese. In Wisconsin, it's closer to 26 percent."
rationale: The numbers in the claim are not accurate. Recent U.S. adult obesity estimates from CDC sources and national surveys place the national adult obesity prevalence in the low-to-mid 30s percent (or higher depending on the dataset/method), and Wisconsin’s adult obesity prevalence is reported around the low-to-mid 30s as well—not as low as ~26%.

claim: Says Jeff Foxworthy wrote a ‘fence test’ for Republicans and Democrats.
rationale: There is no reliable attribution that comedian Jeff Foxworthy authored a formal “fence test” for Republicans and Democrats. Foxworthy is known for humorous “You might be a redneck” routines, and various partisan “tests” and memes have been circulated online often misattributed to celebrities; the specific ‘‘fence test’’ appears to be one of those anonymous or misattributed items. Given lack of verifiable sourcing, the claim that Foxworthy wrote it is likely false.

claim: Georgia has saved $20 million through changes in criminal sentencing.
rationale: The claim is too specific but lacks context (which ‘Georgia’ and what time period). I am not aware of any authoritative source that reports exactly $20 million saved statewide from sentencing changes; reports on Georgia’s justice reforms have cited different and often larger savings estimates or varying figures by program or year. Without a precise citation the $20 million figure appears unsupported.

claim: There are "360,000 (deaths) a year from swimming pools. But we don’t shut the country down for that."
rationale: The figure 360,000 annual deaths from swimming pools is not supported by available data. WHO estimates roughly 200–300 thousand global drowning deaths per year (all settings combined), and only a small fraction of drownings occur in swimming pools; national data (e.g., the U.S.) show only a few thousand drowning deaths annually with pool deaths far lower. The claim greatly overstates pool-specific mortality and conflates broader drowning totals with pool deaths.

claim: "Russia has more diversity in its governmental representation than we do in Texas."
rationale: The claim is false. Russia's national government is highly centralized and dominated by a single ruling party and leadership that is overwhelmingly ethnic Russian and male, with limited space for political opposition or minority representation. By contrast, Texas — while imperfect — operates under competitive elections with visibly greater representation of racial/ethnic minorities, women, and multiple parties at state and local levels, making its governmental representation more diverse in practice than Russia's national leadership.

claim: Bill Nelson’s vote for the Affordable Care Act "cuts $500 billion from Medicare to pay for new government programs."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act included roughly $500 billion in Medicare savings over a 10‑year window, but those were mostly reductions in payments to providers and Medicare Advantage plans and other cost-control measures, not direct cuts to seniors’ guaranteed benefits. While some of the savings helped finance coverage expansions and deficit reduction, presenting it as simply “cutting $500 billion from Medicare to pay for new government programs” is misleading about what was cut, who was affected, and the timeframe.

claim: Federal spending is "the highest it's been as a share of our economy in 60 years (and) revenue is the lowest it's been as a share of our economy in 60 years."
rationale: The statement mixes a largely true point about outlays with a false one about revenues. Federal outlays spiked in 2020 to levels not seen since World War II (so indeed higher than in the past 60 years), but federal revenues as a share of GDP were lower in 2009 during the Great Recession (and thus 2020–21 receipts were not the lowest in six decades). Because the revenue claim is incorrect, the combined claim is false.

claim: "As we watch the news from Colorado with horror and sympathy for the families, we should remember that each day more than 80 Americans are killed by gunfire, unnecessary tragedies."
rationale: Recent U.S. vital statistics show annual firearm deaths in the tens of thousands (roughly 40,000–50,000 in recent years). Dividing those yearly totals by 365 yields well over 80 deaths per day, so the plain reading of the claim is accurate. Note this count includes suicides, homicides, and unintentional shootings.

claim:
Says U.S. Sen Sherrod Brown "promised that the first stimulus bill would fund the
Brent Spence Bridge."
rationale: There is no public record that Sen. Sherrod Brown promised the very first COVID-19 stimulus bill would fund the Brent Spence Bridge. Brown has repeatedly advocated for federal funding for the bridge, but the initial stimulus (CARES Act) did not include such earmarked bridge funding and funding discussions occurred later in separate infrastructure negotiations. Thus the claim that he promised the first stimulus would fund the bridge is not supported by the legislative record or his public statements.

claim: Says Barack Obama "robbed Medicare (of) $716 billion to pay for ... Obamacare."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act included roughly $716 billion in projected Medicare savings over a 10‑year window as estimated by the CBO and Joint Committee on Taxation, but those were statutory reductions in projected Medicare spending (mainly lower growth, cuts to certain provider and Medicare Advantage payments), not a secret “robbery” by President Obama. The savings were enacted by law and were counted as offsets and deficit reduction; they did not involve confiscating existing beneficiary benefits in bulk though some programs and payments were trimmed.

claim: "Biden’s banking nominee demands all ‘private bank accounts’ be eliminated"
rationale: This is a mischaracterization. Biden’s 2021 banking nominee (Saule Omarova) proposed expanding the Federal Reserve’s role and discussed public accounts and tighter regulation of commercial banks, but she did not call for eliminating all private bank accounts and explicitly denied wanting to abolish private banking. Media fact-checks and her own writings show she advocated options like a Fed retail account, not wholesale elimination of private deposit accounts.

claim: "Newspapers have framed this election as my fight against the Illinois mafia."
rationale: The claim asserts a widespread newspaper framing of an election as "my fight against the Illinois mafia," which is a broad, verifiable assertion about media consensus. Without specific citations or a named election/candidate, there is no evidence that newspapers uniformly framed any election in that way; media coverage is diverse and such a uniform characterization would be unlikely and would require documentation. Therefore the claim is not supported as stated.

claim: "There are no tax increases in this debt limit bill. Period."
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim about an unspecified "debt limit bill," and without the bill text this cannot be verified. In practice, debt-limit agreements frequently include tax-related provisions (compliance measures, revenue offsets, closing loopholes, or timing changes) that can raise government revenue even if not labeled as a direct tax hike. Because the claim is absolute and context is missing, it is not reliably true.

claim: "In the last two years, super PACs raised more than $180 million -- with roughly half of it coming from fewer than 200 super-rich people and roughly 20 percent from corporations."
rationale: The claim is vague about the time window and its numbers do not match public reporting from recent federal election cycles. Nationwide super PAC fundraising over two-year cycles has commonly totaled well more than $180 million (often hundreds of millions to over a billion), and while a large share often comes from a small number of very wealthy donors, the exact "fewer than 200" and "roughly 20% from corporations" figures are not supported as a general fact and vary by cycle. The corporate share is also difficult to pin down because donors use LLCs and nonprofits and reporting varies.

claim: Between 40 and 50 percent of tax filers do not owe any income tax.
rationale: For the United States in several recent pre-pandemic years, roughly 40–50% of tax units reported zero or negative federal individual income tax liability after deductions and credits, so the broad claim is accurate for that context. However the exact percentage varies by year and by whether refundable credits and nonfilers are counted, and pandemic-era relief temporarily raised the share above this range.

claim: "Masks will kill quite a few people, it’s well known that they reduce blood oxygen levels and those with respiratory and cardiac disorders will die."
rationale: The claim is false. Numerous studies and guidance from major health agencies show that cloth, surgical, and standard N95 masks do not cause clinically meaningful reductions in blood oxygen or dangerous CO2 retention in the general public, and there is no evidence of widespread deaths caused by mask use. While masks can be uncomfortable and may require individual medical advice for people with severe respiratory failure, the blanket assertion that masks will 'kill quite a few people' is unsupported.

claim: There are nanoparticles in the COVID-19 vaccine that will help people "locate you" via 5G networks.
rationale: The claim is false. COVID-19 vaccines do not contain electronic or radio-traceable nanoparticles that allow 5G networks to locate people; there is no plausible physical mechanism or credible evidence for injectable devices that can be detected or powered by 5G. Some vaccines (mRNA vaccines) use lipid nanoparticles to deliver genetic material, but these are biodegradable delivery vehicles without circuitry, power source, or radio transceivers. Regulatory filings, manufacturing descriptions, and mainstream scientific sources do not support the assertion.

claim: Perpetrators of school shootings "have been drugged in many cases … many of these young boys have been on Ritalin since they were in kindergarten."
rationale: This broad claim is not supported by available evidence. Investigations and reputable fact-checkers find that perpetrators of school shootings have varied and inconsistent medication histories—a minority had been prescribed psychiatric drugs and there is no support for the assertion that many were "drugged" or had been on Ritalin continuously since kindergarten. The statement conflates correlation with causation and overgeneralizes from a few cases.

claim: Six states "decided to stop counting" votes as Donald Trump was "headed for a win" on election night.
rationale: There is no evidence that six states collectively 'decided to stop counting' votes while Trump was 'headed for a win.' Election officials in some jurisdictions paused or delayed tabulation overnight as normal procedure or because state law and ballot-processing rules (especially for mail ballots) require certain timing; these pauses were not a coordinated stoppage intended to reverse a lead. Media call changes reflected incoming late-counted absentee and provisional ballots, not a mysterious halt and restart.

claim: "People were hopeless. Sixty percent of the population, 70 percent of the population wanted to live somewhere else. . . . By the time I left, 70 percent wanted to stay."
rationale: The statement gives specific population percentages but provides no source, location, timeframe, or evidence and even contains an internal contradiction (majority wanting to leave, then later a majority wanting to stay). Without verifiable polling or documentary support the claim cannot be treated as factual. I therefore judge it false as presented.

claim: "However, it took $19.5 million in Oregon Lottery funds for the Port of Newport to eventually land the new NOAA Marine Operations Center-Pacific."
rationale: Contemporary reporting and state documents show the Oregon Legislature authorized about $19.5 million in lottery-backed funds to assist the Port of Newport in acquiring land and preparing the site, actions that enabled NOAA to locate the Marine Operations Center-Pacific there. The money was used by the port for property acquisition and site readiness rather than as direct NOAA construction funding, but it was instrumental in securing the facility.

claim: In Sauk City, Wisconsin, "the ID office" that provides identification for voting "is only open on the fifth Wednesday of every month" -- a total of four days in 2016.
rationale: There is no evidence that any municipal or DMV office in Sauk City restricted issuance of ID to only the fifth Wednesday of each month. While 2016 did have four months with a fifth Wednesday (March, June, August, November), municipal clerk or DMV offices that provide identification normally maintain regular, recurring hours and would not plausibly be open only on those isolated days.

claim: President Obama’s health care law says "when you sell your house now you have to pay a 3.8 percent tax."
