rationale: The claim is incorrect: people do apply to the United States for protection—most clearly in the form of asylum applications filed with U.S. authorities by individuals already in or at the border. For refugee resettlement from abroad, many cases are referred by the UNHCR, U.S. embassies, or designated NGOs to the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program, but that referral process does not make the statement "nobody applies to the United States" true.

claim: "Illegal immigration and the crime rate are as low as they’ve been in decades."
rationale: The claim conflates two different measures and is not supported by data. Border encounters and crossings have been at multi‑year highs in recent years, and while some crime rates fell from 1990s peaks they rose notably in 2020–2021 and have not uniformly returned to decades‑low levels. Whether one metric is ‘‘as low as in decades’’ depends on the specific measure and timeframe, but as stated the blanket claim is inaccurate.

claim: Al Sharpton went to Ferguson, Mo., and is "declaring as a matter of fact that ... Michael Brown didn't use any deadly force or posed no deadly threat to the officer."
rationale: There is no clear public record of Al Sharpton issuing a categorical, singular factual declaration that Michael Brown did not use deadly force or posed no deadly threat; Sharpton visited Ferguson and repeatedly argued Brown was unarmed and criticized the officer’s actions, but his statements were part of advocacy and contested eyewitness accounts. Official investigations produced conflicting findings, so portraying Sharpton as definitively declaring a settled factual conclusion is inaccurate.

claim: Jason Carter supports using Georgia tax dollars to promote Obamacare
rationale: This claim overstates and mischaracterizes Jason Carter’s position. Carter publicly supported Medicaid expansion and outreach to help Georgians enroll under the Affordable Care Act, but he did not clearly endorse a policy of using Georgia state tax dollars to run advertising campaigns promoting ‘Obamacare’ (his emphasis was on expanding coverage and using available federal funds and local outreach). The statement conflates support for enrollment/expansion with a specific pledge to spend state tax revenue on promotion.

claim: The shooting in Boulder, Colo., was a "false flag like most of the others."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Boulder, Colorado, supermarket shooting was a "false flag." Law enforcement identified, arrested, and charged a named suspect and investigators and multiple reputable news organizations reported on physical evidence and witness accounts tying that individual to the attack. The broader assertion that "most of the others" are false flags is a sweeping conspiracy claim unsupported by available facts about mass-shooting investigations.

claim: "In 1968, a full-time worker earning minimum wage, could actually support a family of three above the poverty line. Today, that same worker would earn less than the poverty line for a family of two."
rationale: The federal minimum wage in 1968 was $1.60/hr, which at full-time (2,080 hours) yields about $3,328 — above the 1968 Census poverty threshold for a three-person family (roughly $3,000–$3,200). The current federal minimum wage ($7.25/hr) yields about $15,080 annually, which is below recent U.S. poverty thresholds for a two-person family (roughly $16,000+ in recent years). Thus both parts of the claim align with historical minimum-wage and poverty-threshold data.

claim: "If we use (Tax Increment Financing) funding, that's going to take funds from the general fund for Pinellas County, as it will take funds from the general fund for the city of St. Pete."
rationale: Tax increment financing (TIF) captures the increase in property tax revenue above a set base and directs that incremental revenue to pay for redevelopment projects. Because those incremental dollars are diverted away from the normal tax receipts, using TIF typically reduces near‑term general fund receipts for overlapping taxing jurisdictions such as Pinellas County and the city of St. Petersburg (though the base levy still flows to the general fund and there may be long‑term benefits).

claim: "While all COVID-19 news has been going on, the U.S. Government has been sneakily trying to remove end-to-end encryption" which means "the government will be able to see all of your messages and listen to all of your calls."
rationale: This claim overstates and mischaracterizes reality. While U.S. law-enforcement officials and some legislators have publicly proposed or supported measures (and bills) that could pressure companies to weaken or limit end-to-end encryption, there was no secret government program that successfully removed E2EE across services; major E2EE offerings remain in use. The assertion that the government therefore "will be able to see all of your messages and listen to all of your calls" is speculative and false unless a law or technical change were enacted that eliminated encryption universally, which has not occurred.

claim: "I helped win one of the biggest private lawsuits against Medicare fraud in history. The government declined to pursue the case, so my firm did, and we recovered $324 million for taxpayers."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific assertion as stated because no case name, year, or named parties are provided to confirm a $324 million recovery tied to a private firm after the government declined intervention. While the False Claims Act allows private relators to pursue suits if the government declines, most of the largest Medicare fraud recoveries reported publicly are in the billions, and I found no clear, attributable $324 million qui tam recovery matching this description. Without documentary evidence (DOJ press release, court judgment, or news reporting) the claim is unverified and therefore judged false for lack of support.

claim: When he was Milwaukee County executive, "eight years in a row we pushed through budgets that did not increase the tax levy from the previous year."
rationale: This statement is inaccurate as a literal claim about eight consecutive years of no tax-levy increase for Milwaukee County. Public budget records and local fact-checking show the county levy did not remain flat every year during the referenced executive’s tenure; measures such as debt service, levy transfers, or adopted budgets produced year-to-year levy increases in at least some years. Therefore the blanket eight-year assertion is misleading.

claim: Says Melania Trump’s dress at Mount Rushmore speech was designed from "drawings of several young victims of sex trafficking."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or statement from the designer/stylist showing Melania Trump’s Mount Rushmore dress was based on drawings by young victims of sex trafficking. Contemporary fact-checks and mainstream reporting found the claim originated on social media and remained unsubstantiated.

claim: "Of the top five cities for staged automobile accidents, three are in Florida. … We rank No. 1 in the country in staged auto accidents."
rationale: There is no consistent, authoritative national dataset that supports the blanket claim that three of the top five cities for staged auto accidents are in Florida or that 'we' (presumably Florida) rank No. 1 nationally. Rankings depend on the data source, year, and how ‘staged’ crashes are defined; different insurance and law‑enforcement reports list different cities and years. Without a cited, current source, the statement is unverified and likely inaccurate as a universal claim.

claim: Louisiana gets "not one single penny" from Gulf Coast offshore oil revenues.
rationale: The claim is incorrect: Louisiana does receive money tied to Gulf offshore oil and gas. The state collects royalties and severance taxes on state and federal leases and receives federal revenue-sharing distributions to Gulf producing states and coastal political subdivisions under laws such as the Gulf of Mexico Energy Security Act (GOMESA).

claim: "When I took office, the deficit was nearly 10 percent of our economy. Today, it's approaching 3 percent."
rationale: The claim misstates the magnitudes. At the start of the Biden administration the federal deficit was well above 10% of GDP (the large COVID-era shortfall in 2020 was roughly in the mid‑teens percent of GDP), and recent annual deficits have been substantially above 3% of GDP (most recent unified deficits have been in the mid‑single digits percent of GDP), so the two percentages cited are not accurate comparisons.

claim: "1928 was last time Republicans had the White House, the House and the Senate."
rationale: This is false. Republicans later held the presidency and both chambers after the 2002 elections: George W. Bush was president and Republicans controlled the House and Senate beginning in January 2003 (through 2007). Thus 1928 was not the last time Republicans had the White House and both chambers.

claim: David Perdue did not support the 2014 farm bill that U.S. Sens. Isakson and Chambliss did.
rationale: David Perdue was not a U.S. senator until January 2015 and therefore did not vote for or officially cast Senate support for the 2014 Agricultural Act. Georgia senators Saxby Chambliss and Johnny Isakson voted in favor of the 2014 farm bill. While Perdue may have expressed opinions about farm policy as a candidate, he did not vote to support that bill in 2014.

claim: "If we had been on 'Obamacare' and a bureaucrat was trying to tell me when I could get that CAT scan, that would have delayed my treatment."
rationale: The claim is a speculative counterfactual that mischaracterizes how imaging is scheduled under the Affordable Care Act. In practice clinicians order CT/CAT scans and providers schedule them; insurers (public and private) may require prior authorization in some cases, but that requirement is not unique to the ACA nor does the law create a single "bureaucrat" who schedules care. There is no evidence that being on "Obamacare" would automatically have delayed necessary imaging in the way asserted.

claim: Says Donald Trump has written 10 checks to Hillary Clinton "and four of those checks were not to her Senate campaign. … It was to her presidential campaign."
rationale: Campaign finance records and reporting from fact-checkers do not support the claim that Donald Trump wrote ten checks to Hillary Clinton with four specifically to her presidential campaign. Available FEC data and news coverage show only a small number of past donations by Trump to various Democrats and no evidence matching the specific counts alleged; the claim appears to conflate or invent transactions.

claim: "So far, out of 175 arrested in Kenosha, 102 were not from Kenosha. Rioting has become its own industry."
rationale: The specific numeric claim is not borne out by contemporaneous official arrest summaries and reputable reporting, which gave different residency breakdowns that varied by date and definition (city vs county). The follow-up phrase 'Rioting has become its own industry' is a subjective opinion, not a verifiable factual statement.

claim: "Illegal immigrants currently occupy 8 million jobs."
rationale: The claim is not supported by mainstream estimates. U.S. research organizations (Pew, Migration Policy Institute, DHS estimates) generally put the number of unauthorized/undocumented immigrants employed in the United States closer to the mid-single millions (roughly 6–7 million) rather than a precise current figure of 8 million, and estimates vary by year and methodology. The statement also treats ‘occupy 8 million jobs’ as a precise and current count despite data lags and issues counting multiple job-holders.

claim: More than one-quarter of America’s young adults are too fat to serve in the U.S. military
rationale: Department of Defense analyses and multiple reports have estimated that roughly one-quarter to one-third of Americans in the key recruitment ages (often cited as 17–24) exceed the military’s weight/body-fat standards, so the statement that more than one-quarter are too heavy to serve is consistent with published estimates. The exact share varies by age window, branch standards and the metric used (BMI vs. body-fat), but standard summaries routinely put the figure just above 25%.

claim: The snow is government-generated or fake.
rationale: The claim is false. Snow is a well-understood natural meteorological phenomenon formed when atmospheric water vapor condenses and freezes into ice crystals and falls as precipitation; governments do not generate or replace all natural snowfall. Although artificial snowmaking machines are used locally (e.g., ski resorts), that limited technology does not account for widespread or naturally occurring snow events.

claim: Attorney general candidate Brad Schimel "is in cahoots with Wisconsin Right to Life to make abortion a crime in Wisconsin."
rationale: The claim asserts a specific conspiratorial arrangement that Brad Schimel and Wisconsin Right to Life are actively working together to criminalize abortion in Wisconsin; there is no public evidence of a covert agreement or plan to that effect. Public record does show Schimel is a pro‑life Republican who has defended abortion restrictions and has received support from anti‑abortion groups, but those facts do not prove the stronger allegation of being “in cahoots” to make abortion a crime. Without documented communications, coordinated strategy, or legal actions explicitly creating new crimes at their joint direction, the statement is unsubstantiated.

claim: "The last major oil spill from a drilling accident in America happened over 40 years ago in 1969."
rationale: This is false. While the 1969 Santa Barbara blowout was a major U.S. drilling spill, a far larger drilling accident occurred in the United States in 2010: the Deepwater Horizon (Macondo) disaster in the Gulf of Mexico, which released millions of barrels of oil. Therefore the "last major" drilling spill did not occur in 1969.

claim: The typical elementary school teacher pays $7,239 in federal income taxes, and firefighters pay $5,328, while Donald Trump paid $750.
rationale: The claim mixes a specific, widely reported figure about Donald Trump (he paid $750 in federal income tax for 2016, and reports indicated $750 for 2017 as well) with unsourced, context‑dependent figures for “typical” elementary teachers and firefighters. The teacher and firefighter numbers are not tied to a clear year, source, or whether they are medians or means and thus are misleading as presented. Because of those omissions and lack of comparability, the blanket claim as stated is false.

claim: "In the last year, Wisconsin ranked third in Midwest job growth."
rationale: The claim gives no specific 12‑month period or source and cannot be verified as stated. Annual and 12‑month job growth rankings among Midwest states fluctuate by month and by data source (BLS payrolls, CES, state reports), and Wisconsin has not been consistently third in recent 12‑month comparisons. Without a specific timeframe and source, the statement is unsupported and likely inaccurate.

claim: "Right now, women are able to access an abortion in the later stages of their pregnancy under certain conditions with approval of their medical doctors. I’ve done nothing to change that."
rationale: The claim combines a partly true factual statement about medical exceptions with an unverifiable political assertion. While many places allow later-term abortions only in limited circumstances (e.g., to protect the woman’s life or health, often with physician certification), access varies greatly by jurisdiction and many policymakers have enacted new restrictions or bans since the Dobbs decision. The speaker’s blanket claim that they "have done nothing to change that" is unverified and misleading given the widespread legal changes and differing roles officials may have.

claim: Quotes incoming U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez as saying "under capitalism, man oppresses man. Under socialism, it’s the other way around."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said this aphorism; the one-liner predates her and has been widely misattributed to many figures. Major fact‑checking and archival records attribute the joke to earlier, anonymous or various historical sources rather than to AOC.

claim: After a "major water main break," Georgia election workers counted "18,000 ballots, all for Biden" that they pulled from suitcases and with no election observers present.
rationale: This claim is false. Multiple nonpartisan fact-checkers and Georgia election officials reviewed the incident and found no evidence that 18,000 ballots were pulled from suitcases and counted solely for Biden without observers; ballots were handled in sealed containers, observers (including bipartisan representatives) had access, and audits/recounts did not uncover a single 18,000-vote pro-Biden dump. The claim appears to conflate or mischaracterize routine ballot storage/transport and a separate plumbing incident.

claim: "Trump Management was charged with discriminating against African-Americans and breaking federal law."
rationale: The U.S. Department of Justice filed a federal civil lawsuit in 1973 accusing Trump Management of discriminating against Black renters in violation of federal fair-housing law. The case was resolved with a 1975 consent decree imposing remedies; the company did not obtain a criminal conviction nor admit guilt.

claim: "Expanding Medicaid, which if we had done at the beginning of the Abbott administration, would have brought in $100 billion to this state's economy."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and not supported as stated. Estimates of the fiscal impact of Medicaid expansion for a state like Texas vary widely by model and timeframe; some advocacy analyses have estimated around $100 billion in additional federal payments or economic activity over a multi‑year period (often 10 years), but there is no authoritative consensus that expanding Medicaid at the start of Governor Abbott's term would have definitively "brought in $100 billion" to the state's economy. The figure depends on assumptions (time period, whether counting federal reimbursements vs. total economic output, and behavioral responses), so the unqualified assertion is misleading.

claim: "Here in Pennsylvania, the annual cost for infant childcare is over $10,000 per child, which is more than most families pay in rent and almost the same cost as in-state college tuition."
rationale: The claim mixes accurate and inaccurate elements. Average infant child care in Pennsylvania is commonly reported around $10,000–$12,000 per year, which can be comparable to in-state public university tuition at some schools, but median annual rent/household housing costs in Pennsylvania (roughly $12,000–$15,000 per year for typical rents) are often higher than $10,000, so it is not true that infant childcare costs are "more than most families pay in rent." The statements about rent and universal parity with in-state tuition are therefore misleading.

claim: Says Nevada state Sen. Michael Roberson "forced Common Core for Nevada schools."
rationale: The claim overstates Roberson's role. Nevada's adoption and implementation of Common Core were actions taken by the state Board of Education, the legislature, and the governor as part of a statewide process; a single state senator could not unilaterally 'force' the standards. While Michael Roberson may have supported or voted for related measures or funding, responsibility for adoption was collective and institutional, not the act of one legislator.

claim: "The total (state) payroll has gone down. The total amount of the number of workers in the state has gone down. I like the fact that the bulk of that is just by retirements."
rationale: The claim is unverified and likely false as stated because it gives no specific state, timeframe, or data source. State payroll totals and employee headcounts fluctuate by state and year and can fall for many reasons (hiring freezes, layoffs, attrition), so asserting the bulk of the reduction is due to retirements requires payroll and HR data that are not provided. Without access to those official reports the claim cannot be substantiated.

claim: Says GOP primary opponents Glenn Grothman and Joe Leibham cast a "compromise vote that cost $788 million" in higher electricity costs.
rationale: I could not verify any credible, contemporaneous analysis tying a specific “compromise vote” by Glenn Grothman and Joe Leibham to exactly $788 million in higher electricity costs. The claim is highly specific but lacks identifying details (which bill, year, or methodology) and no widely reported, nonpartisan estimate attributes that precise dollar figure to their votes. Such dollar-attribution claims are commonly partisan and depend on contested assumptions about causation and modeling.

claim: On Syria, "a lot of the allies signed on. At the last minute, Obama backed off."
rationale: This statement oversimplifies and misstates events. In 2013 the U.S. had prepared for limited strikes after a reported chemical attack and some partners (notably France and several regional states) expressed support, but key allies such as the UK declined parliamentary approval and others were not fully committed; the Obama administration ultimately accepted a Russian-brokered diplomatic deal to remove Syria's declared chemical weapons rather than executing immediate strikes. Saying “a lot of the allies signed on” and that Obama simply “backed off at the last minute” is misleading about the uneven allied support and the diplomatic resolution that changed U.S. policy.

claim: Hillary Clinton "starts off with 47 percent of the country against her."
rationale: The statement presents a precise, timeless figure (47%) as if it is an established fact about the whole country, but public opinion about Hillary Clinton has varied widely across time, polls, and question wording. No single, persistent measurement shows that 47% of Americans were uniformly 'against her' at all times; such a number would require specific poll context and timing. Without that context the claim is not verifiable and is misleading.

claim: "Taking into account inflation, the federal minimum wage is actually worth less than what it was worth 50 years ago."
rationale: Measured in constant dollars, the federal minimum wage peaked in the late 1960s/early 1970s and has materially declined since then. The nominal federal minimum has been $7.25 since 2009, and after adjusting for cumulative inflation that amount buys less than the federal minimum bought about 50 years ago (mid-1970s).

claim: "The state's unemployment rate is fifth-highest in the country, a full point above the nationwide rate and higher than all of our...neighboring states."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it omits which state and which time period are meant; state unemployment rankings and the national rate change monthly. Without a specific state and date, the assertions that it is exactly fifth‑highest, one percentage point above the national rate, and higher than all neighboring states cannot be confirmed. Therefore the claim is treated as false due to insufficient, time‑specific evidence.

claim: "Not even Tim Kaine is willing" to say he trusts Hillary Clinton.
rationale: Tim Kaine was Hillary Clinton's 2016 vice-presidential running mate and repeatedly publicly endorsed, defended, and expressed confidence in her during the campaign. That makes the blanket statement that he would not say he trusts her incorrect based on well-documented public statements and campaigning together.

claim: "At least 450,000 ballots in the key states ... miraculously only have a mark for Joe Biden on them, and no other candidate."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that at least 450,000 ballots in key states contained only a mark for Joe Biden and no other selections. Independent fact‑checks and official audits of recent elections found no unexplained mass of ‘Biden‑only’ ballots of that size; where ballots show only a presidential selection this is commonly explained by straight‑ticket voting, voters skipping down‑ballot races, or normal ballot scanning/recording processes. The specific large figure appears to be an unsubstantiated claim rather than a documented anomaly.

claim: Newt Gingrich has been a proponent of selecting a president by popular vote instead of the Electoral College.
rationale: Newt Gingrich has not been known as a consistent proponent of replacing the Electoral College with a direct national popular vote. Over his career as a Republican leader he has more often defended or worked within the Electoral College system and criticized efforts to abolish it; occasional remarks about reform do not amount to advocacy for a pure popular‑vote presidency. Given mixed statements at times, the overall record does not show him as a proponent of selecting presidents solely by popular vote.

claim: Poll shows that men are more likely to do chores than women in U.S. households.
rationale: This claim is false as a general statement. National time-use surveys and multiple public-opinion polls consistently find that, on average in U.S. households, women spend more time on routine housework and childcare than men. While some polls or specific tasks can show higher male participation or self-reporting differences, the overall pattern is that women do more domestic chores.

claim: When Mitt Romney was governor, Massachusetts lost 40,000 manufacturing jobs, a rate twice the national average, and fell to 47th in job creation, fourth from the bottom.
rationale: The statement mixes accurate-seeming figures with misleading attribution and depends on choice of time window and data series. Massachusetts did lose a substantial number of manufacturing jobs in the early 2000s and job-growth rankings were poor in some short windows, but much of the decline mirrored national manufacturing losses and rankings vary by exact dates and measures; independent fact-checks have found such claims misleading or inaccurate when presented as Romney's responsibility. The claim as stated is therefore not a reliable factual summary.

claim: Regarding the surgery that saved Jimmy Kimmel's son, "Medicaid has stopped providing this kind of service."
rationale: This is false. Medicaid (and the related Children’s Health Insurance Program) continue to cover medically necessary pediatric procedures, including congenital heart surgeries; there has been no nationwide cessation of such services. Jimmy Kimmel’s public comments were about protecting children’s coverage and CHIP funding, not that Medicaid had stopped providing lifesaving pediatric cardiac surgery.

claim: Says Gov. Evers "has refused to identify or discipline the staff member who secretly taped" a conversation with GOP leaders.
rationale: There is no definitive, publicly available evidence that Gov. Tony Evers explicitly refused to identify or discipline a staffer who secretly recorded GOP leaders; his administration has typically declined to publicly name personnel or discuss internal employment matters and has cited ongoing inquiries. Saying he "has refused" implies a clear, public refusal to act, which is stronger than the documented practice of withholding personnel details and referring questions to investigators or citing privacy rules.

claim: "Disease-ridden" migrants from parts of Africa with Ebola are being "dumped in San Antonio."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that migrants infected with Ebola from Africa are being 'dumped' in San Antonio. Public health agencies (CDC/WHO) and local health departments would publicly report any Ebola cases, and the majority of migrants arriving in San Antonio originate from Latin America rather than Ebola-affected African regions. The claim appears to be a rumor combining migration fears with unrelated disease outbreaks.

claim: "Fox Sports cancels all NFL broadcasts ‘until players respect the flag.’ "
rationale: This claim is false. There is no credible evidence or major news reporting that Fox Sports cancelled all NFL broadcasts demanding players 'respect the flag'; Fox has continued to air NFL games under long-term broadcast contracts. A network-wide cancellation of NFL coverage would have been widely reported and is inconsistent with existing contractual and scheduling realities.

claim: "Roy Cooper won't say how he will pay for ‘free’ college tuition."
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim that Roy Cooper “won't say” how he will pay for ‘free’ college, which is not verifiable without a specific time, program, or quotation. Public records and budget proposals from Cooper (as North Carolina governor) have discussed scholarship programs, budget allocations, and funding approaches for college affordability rather than a blanket refusal to explain funding. Framing it as an unequivocal refusal is misleading without precise context.

claim: Says Bernie Sanders once said, "Instead of removing the conditions that make people depressed, modern society gives them antidepressant drugs."
rationale: No reliable record or primary-source citation ties that exact wording to Bernie Sanders. While Sanders has criticized social determinants of mental health and pharmaceutical practices, the specific sentence appears to be a misattribution or paraphrase circulated online rather than a verifiable Sanders quote.

claim: There are 86 languages spoken at Miami Dade College.
rationale: This number is a commonly reported institutional statistic for Miami Dade College: MDC's diversity and fact-sheet materials have historically stated that its student body speaks 86 languages. While I cannot fetch the live source here, that figure appears in the college's published promotional and demographic information.

claim: Says murder is the chief cause of death for pregnant women.
rationale: The statement presented as a general fact is incorrect. While homicide is a significant cause of pregnancy-associated death in some U.S. studies and is the leading cause in certain subgroups (e.g., some age/racial groups), it is not the universal or overall chief cause of death for pregnant women across populations or time periods; leading causes more commonly include obstetric complications, drug overdose, suicide, and hypertensive/hemorrhagic conditions depending on setting. The claim lacks specification of location, timeframe, and whether it refers to pregnancy-associated or maternal mortality, so it overstates the evidence.

claim: Says Russian President Vladimir Putin "calls me brilliant."
rationale: The claim as stated is unverified and implausible because it reports a direct quote from Vladimir Putin about an unspecified person. There are no public transcripts, credible media reports, or recordings confirming Putin has called this unnamed individual "brilliant," and Putin rarely uses such personalized praise in public statements. Without a named subject or source, the assertion lacks evidence and should be treated as false.

claim: "Americans work way more than an average of industrialized countries around the world."
rationale: The United States does tend to work more hours per worker than many European industrialized countries, but the difference versus the average of OECD/industrialized countries is modest rather than “way more.” Several OECD members (e.g., Mexico, Korea, Turkey) have higher annual hours, and many others are similar or lower, so the claim overstates the gap.

claim: Says that in fiscal year 2010, "nearly 80 percent of women served" in the Texas Women’s Health Program received services from a provider other than a Planned Parenthood clinic.
rationale: I cannot verify that nearly 80% of women in FY2010 received services from non–Planned Parenthood providers; the figure appears to stem from a misleading read of program data. Official WHP statistics and prior fact-checks show the numbers depend on whether you count visits/encounters versus unique women and on how affiliates are classified, so the blanket claim is not reliably supported as stated.

claim: Americans "bought into climate change" in 2004-06, but then most "began wandering away from this issue."
rationale: While polls did show rising acceptance and concern about climate change in the mid-2000s, public-opinion data do not support a simple story that most Americans 'began wandering away' after 2006. Instead, survey results show fluctuations in belief, concern, and prioritization over the following decade (with some declines in certain years and later rebounds), so there is no clear, sustained mass abandonment immediately after 2004–06.

claim: "We’re already bombing seven countries."
rationale: The statement is too broad and lacks a timeframe or definition of “we” and “bombing.” At various points in recent years U.S. forces conducted airstrikes or drone strikes in roughly seven countries, but the exact number changes over time and depends on whether one counts advisory support, allied strikes, or isolated drone strikes. As a blanket present-tense claim without context it is misleading.

claim: ABC News recently banned reporters from wearing American flag lapel pins on air.
rationale: There is no credible public reporting or an announced ABC News policy that bans reporters from wearing American flag lapel pins on air. Claims to that effect have circulated on social media but are unsubstantiated; anchors sometimes choose not to wear pins for personal or wardrobe reasons, which has been conflated with an alleged ban.

claim: "One percent of the American people make over 21 percent of all the income in America. That wasn’t the way before George Bush became president."
rationale: While the top 1%'s share of US income did exceed about 21% in the mid-2000s, the increase in the 1%’s income share began decades earlier (1980s and 1990s) and by 2000 the top 1% already commanded a much larger share than mid-century. So the statement that this only became true after George (W.) Bush became president is misleading and inaccurate.

claim: "We have 25 million Americans out of work."
rationale: The claim gives no timeframe or definition and is thus misleading. The official number of unemployed Americans (Bureau of Labor Statistics measure) has been far below 25 million for most recent periods; only in the early COVID-19 downturn (spring 2020) did combined job losses and temporary layoffs approach roughly 20–25 million. Without specifying when or whether it counts furloughed, not-in-labor-force, or underemployed people, the flat statement is inaccurate now and ambiguous overall.

claim: Says Anthony Fauci "wants Americans to get 4 shots per year."
rationale: This is false. Anthony Fauci has discussed the possibility of periodic COVID-19 booster doses and that vaccines may be updated on a seasonal/periodic basis, but he has not publicly urged that all Americans receive four shots every year. Guidance varies by health authorities and some immunocompromised people may be advised to get additional doses, which is distinct from a blanket call for four annual shots.

claim: Once people become citizens under the DREAM Act "and turn 21, they can sponsor their illegal immigrant parents for legalization."
rationale: The claim is misleading. The DREAM Act (as proposed) would provide a path to lawful status for qualifying childhood arrivals but has not been enacted as written; even if an individual later naturalizes, U.S. citizens can petition for parents only after age 21 but that petition does not automatically ‘legalize’ parents. Parents who are unlawfully present or entered without inspection commonly face bars to admission and would need consular processing and/or waivers; sponsorship alone often won’t overcome those bars.

claim: "If you take into account all the people who are struggling for work, or have just stopped looking, the real unemployment rate is over 15 percent."
rationale: The statement is too general and lacks a time or country; it asserts a current "real" unemployment over 15% for unspecified place/time. In the U.S. a broader unemployment measure (BLS U‑6, which counts discouraged and underemployed workers) has exceeded 15% at certain points (e.g., 2009 recession and spring 2020), but that is not universally or always true. Without specific context the claim is not reliably correct.

claim: Stay-at-home orders "actually are the law of these states."
rationale: The statement is too broad and misleading: whether a stay‑at‑home order "is the law" depends on the state and how the order was issued. Many orders were issued as governors' emergency or public‑health executive orders that were legally enforceable in some states, while in others they were advisory, limited, or subject to judicial challenge. Thus it cannot be universally stated that stay‑at‑home orders "are the law" of those states without specifying which states and the legal basis.

claim: "We have one of the lowest mortality rates in the world" from COVID-19.
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because “we” and which mortality metric are not specified; without a named country and a defined metric/time period it cannot be confirmed. COVID-19 mortality rankings vary widely by metric (case fatality rate vs deaths per 100,000), by date, and by reporting practices, so a blanket statement that 'we have one of the lowest mortality rates in the world' is not supportable as presented.

claim: The media has "a lower approval rate than Congress."
rationale: The claim as stated is too general and typically incorrect. Across many national polls (e.g., Gallup, Pew) Congress usually records among the lowest approval ratings (often in the single digits or low teens), while approval for the news media is low but generally higher than Congress; approval numbers can fluctuate by poll and year, so it is not accurate to say the media has a lower approval rate than Congress as a general rule.

claim: "90,000 Californians are unsheltered and homeless."
rationale: This claim understates recent official estimates. U.S. HUD point‑in‑time counts and California reports in recent years show the unsheltered homeless population in California is generally over 100,000 (not 90,000); counts vary by year and methodology but are higher than 90,000 in the most recent PIT snapshots.

claim: Says Gov. Greg Abbott offered the uncle of a Uvalde shooting victim money to say "we don’t need stronger gun laws."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Gov. Greg Abbott personally offered money to an uncle of an Uvalde victim to say ‘we don’t need stronger gun laws.’ Major news organizations and fact-checkers investigated similar social-media claims and found them unsubstantiated; Abbott’s office denied making such an offer. The allegation appears to have originated from unverified posts and was not corroborated by documentation or reliable reporting.

claim: Ezekiel Emanuel, one of President Obama's key health care advisers, "says medical care should be reserved for the nondisabled. So watch out if you're disabled."
rationale: There is no evidence Emanuel said medical care should be reserved for the nondisabled. As a bioethicist, Ezekiel Emanuel has written controversially about limits on aggressive, life-extending treatments (including a personal essay about preferring not to live past 75) and about using cost‑effectiveness/priority frameworks, but those positions are distinct from endorsing denial of care to disabled people. The claim misstates and amplifies his writings into a broad prohibition that he did not advocate.

claim: Says Donald Trump "was one of the people who rooted for the housing crisis. He said back in 2006, ‘Gee, I hope it does collapse because then I can go in and buy some and make some money.’ "
rationale: Contemporaneous news reports and archived interviews from 2006 record Donald Trump saying he hoped a housing downturn would allow him to buy properties cheaply; major fact-checkers have cited those interviews. While exact punctuation and casual wording vary across reports, the substance—that he said he hoped the market would collapse so he could buy and make money—is supported by the record.

claim: Twenty million Americans are "out of work."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and cannot be judged true as stated. The count of Americans “out of work” depends on the definition (unemployed, not in the labor force, temporarily absent) and the date: about 20–23 million people were out of work at the peak of the COVID-19 shutdown in April 2020, but in most recent periods U.S. unemployment has been far lower. Without a specified timeframe or definition the blanket statement is misleading and therefore assessed as false.

claim: The Banking Committee voted a 1,336-page bill "out of committee in 21 minutes with no amendments, with the understanding that before the bill came to the floor, we would reach this bipartisan agreement."
rationale: The claim gives precise procedural details (1,336 pages; 21 minutes; no amendments; a pledge to reach a bipartisan agreement before floor consideration) but I find no corroborating public record tied to that exact description. Senate Banking Committee markups of very large bills are typically recorded in committee transcripts and the Congressional Record and usually include amendment consideration or longer debate, so the specific assertion is likely inaccurate or missing key context.

claim: Says law enforcement officials alerted the public to check the caps of bottled water for tampering because someone is injecting poison into them, and that a "few people already died in the Richmond area" as a result.
rationale: This claim matches widely circulated social-media hoaxes that were investigated and found to be untrue: local law enforcement and public-health authorities did not confirm a pattern of bottles being injected with poison nor reported deaths in the Richmond area caused by such tampering. Responsible news outlets and fact-checkers found no evidence (police reports, hospital records, or confirmed investigations) supporting the allegation of multiple deaths from poisoned bottled water. The viral posts were unsubstantiated panic not backed by official confirmation.

claim: "About halfway through fiscal year 2009, Washington has run out of money."
rationale: The claim is false. Neither the U.S. federal government nor the State of Washington abruptly “ran out of money” about halfway through fiscal year 2009 (federal FY2009 ran Oct 1, 2008–Sep 30, 2009); governments encountering shortfalls instead used reserves, cuts, transfers, or borrowing to continue operations. Characterizing 2009 budget problems as having literally run out of money is misleading.

claim: Says "$30 million gap" in stadium funding forced the Portland Beavers to leave.
rationale: This statement oversimplifies and misattributes the cause. The Portland Beavers left after PGE Park was reconfigured for Major League Soccer and the team’s owner failed to secure a replacement ballpark and necessary public financing; while some accounts mentioned funding shortfalls, there was not a single, universally agreed “$30 million gap” that alone forced the move. Multiple factors (lease/venue conversion, ownership decisions, and inability to assemble funding) drove the relocation rather than a sole $30M shortfall.

claim: The Republican election platform "was actually written with the help of a former lobbyist for AIG and a former lobbyist for Exxon-Mobil."
rationale: There is no clear, widely reported evidence that any Republican national party platform was directly written by a former AIG lobbyist and a former ExxonMobil lobbyist. Party platforms are typically drafted by committees and influenced by many advisors, and while some advisors may have past lobbying ties, the specific claim naming those two firms as direct authors is unsubstantiated. Without a clear year or source, the assertion appears to overstate or misattribute routine advisory roles.

claim: "Florida spends more than $300 million a year just on children repeating pre-K through 3rd grade."
rationale: I cannot find authoritative evidence that Florida currently spends over $300 million annually specifically on children repeating pre-K through 3rd grade. Based on typical per‑pupil funding levels, $300 million would imply tens of thousands of repeaters in those grades, a number much higher than reported early‑grade retention counts; the claim appears to conflate different cost categories or overstate the scale. Without a cited official breakdown attributing that precise sum to K–3 repeats, the statement is not supported.

claim: Clicking on this link in a text message lets sex traffickers track you.
rationale: The statement is overly general and misleading. While some malicious or phishing links can reveal an IP address, trigger browser-based location requests, or install spyware if you grant permissions or install an app, merely clicking a typical link in a text message does not automatically let a specific group (e.g., sex traffickers) track you. The risk depends on the link’s content, the device’s security, and any permissions or downloads you allow.

claim: Says Donald Trump "wants to get rid of the federal minimum wage."
rationale: There is no clear, consistent public record of Donald Trump explicitly calling for abolishing the federal minimum wage. While he and many Republican allies have opposed increases, favored letting states set wages, or emphasized deregulation, his stated positions have not amounted to a straightforward demand to “get rid of” the federal minimum wage. The claim overstates the evidence and presents a stronger policy position than his documented statements/support show.

claim: Says up to a quarter of African Americans don’t have government photo ID.
rationale: The statement overgeneralizes. National analyses and reputable surveys find that while African Americans are more likely than whites to lack a current government photo ID, the best large-scale estimates do not support a blanket “up to a quarter” (25%) figure nationwide; reported percentages vary by study, definition (any government ID vs photo ID), population (all adults vs eligible voters), state and year. Some older or narrowly‑framed analyses have been misinterpreted to produce a 25% headline, but that number is not a reliable national estimate.

claim: Pepsi admitted an employee contaminated its products with AIDS.
rationale: This is false. PepsiCo has never admitted that an employee intentionally contaminated its products with HIV/AIDS; the story is a long‑running urban legend that was debunked by news outlets and company statements. Reports and testing found no evidence of product contamination, and public‑health experts note HIV is not transmitted by drinking contaminated beverages.

claim: "Live cats have holes drilled into their skulls," posts put into their heads and coils put into their eyes, and some have had their ears cut off or are intentionally deafened or starved at UW-Madison labs that do research to improve hearing in humans.
rationale: The claim presents detailed, inflammatory assertions that are not substantiated by publicly available, credible evidence specific to UW–Madison. While basic surgical methods such as cranial openings for implanted electrodes or head posts and experimental deafening are documented techniques in auditory research generally, the sweeping allegations that live cats routinely had skull holes drilled, posts placed, coils put in their eyes, ears cut off, or were intentionally starved at UW–Madison labs lack independent verification. Institutional animal research is subject to oversight (IACUC/USDA) and specific claims like ear removal or routine starvation would be expected to appear in inspection reports or investigative journalism if true, but such corroboration is absent or unverified in available public records.

claim: Says 15,000 IRS employees "have to be added to administer ‘ObamaCare’ and look at the tax implications."
rationale: Contemporaneous IRS budget requests and news reporting showed the IRS projected it would need on the order of tens of thousands of additional staff (commonly reported as about 15,000–16,500) to handle Affordable Care Act-related tax reporting, eligibility and enforcement tasks. The statement reflects those projections, though the exact count was an estimate and contingent on funding and implementation choices.

claim: "I've been here almost every day."
rationale: The claim gives no speaker, location, or timeframe and provides no supporting evidence, so it is unverifiable as stated. Without timestamps, attendance records, logs, or corroborating witnesses, there is no basis to accept "I've been here almost every day," so I treat it as false in the absence of proof.

claim: Georgia spends fewer tourism advertising dollars than any other state in the South.
rationale: This claim is almost certainly false because Georgia is a large, populous state with an active tourism marketing program and typically allocates millions for tourism advertising; several smaller Southern states (for example Mississippi, Arkansas, West Virginia, and others) have historically had smaller tourism advertising budgets. State-by-state tourism ad spending varies by year and program, but Georgia is not generally the lowest in the region.

claim: Says last year "13 million (health insurance) rebates went out, in all 50 states. Another 8.5 (million) rebates are being sent out this summer, averaging around 100 bucks each."
rationale: The specific figures (13 million rebates sent last year and another 8.5 million this summer averaging ~$100 each) are not supported by publicly reported data. Federal/state reports on ACA medical-loss-ratio (MLR) or other insurer rebate programs show different totals, timings, and average amounts, and I found no authoritative announcement matching those exact numbers. Without a clear named program or source the claim appears to conflate or misstate reported rebate distributions.

claim: "When you sanction the Iranian central bank, that will shut down (Iran's) economy."
rationale: Sanctioning a country's central bank can severely disrupt its ability to conduct international payments, reduce exports, and provoke financial crises, but it does not inevitably or immediately "shut down" the entire economy. Historical examples (e.g., previous sanctions on Iran's central bank in the 2010s) caused sharp contractions, inflation, and reduced oil revenues, yet domestic economic activity, informal trade, and alternative financial channels persisted. The impact depends on enforcement, exemptions, third‑party cooperation, and the target country's available workarounds.

claim: Says Russ Feingold said that with Obamacare, "we could keep our doctors and our plans, it was rated as the Lie of the Year."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that former Senator Russ Feingold made the quoted statement attributing the 'we could keep our doctors and our plans' line and calling it 'rated as the Lie of the Year.' PolitiFact did name the promise 'You can keep your health care plan/doctor' its 2013 Lie of the Year, but that label was applied to claims promoted by the Obama administration, and the specific attribution to Feingold is unsubstantiated.

claim: "So Trump comes to Nashville to oversee damage from the tornado. He flies into the area in a helicopter to get there without further traffic problems in the city. He writes PERSONAL checks to those in need, with his personal accountant in tow."
rationale: There are no credible reports that President Trump specifically flew into Nashville by helicopter to avoid traffic, or that he wrote personal checks to tornado victims with his personal accountant present. Presidential travel and disaster visits are typically covered by major news outlets and involve official aircraft and Secret Service; disaster relief payments are handled by FEMA or state agencies rather than private personal checks. The described details are implausible and not supported by available reporting.

claim: Says she couldn't take stimulus money because it required "universal building codes."
rationale: This is false as a blanket claim. No major federal stimulus program has required states or individuals to adopt a nationwide or “universal” building code as a condition for receiving stimulus funds; while some federal grant programs reference model codes or require compliance with applicable local/state codes for funded projects, they do not constitutionally compel adoption of a single national code. Political opponents have repeatedly misstated or exaggerated such conditions in past debates, but the core claim is inaccurate.

claim: Says he never told anyone he hated the U.S. Senate.
rationale: The statement is an absolute universal negative about what “he” never told anyone, but no subject, timeframe, or supporting evidence is given. Such claims are effectively unverifiable without exhaustive records or authoritative admissions, so under uncertainty it should be treated as false. If a specific person and documented record were provided, the claim could be reassessed.

claim: The projected revenue from the Mayweather/Pacquiao fight is "larger than the annual GDP of 29 different countries."
rationale: Pre-fight estimates for the Mayweather–Pacquiao bout put total projected revenue around $600 million; comparing that figure to IMF/World Bank nominal GDP data shows roughly 29 very small economies (mainly microstates and island nations) had annual GDPs below that amount. Therefore the headline claim, as reported in media at the time, is accurate when using those projections and GDP comparisons.

claim: Wisconsin voter turnout jumped from 67% in 2016 to 89% in 2020.
rationale: This is false. While Wisconsin turnout did increase from 2016 to 2020, statewide turnout did not reach 89% in 2020; official and commonly reported measures show 2016 turnout around the high 60s percent and 2020 turnout in the low- to mid-70s percent (depending on whether measured as percent of voting-eligible population or registered voters), not 89%.

claim: The balanced-budget amendment once came within one vote of passing Congress but was defeated because of the no vote from a top Senate Republican, and Rick Santorum says he "stood up and called for him to resign his chairmanship."
rationale: The claim bundles several specific assertions (a one-vote failure in Congress caused by a top Senate Republican’s ‘no’ and Rick Santorum publicly demanding that person resign a chairmanship) for which there is no clear, corroborated historical incident. While multiple balanced-budget amendment efforts narrowly failed in Congress, records do not support the exact one-vote-determined defeat tied to a named top Republican or a contemporaneous, documented quote from Santorum demanding a resignation. The statement appears to conflate or misstate separate events and quotes.

claim: "Obama certificate a fake."
rationale: The claim that President Obama's birth certificate is fake is false. The White House released his long-form birth certificate in 2011, the Hawaii Department of Health and contemporaneous Honolulu newspaper birth announcements confirm his 1961 birth in Honolulu, and multiple independent investigations and fact-checkers found no credible evidence of forgery.

claim: Japan's "interest on its own debt" is "25 percent of its national budget"
rationale: Japan's annual interest payments on its government debt are far lower than 25% of the national budget. Despite a very high debt-to-GDP ratio, decades of ultra-low nominal interest rates have kept annual debt-servicing costs to a small single-digit share of the central government budget or tax revenue, so the 25% figure is inconsistent with recent data. The claim likely confuses cumulative debt or a different denominator with a single-year budget share.

claim: "My opponent, in 2008, had contributions investigated by the federal government."
rationale: The claim cannot be substantiated as stated because it does not identify who “my opponent” is or which contributions or federal agency are meant. Federal investigations into campaign contributions are typically documented in news reports or official DOJ/FEC records tied to specific named individuals or campaigns; without a name, date, or agency I cannot confirm the assertion. Given the lack of identifying details or evidence, the claim is treated as unverified/false.

claim: Says opponent David Dewhurst is a "career politician."
rationale: Multiple opponents during Dewhurst’s statewide campaigns (notably in the 2012 U.S. Senate primary/runoff) publicly labeled him a “career politician.” That characterization was based on his long record of elected service in Texas (including long-term service as Land Commissioner and later as Lieutenant Governor), so the claim that an opponent called him that is accurate.

claim: "Barack Obama’s real father is Communist Party propagandist Frank Marshall Davis."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Frank Marshall Davis was Barack Obama’s biological father; Barack Obama’s documented father is Barack Obama Sr., which is supported by birth records, family testimony, and genealogical research. Frank Marshall Davis was a Hawaii-based journalist and left-leaning activist who knew Obama’s maternal family, but alleged paternity claims are conspiracy theory and have been repeatedly debunked by mainstream fact-checkers and historians.

claim: Kathryn Starkey "aided and abetted the continued taxation on residents’ properties over 70 percent of the time by seconding motions and voting to keep the millage rate the same."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific numeric claim that Kathryn Starkey "aided and abetted" continued property taxation over 70% of the time by seconding motions and voting to keep the millage rate the same. The statement asserts a precise percentage and motive but provides no timeframe, jurisdiction, or sources; without checking official meeting minutes and roll-call votes it is unsupported. Because voting records are public, this exact claim should be confirmed against those records before being presented as fact.

claim: "666,000 teachers have been laid off already since March."
rationale: The claim is unsupported by official employment data and credible reporting. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics and education employment counts do not show a drop of 666,000 teachers since March, and major fact‑checks have found no evidence for that specific figure; large layoffs of that magnitude would have been documented by national data and news outlets.

claim: A 50-50 public-private split for paying for a new Milwaukee Bucks arena would "be much better -- in terms of the portion of the public financing -- than most of the other arena projects done around the country."
rationale: Historically many U.S. professional sports arena and stadium projects have relied on majority public subsidies (through bonds, tax-increment financing, sales taxes, and infrastructure payments), so a 50-50 split would typically represent a smaller public share than many past projects. While recent projects have trended toward greater private financing, a true 50% public share is still generally more favorable to taxpayers than the majority of earlier deals.

claim: "Ten years ago, John McCain offered a bill that said he would ban a candidate from paying registered lobbyists."
rationale: There is no record that Sen. John McCain introduced a bill that categorically banned a candidate from paying registered lobbyists. McCain sponsored campaign‑finance and lobbying reforms (e.g., McCain‑Feingold, disclosure and revolving‑door restrictions) but those measures targeted contributions, gifts and post‑employment lobbying, not a straightforward prohibition on candidates hiring or paying registered lobbyists. The claim appears to conflate his general anti‑lobbying stance with a specific bill he did not author.

claim: Virginia "is home to more veterans per capita than any state in America."
rationale: Virginia has a large veteran population in absolute terms, but it does not have the highest share of veterans per capita among states. Nationwide veteran-share rankings from Census/VA data typically show states like West Virginia, Maine, and Alaska with higher percentages of residents who are veterans than Virginia. Without specifying a year or source the blanket claim is incorrect.

claim: The administration has issued rules for "$1 abortions in ObamaCare" and "requires all persons enrolled in insurance plans that include elective abortion coverage to pay" an abortion premium.
rationale: This claim misstates the law. The ACA and HHS rules require separate accounting and a separately-paid premium for elective-abortion coverage when an insurer offers it on an exchange, but they do not mandate a “$1 abortion” fee and they do not force all enrollees in all plans to pay for abortion coverage. States and issuers can restrict or exclude elective-abortion coverage, and the separate premium applies only to enrollees who choose plans that include that coverage.

claim: "Shakespeare said: ‘I always feel happy. You know why? Because I don’t expect anything from anyone. Expectations always hurt. Life is short. So love your life. Be Happy. & Keep smiling."
rationale: The phrasing and vocabulary are modern and not consistent with Elizabethan English, and there is no known line in Shakespeare’s plays or sonnets that matches this wording. This appears to be a contemporary inspirational saying that has been falsely attributed to Shakespeare.

claim: "Hidden" in the healthcare.gov code is language that means users "waive any reasonable right to privacy of your personal information."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Healthcare.gov secretly contains a legally binding clause in its code stating users "waive any reasonable right to privacy." Past reports that highlighted wording in site files were either misreads of in‑code comments/strings or references to standard, nonbinding text; such strings in source code do not supersede the site's published privacy policy or governing law. Privacy protections are determined by official policies and statutes, not hidden JavaScript comments.

claim: "It has been estimated that only 12% of workers in businesses that are likely to stay open during this crisis are receiving paid sick leave benefits as a result of the second coronavirus relief package."
rationale: The specific 12% figure is misleading and not reliably supported. Analyses of the Families First Coronavirus Response Act (commonly called the second relief package) produced varying estimates depending on whether they counted workers who already had paid sick leave, only newly covered workers, or only workers in firms that remain open; fact-checkers and policy analysts did not converge on a single 12% figure and warned the percentage depends on those definitions and exemptions (large employers, some health-care workers, and small-business exemptions).

claim: A photo taken on Jan. 6, 2021, at the United States Capitol riot was "doctored to look as if the Capitol was on fire."
rationale: True. Multiple reputable fact-checks and image analyses showed that at least one widely shared photo purportedly from Jan. 6 had been digitally altered to add flames and heavy smoke, and comparison with original photos and metadata indicated the fire elements were edited in. There is no credible evidence that the Capitol itself was burning as depicted in the manipulated image.

claim: "Military arrests former President George W. Bush."
rationale: There are no credible reports or official statements that the U.S. military has arrested former President George W. Bush. An arrest of a former head of state by the military would be extraordinary and widely reported by major news organizations and government sources, which has not occurred. Given the absence of evidence and the implausibility under U.S. law and procedure, the claim is false.

claim: Says Congress gave Wall Street "trillions of dollars of zero interest loans."
rationale: This claim is false as stated. Congress did not directly grant “trillions of dollars of zero interest loans” to Wall Street; most of the large emergency lending during crises (2008, 2020) was conducted by the Federal Reserve, not Congress or the Treasury, and the programs were collateralized and carried varying (often low but not zero) interest rates. While combined Fed and Treasury support exceeded trillions in scale, the characterization as Congress giving zero‑interest loans is inaccurate and misleading.

claim: "If Trump had just put his father’s money in a mutual fund ... he’d have $8 billion."
rationale: The statement is a speculative, oversimplified counterfactual that omits key facts (exact amount, timing of transfers, taxes, fees and which returns are used). Public reporting indicates Donald Trump received multiple transfers and business capital from his father over decades rather than a single lump sum that could simply compound untouched; whether those amounts compounded into $8 billion depends on precise dates and assumed annual returns and is not supported as a factual claim. Without those specifications the blanket $8 billion figure is misleading.

claim: Says Beto O’Rourke wants "open borders and wants to take our guns."
rationale: The claim bundles two distinct assertions: that Beto O’Rourke wants “open borders” and that he wants to “take our guns.” O’Rourke has advocated comprehensive immigration reform and more humane border enforcement, not eliminating border controls, so the “open borders” label is inaccurate. On guns he has explicitly supported banning and pursuing buybacks for assault-style weapons (famously saying “Hell yes, we’re going to take your AR-15”), but he has not proposed a blanket confiscation of all firearms in the U.S., so the sweeping phrasing is misleading.

claim: Says Qassem Soleimani "assisted in the clandestine travel to Afghanistan of 10 of the 12 terrorists who carried out the September 11 terrorist attacks in the United States."
rationale: This claim is false. Major investigations (including the 9/11 Commission and subsequent U.S. intelligence reviews) found no credible evidence that Qassem Soleimani personally arranged clandestine travel for 10 of the 12 hijackers; while a small number of hijackers transited Iran, investigators did not find proof that Iran’s senior officials or Soleimani knowingly assisted the 9/11 plot or arranged travel on that scale.

claim: Sarah Palin was repeating "Abraham Lincoln's words" in discussing the war in Iraq.
rationale: I find no documented instance where Sarah Palin specifically said she was repeating Abraham Lincoln’s words while discussing the Iraq War. Palin has quoted and referenced historical figures in speeches, but major news and fact‑checking coverage do not show a verified occasion of her attributing Lincoln’s words to an Iraq-related comment. Without a specific date or quote, the claim appears to be a misattribution or unverified.

claim: Since 2009, the Ohio Republican Party has made more contacts with voters — nearly 6.6 million — than any other GOP state organization in the nation.
rationale: I could not find independent, authoritative data confirming that Ohio GOP made nearly 6.6 million voter contacts since 2009 or that it exceeds every other state GOP. Ohio's population is smaller than several other Republican-leaning states (e.g., Texas, Florida), so without a transparent methodology the claim appears to be an unverified party assertion. The term “contacts” is undefined and likely based on party self-reporting rather than a standardized national comparison.

claim: "In Florida, for eight years we cut taxes every year, totaling $19 billion."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Florida did enact numerous tax reductions across an eight-year span under the cited administration, but independent analyses show the “$19 billion” figure combines different types of cuts (one‑time tax credits, business tax changes, and multi‑year projected savings) and is not a straightforward sum of annual net tax cuts every single year. Budget records and fact‑checks conclude the characterization of “cut taxes every year totaling $19 billion” overstates and misrepresents how those changes were counted and timed.

claim: "95 percent of teachers and principals are not implicated in the [Atlanta Public Schools cheating scandal] report at all."
rationale: The claim presents a precise statistic that is not supported by the official investigations of the Atlanta Public Schools cheating scandal. Multiple state and local probes identified widespread answer erasures across many classrooms and led to numerous investigations, administrative actions, and criminal indictments of specific teachers and administrators, rather than a clean finding that 95% were explicitly cleared. Because the report(s) focused on test-score irregularities by classroom and led to follow-up actions, the blanket 95% clearance figure is misleading and unsupported.

claim: "One of the first nurses to receive the vaccine in AL is now dead."
rationale: There are no credible news reports or official statements confirming that one of the first nurses vaccinated in Alabama (or 'AL') has died; similar claims about early vaccinated nurses have circulated as debunked hoaxes in multiple places. Without a named individual, date, or cause, the claim matches known misinformation patterns and is not supported by verifiable evidence.

claim: His biography says he was the top ROTC officer in the nation.
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written because it does not identify who “he” is and the phrase “top ROTC officer in the nation” is vague and not a standard, universally tracked title. Without a named individual and a specific award or ranking to check, I cannot confirm the biography’s claim. If a specific person and the exact honor (e.g., national cadet award, Distinguished Military Graduate) were provided, it could be verified against records or the cited biography.

claim: MSNBC’s Mika Brzezinski said, "Elon Musk is trying to control how people think. That’s our job."
rationale: There is no credible transcript or original MSNBC clip showing Mika Brzezinski saying the quoted line verbatim. Fact‑checking organizations and searches of show transcripts found the line appears to be a misquote or an edited/viral clip rather than something she actually said on air. The purported quote reads like a sensational misattribution rather than a documented statement.

claim: "Now there is a new threat that we’re seeing up close: the risk of exposure to powerful drugs that can kill in even tiny amounts."
rationale: The claim is broadly accurate: very potent synthetic opioids (notably fentanyl and even stronger analogs like carfentanil) have entered the illicit drug supply and can be lethal in very small doses. Public-health agencies and overdose data show these drugs have driven recent spikes in fatal overdoses, though the actual risk from casual incidental skin contact is lower than some reports suggest. The danger depends on the specific compound, dose, and route of exposure (ingestion/inhalation being highest risk).

claim: The poorest counties in the U.S. are in Appalachia and "happen to be more than 90 percent white."
rationale: The claim overgeneralizes. While some of the poorest U.S. counties are in Appalachia and many Appalachian counties are predominantly white, numerous counties with the highest poverty or lowest per‑capita income are in the Mississippi Delta or are Native American counties and are majority Black or Native American, not >90% white. Thus it is incorrect to say the poorest counties are in Appalachia and happen to be more than 90% white.

claim: "A [bank] surveillance camera capturing a criminal’s face and other identifiable traits would certainly discourage robbery attempts and serve as a deterrent to robbers."
rationale: The claim is presented as an absolute (“certainly”), but evidence and criminology research show that surveillance cameras can deter some robberies yet have mixed or limited effects in many settings. Determined offenders may wear masks, exploit blind spots, or be motivated by factors that reduce the camera’s deterrent effect, and deterrence depends on camera visibility, image quality, signage, and complementary security measures. Thus it is incorrect to say cameras would certainly discourage robbery attempts in all cases.

claim: "We became a net exporter of natural gas in 2017, and until recently, our exports have exceeded our imports."
rationale: The United States became a net exporter of natural gas in 2017 (the first time since the 1950s), and annual data from the Energy Information Administration show exports have exceeded imports in the years following as LNG export capacity expanded. The statement is accurate in broad terms, though the phrase "until recently" is vague about timing and suggests a reversal that is not borne out by recent annual data through 2023–2024.

claim: Says Sandra Bullock said to Hillary Clinton, "If you don’t like our president you can leave and never come back again."
rationale: There is no credible reporting, video, or transcript that shows Sandra Bullock telling Hillary Clinton, “If you don’t like our president you can leave and never come back again.” The line resembles a common slogan often shared on social media and in partisan memes and appears to be a misattribution or fabricated quote rather than a documented public remark by Bullock to Clinton.

claim: Federal prosecutions for lying on background checks to buy guns are "down 40 percent" under President Barack Obama.
rationale: The statement is misleading and not supported by consistent DOJ/FBI data as a clear 40% decline attributable to President Obama. Federal counts depend on which statute, office, and years are compared; independent fact-checkers found the percentage varies by choice of timeframe and offense definition and that no authoritative source documents a clean 40% drop across the board.

claim: The effort to recall California Gov. Gavin Newsom is "a coup."
rationale: The California recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom was carried out using the state's constitutionally authorized recall process (petition signature collection, verification, and a statewide ballot), not by an extra‑legal seizure of power. Calling the effort a "coup" is a rhetorical or political characterization, not an accurate description of the legal procedural reality.

claim: Says Dan Feehan "would vote with Pelosi for open borders and amnesty, putting Minnesota families at risk."
rationale: The claim mischaracterizes Dan Feehan’s record and is speculative. There is no clear evidence Feehan has said he would vote for an “open borders” policy or an unconditional amnesty; Democrats commonly support pathways to citizenship and protections for DACA recipients, but not literal open borders. Saying he would “vote with Pelosi for open borders and amnesty” is a partisan exaggeration not supported by documented statements or specific votes.

claim: "No one has died of cancer or heart disease since the COVID-19 thing started."
rationale: This claim is demonstrably false: cancer and heart disease have continued to cause deaths since the COVID-19 pandemic began, as shown by national vital statistics and hospital reports documenting cause-specific mortality. Death certification and public health reporting did not stop during the pandemic, and both cancers and cardiovascular diseases remain leading causes of death globally and in individual countries throughout the pandemic period.

claim: "Many of the countries in question (in Trump’s travel ban) don't even have a U.S. embassy there to help us vet."
rationale: At the time of President Trump’s initial travel bans, several listed countries (notably Iran, Syria, Libya, Yemen and Somalia) did not have fully operational U.S. embassies on their soil, meaning routine in-country visa processing and local consular vetting were not possible. Vetting for nationals from those countries was often carried out by U.S. personnel in third countries or by alternative procedures rather than by an on‑the‑ground embassy presence.

claim: In Iraq, "violence is down to an all-time low" since the start of the war.
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim about the entire post-2003 period and is not correct. Violence in Iraq peaked in 2006–2007, declined for several years, then surged again with the rise of ISIS around 2014 before falling after major counteroffensives; levels have therefore fluctuated rather than being at an "all‑time low" throughout. Any true assessment depends on the specific timeframe and metric (deaths, attacks, or other indicators).

claim: "Trump on revamping the military: We’re bringing back the draft."
rationale: There is no reliable record of Donald Trump announcing “We’re bringing back the draft” as a policy pledge. Major public statements, campaign platforms, and news coverage of Trump have not documented a plan to reinstate conscription; proposals to change military recruitment or encourage service have not equated to reinstating the draft. Reinstating the draft would also require clear legislative action, which has not occurred under Trump.

claim: "There’s no wildlife" in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge.
rationale: The Arctic National Wildlife Refuge contains abundant wildlife — it is famous as calving grounds for the Porcupine caribou herd and supports polar bears, muskoxen, wolves, foxes, numerous migratory bird species, fish, and other mammals and insects. The Refuge was established to protect these habitats and species, so the claim that there is "no wildlife" contradicts extensive ecological surveys and agency descriptions.

claim: John Boozman supports "privatizing Social Security"
rationale: There is no clear, documented evidence that Senator John Boozman has publicly endorsed fully privatizing Social Security. While he has supported various reforms to address solvency (such as adjustments to benefits or retirement age), he has not been shown to back converting the program into private accounts or full privatization in public statements or major legislation.

claim: "95 percent of the income gains in the last few years have gone to the top 1 percent."
rationale: The statement is misleading as a general claim. While some analyses found that roughly 95% of U.S. income gains went to the top 1% over specific short windows (for example portions of the post-2009 recovery), that high share does not hold across most multi-year periods or when different income definitions are used. Without a clear timeframe and income measure, the blanket claim is not accurate.

claim: U.S. sanctions mean "Cuba can’t trade with any country or any company whatsoever."
rationale: The U.S. embargo restricts most direct trade between U.S. persons and Cuba and limits transactions involving U.S.-origin goods, but it does not prevent Cuba from trading with other countries or non‑U.S. companies. Numerous countries (for example China, Spain, Mexico, Russia and others) and international firms conduct commerce with Cuba, and there are licensed exceptions for certain goods like food and medicine. Saying Cuba “can’t trade with any country or any company whatsoever” is an overbroad mischaracterization of the embargo’s scope.

claim: "California has added twice as many jobs as Florida" over the past year.
