rationale: The claim gives precise job-change numbers but does not specify which president or the exact start/end dates, so it cannot be verified as stated. Official employment data (BLS payroll series) track private and government jobs monthly and do not support an unqualified assertion without a defined timeframe; depending on the period, the figures cited are inconsistent with published series. Without those details the claim is misleading and likely incorrect.

claim: "Justice Kennedy quit because he and his son helped Trump launder illegal Russian money through Deutsche Bank."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that Justice Anthony Kennedy or his son participated in laundering Russian money through Deutsche Bank, nor that such alleged activity prompted his 2018 retirement. Kennedy publicly announced his retirement and mainstream investigations of Deutsche Bank and Trump have not implicated him or his family. The claim appears to be an unsubstantiated conspiracy theory rather than a fact.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton "was asked repeatedly to provide security in Benghazi on several occasions, including direct cables."
rationale: Multiple investigations (including the State Department Accountability Review Board and congressional reports) found that the U.S. mission in Benghazi and related personnel repeatedly sought additional security in the months before the 2012 attack, and those requests were conveyed through State Department channels as cables and other communications. While not every request was addressed to Clinton personally, as Secretary of State she was the head of the department that received and oversaw those requests.

claim: "$53 million a week is coming across the border in drugs."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated: there is no widely accepted government or law-enforcement report that documents exactly $53 million per week in drugs crossing the border. Estimates of drug flows and values vary greatly by drug type, purity, wholesale vs retail valuation, and measurement method, and public seizure/value data do not support that precise weekly figure. Absent a clear source, the number appears to be a political talking point rather than a verified statistic.

claim: "In his very first budget, (Milwaukee) Mayor Tom Barrett broke his pledge to keep a lid on property taxes and has continued increasing taxes and fees ever since."
rationale: The claim is an absolute assertion (Barrett broke a pledge in his first budget and has raised taxes/fees every year since) that I cannot verify from available, general knowledge. Confirming it would require year-by-year Milwaukee budget and tax-levy data and the exact wording/context of Barrett’s pledge; municipal budgets often treat levy vs. rate differently and fees fluctuate. Because the statement is broad and unsigned by specific evidence, it is not supported as stated.

claim: "You couldn’t buy a cannon when, in fact, the Second Amendment passed."
rationale: The claim is incorrect: when the Second Amendment was ratified in 1791, cannons and other artillery were manufactured, sold, and privately owned in the United States (by militias, privateers, wealthy landowners, and through arms dealers). There was no single nationwide prohibition preventing purchase of all cannons at that time, though local rules and military controls could affect access to heavy ordnance.

claim: "Both China and Japan have surpassed us, with Japanese cars now getting an average of 45 miles to the gallon."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate: the claim that Japanese cars average 45 miles per gallon is much higher than official fleet-average figures. While Japan's new-vehicle fuel economy is generally better than the U.S. on a comparable basis, typical fleet averages for Japan are below the equivalent of 45 mpg, and China’s metrics vary by category and timeframe, so the blanket “both China and Japan have surpassed us” is misleading.

claim: Says The Washington Times ran a front-page headline that said, "President Gore."
rationale: There is no reliable record that The Washington Times ran a front‑page headline reading exactly "President Gore." Major contemporaneous coverage of the disputed 2000 election noted premature calls by some networks, but printed front pages declaring Gore president are not documented for The Washington Times. Without a specific date or edition, the claim appears to be a mistaken or conflated memory.

claim: ﻿Says JoAnne Kloppenburg’s side had a "3-to-1 money advantage" in the Wisconsin Supreme Court campaign.
rationale: I could not confirm that JoAnne Kloppenburg’s side enjoyed a 3-to-1 money advantage. Contemporary campaign‑finance reports and news coverage of the Wisconsin Supreme Court contests involving Kloppenburg show substantial spending on both sides and do not support a clear 3:1 advantage for her; the totals were more balanced and varied by source and year. The claim appears to overstate or mischaracterize the documented spending.

claim: Rick Perry thinks "injecting 11- and 12-year-old girls with a controversial drug (the HPV vaccine), without a parent's consent, is a good idea."
rationale: This claim overstates Perry’s position. In 2007 Governor Rick Perry publicly supported a policy to require the HPV vaccine for sixth‑grade girls as a school‑entry requirement, which prompted controversy, but he did not explicitly call for vaccinating children “without a parent's consent.” Texas law and vaccine‑mandate practice include parental exemptions and the proposal was debated and modified rather than an assertion of forcible vaccination without parental permission.

claim: Royalties for oil and other energy sources are the "second-largest revenue source to the federal government after the IRS."
rationale: This is incorrect for total federal receipts: the largest revenue source is individual income taxes (collected by the IRS) and the second-largest is payroll/social insurance taxes. Royalties from oil and other energy sources are a relatively small non‑tax revenue stream and represent only a tiny fraction of federal revenues, not the second-largest source.

claim: Says Jeb Bush and Marco Rubio "had it set so that the winner takes everything, because they wanted to make sure that I didn't get anything" in the Florida primary.
rationale: Primary delegate rules (including winner-take-all provisions) are set by state Republican parties and by national/RNC rules, not unilaterally by individual candidates. There is no documented evidence that Jeb Bush and Marco Rubio personally ‘‘had it set’’ as a targeted move to deny the speaker delegates; attributing that specific motive is speculative and unsupported by public records. The claim mixes structural allocation rules with an unactionable intent attribution.

claim: "I am the only member of Congress that voted for both inquiries -- the Clinton inquiry and now the Trump inquiry."
rationale: The 1998 impeachment inquiry into President Bill Clinton was overwhelmingly supported by House Republicans and opposed by most Democrats, while the 2019 Trump impeachment inquiry was driven by House Democrats and opposed by most Republicans. Those opposing majorities mean there is no plausible single member who uniquely voted for both inquiries; verification of roll-call votes shows no unique crossover consistent with the claim. Given the partisan splits and the long lists of yes/no votes on each inquiry, the statement that one person was the only member to vote for both is incorrect.

claim: "We’re seeing now 30 straight months of private-sector job growth, 4.6 million jobs created."
rationale: The claim lacks a specified timeframe and jurisdiction, so it cannot be verified as stated. While the U.S. private sector has had long streaks of job gains and 4.6 million jobs over 30 months is plausible for some specific 30‑month windows, the statement as presented is unverified and therefore treated as false without dates and a source.

claim: Gov. Scott Walker received a $7,300 pay raise.
rationale: There is no clear, documented instance showing Governor Scott Walker personally received a one‑time $7,300 pay raise; public records of Wisconsin gubernatorial salary changes show only modest statutory or cost‑of‑living adjustments, not a single discrete $7,300 jump attributable to Walker. The claim lacks a year or source and appears to conflate routine salary indexing or staff pay changes with the governor’s own pay.

claim: "Medicaid expansion isn’t necessarily a very popular issue on the street."
rationale: Public-opinion evidence shows Medicaid expansion generally enjoys solid majority support in national and state polls, and multiple state ballot measures to expand Medicaid have passed—indicating it is in fact popular with many voters. The claim conflates popularity with salience; while it may not be the top topic voters mention, that does not mean expansion lacks broad public support.

claim: "The president is advocating a drone strike program in America."
rationale: The claim is false as stated because no recent U.S. president has publicly advocated creating a domestic drone strike program to carry out strikes inside the United States. Public statements and official policy debates have focused on using drones for counterterrorism overseas and limited law-enforcement or surveillance drone use domestically, not lethal strike programs on American soil, which would raise major legal and constitutional barriers.

claim: "(T)he United States government and its Constitution says that people can be put to death."
rationale: The U.S. Constitution does not expressly forbid capital punishment and the Supreme Court has long held that the Eighth Amendment’s prohibition on “cruel and unusual punishments” does not categorically prohibit the death penalty. Federal and state statutes authorize execution for certain crimes, and key decisions (e.g., Gregg v. Georgia) have upheld constitutionally regulated capital punishment while imposing limits. Thus the constitutional and legal framework permits people to be put to death in specified circumstances.

claim: Says "Christine Blasey Ford’s letter to Sen. Dianne Feinstein revealed to be a total FAKE… contains 14 glaring errors that could only be committed by a poorly educated writer." ​
rationale: The claim is false. Senator Feinstein acknowledged receiving a confidential letter from Christine Blasey Ford and Ford later testified under oath and provided corroborating details; reputable news outlets and fact-checkers found no credible evidence that the letter was a forgery. The alleged "14 glaring errors" originate from partisan online posts and speculative analyses, not from forensic or official findings.

claim: "One third of our age group (Millennials) have moved back in with their parents."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and unsupported as stated. Statistics about Millennials living with parents vary by country, exact age range, and year; some surveys report around one‑third of certain young-adult cohorts live with parents, but that is not equivalent to ‘moved back in’ for one third of all Millennials and depends on timeframe (e.g., post‑recession or COVID spikes). Without a specified population and period, the blanket statement is not reliably true.

claim: State Rep. Elena Parent "supported Governor Nathan Deal’s plan to slash the HOPE scholarship."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that State Rep. Elena Parent publicly endorsed or voted to back Governor Nathan Deal’s proposal to slash the HOPE scholarship. Parent is a Democratic legislator known for supporting education funding, and available public records and statements do not show she supported Deal’s cuts. The claim appears to misattribute support to her without documented backing.

claim: Obama "voted against funding our troops."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Barack Obama did not categorically vote against funding U.S. troops; as a senator he supported many appropriations for military pay and veterans and sometimes voted for supplemental funding while opposing specific war-policy tied bills or funding packages he felt lacked conditions or oversight. Without a specific bill or vote identified, the blanket statement that he "voted against funding our troops" is inaccurate.

claim: Says Thom Tillis "refuses to say what we should do to combat ISIS."
rationale: I cannot verify a specific, documented instance where Sen. Thom Tillis categorically 'refused to say what we should do to combat ISIS.' The claim is vague about timing and context; politicians often decline to give operational military details, so without a cited occurrence this assertion is unverified and likely misleading. Given the lack of corroborating evidence, I rate it as false pending a precise citation.

claim: "There is no reason to allocate 60 percent of bridge space to satisfy two percent of all travelers."
rationale: The statement is a normative opinion presented as a universal fact and cannot be verified without context. Whether dedicating 60% of bridge width to modes used by 2% of travelers is justified depends on measurable factors (safety, legal obligations, modal priority, congestion management, equity, environmental goals) and local data, so the blanket assertion is not factually supportable.

claim: Says the T.R.U.M.P. Act, which would force presidential candidates to release their tax returns to run in North Carolina, "has a lot of support – by a majority of North Carolinians and members of both parties."
rationale: National polls show broad support for requiring presidential candidates to release tax returns, but there is no clear, consistent evidence that a majority of North Carolinians — and specifically a majority of members of both parties — back this particular T.R.U.M.P. Act. Republican voters in most surveys are substantially less likely than Democrats to support such a mandate, so the claim overstates a bipartisan majority without citing a specific recent state-level poll.

claim: "More than one in five of veterans aged 20 to 24 can’t find a job to support their family or to ease the transition to civilian life."
rationale: The claim asserts over 20% of veterans aged 20–24 “can’t find a job,” but official labor statistics and major surveys do not support a >20% unemployment or job‑seekers rate for that veteran age group in recent years. Labor data (BLS) report veteran unemployment rates by age that have been well below one-in-five in typical recent periods, and the claim’s wording (“can’t find a job to support their family or to ease the transition”) is not a standard measured metric. Without a specific source/timeframe this statement overstates what national data show.

claim: "It costs a hell of a lot more money to put somebody in jail than send them to the University of Virginia."
rationale: Broadly true: typical U.S. estimates show the annual cost to incarcerate one person is often tens of thousands of dollars (commonly $30k–$60k or more), while sending an in-state student to a public university like the University of Virginia (tuition, fees and often room/board) is generally lower on an annual basis. Thus it is reasonable to say incarceration frequently costs substantially more than sending someone to UVA, though exact figures vary by jurisdiction and residency status.

claim: Says Rick Scott’s "hospital company stole millions, defrauding the military’s health care program."
rationale: The hospital company Rick Scott led (Columbia/HCA) was the subject of major federal investigations in the late 1990s and the company paid roughly $1.7 billion to settle claims of Medicare/Medicaid and other federal billing fraud. However, there is no clear evidence that Scott personally ‘stole’ millions or that the settlement specifically alleged targeted theft of the military’s health care program (TRICARE); Scott was not criminally charged. The claim therefore overstates and misattributes the documented corporate misconduct.

claim: Pennsylvania officials are "attempting to silence voters" by sending them letters that say they’ve been exposed to COVID-19 and "must remain quarantined and not vote in person on Election Day."
rationale: There is no evidence of a coordinated effort by Pennsylvania officials to ‘silence voters’ by sending quarantine letters to prevent in‑person voting. The letters described are routine public‑health quarantine notifications advising exposed people to isolate to prevent disease spread; Pennsylvania also provides alternatives such as absentee/mail‑in ballots and curbside voting so exposed or quarantined voters can still cast ballots. Characterizing public‑health isolation orders as an intentional voter‑suppression scheme is unsupported by available facts.

claim: Kasim Reed has kept every promise he made as a candidate.
rationale: An absolute claim that any politician "kept every promise" is implausible and there is no evidence that Kasim Reed fulfilled every pledge he made. Reporting and post‑tenure analysis described a mix of fulfilled, partially fulfilled, and unfulfilled pledges during his time in office, along with controversies and ethics questions that complicate claims of blanket success. Thus the universal statement is false.

claim: Says Florida Gov. Rick Scott "subtracted $1.3 billion from public schools."
rationale: The blanket claim that Gov. Rick Scott “subtracted $1.3 billion from public schools” is misleading. Over Scott’s terms (2011–2019) nominal K–12 appropriations in Florida did not fall by $1.3 billion overall; the $1.3 billion number reflects specific vetoes, transfers, or comparisons to higher proposed budgets or inflation/enrollment-adjusted baselines rather than an across-the-board cut to school funding. Presenting the raw figure without that context misstates what happened to total K–12 funding.

claim: Says when he was governor, "most of the Democrats" voted for his billion-dollar property-tax cuts, but U.S. Senate rival Tammy Baldwin "voted against it."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate as presented. Property-tax changes while Scott Walker was governor were enacted by the Wisconsin Legislature, and Tammy Baldwin was serving in the U.S. House (and later the U.S. Senate) during Walker’s governorship, so she did not cast a vote in the state legislature on those bills. The claim also asserts that “most of the Democrats” supported the cuts; legislative roll-call records show Democratic support varied by measure and time, so that blanket claim is unsupported.

claim: Says Joe Biden tweeted, "the way white people talk leaving minorities confused."
rationale: No record exists of Joe Biden posting that exact phrase from his verified Twitter/X account, and major news outlets and fact-checkers have not reported such a tweet. The wording is inconsistent with Biden's typical public statements and is likely a fabrication, misattribution, or from a parody account or altered screenshot.

claim: "In France, they have a (surveillance) program a thousandfold more invasive" than the United States.
rationale: The claim is a vague, hyperbolic comparison with no measurable metric and no evidence that any French surveillance program is 1,000 times more invasive than U.S. programs. Both countries maintain extensive intelligence and surveillance capabilities (e.g., U.S. bulk-collection programs and French post-2015 laws authorizing bulk data access), but independent assessments and laws do not support a precise multiplicative factor of 1,000. Without a defined metric (volume of data, scope of targets, legal powers, etc.) the assertion is unsupported and implausible.

claim: Says "Scott Walker says he would ban stem cell research"
rationale: There is no clear record of Scott Walker explicitly saying he would ban all stem cell research. His public statements and campaign positions typically distinguished between embryonic/fetal tissue research (which he opposed or favored limits on) and adult stem cell research (which he supported), and opponents sometimes misstated his positions. Absent a direct, verifiable quote pledging a blanket ban, the claim is inaccurate.

claim: "More than 20 million people are at risk of dying from starvation within 6 months in 4 nations."
rationale: This claim overstates and mischaracterizes widely reported UN warnings. UN agencies have warned that more than 20 million people across four crisis areas (commonly cited as Yemen, South Sudan, Somalia and northeastern Nigeria) faced the risk of famine without urgent aid, but official language was typically 'at risk of famine' or 'one step away from famine' and not uniformly 'at risk of dying from starvation within 6 months' for entire nations. The claim's precise timeframe and wording therefore mislead about what the sources stated.

claim: "I've always known this is a real, this is a pandemic. I've felt it was a pandemic long before it was called a pandemic."
rationale: The statement asserts a subjective, internal belief (that the speaker felt it was a pandemic before it was called one). Such personal mental-state claims cannot be independently verified without contemporaneous, dated evidence (e.g., social posts, emails, or public statements made before the official declaration). Absent that corroboration, the claim cannot be treated as a proven fact.

claim: Says "76 percent of all voters in the United States say they want Johnson-Weld, by name, in the presidential debates."
rationale: No reputable national poll from the 2016 cycle or afterward supports that 76% of all U.S. voters specifically named the Johnson–Weld ticket as wanting them in presidential debates. Most national polls showed single-digit to low-double-digit support for third-party candidates and much lower explicit demand to include that ticket by name; debate inclusion rules also depended on sustained ~15% polling. The claim appears to greatly overstate or misrepresent available polling evidence.

claim: "Last week Joe Biden flashed the ‘white power’ sign. President Trump condemned white supremacists yesterday. Why hasn't Joe Biden?"
rationale: The claim mixes unverified timing and an ambiguous hand gesture. There is no credible evidence that Joe Biden intentionally flashed a recognized “white power” sign last week; the circular “OK” or similar hand gestures are often misinterpreted and require video/context to determine intent. Also, Biden has publicly condemned white supremacy on multiple occasions, and the assertion that Trump condemned white supremacists “yesterday” cannot be verified without a specific date.

claim: "Wages adjusted for inflation haven’t risen since the turn of the last century."
rationale: The claim is not accurate as a blanket statement: common inflation-adjusted wage series (for example median usual weekly earnings and other BLS/Census measures) show modest real gains since around 2000, though growth has been slow and uneven and included periods of stagnation and decline (notably around the Great Recession and COVID). Saying wages "haven’t risen" ignores these measured increases and depends heavily on which wage measure, population, and exact start/end dates are used.

claim: Says Melania Trump hired exorcist to "cleanse White House of Obama demons."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Melania Trump formally hired an exorcist to ‘cleanse the White House of Obama demons.’ The story originated in tabloids and anonymous gossip rather than reputable reporting, and major fact-checkers and news organizations found the claim unsubstantiated. While Melania is Catholic and has had religious contacts, those documented interactions do not corroborate an exorcism-for-Obama-demons narrative.

claim: The Baucus health care bill "would drastically restrict the use of flexible spending accounts (FSAs) in order to help pay for health care reform."
rationale: The Baucus (2009) health‑care proposal included specific limits on tax‑favored flexible spending accounts as part of its revenue offsets — notably a proposal to cap annual salary‑reduction FSA contributions (reported at $2,500). That provision was explicitly intended to help pay for the reform, so saying the bill would restrict FSAs to help pay for reform is accurate.

claim: "We had the highest number of (military) sexual assaults ever reported in the last year" and "we had the lowest conviction rate and the lowest prosecution rate."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it does not specify which country's or service's military, nor the exact year or whether “reported” refers to reports filed or estimated incidents. Different militaries and different years show varying trends in reports, prosecutions, and convictions, so a blanket statement cannot be confirmed. Without a specific jurisdiction and time period and comparison baseline, the assertion is unreliable.

claim: "We enacted the biggest tax cuts and reforms in American history."
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim but hinges on how “biggest” is measured. The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act was a large tax overhaul and included the largest corporate rate reduction in U.S. history, but other reforms (notably the 1981 Reagan cuts and some early‑2000s changes) were larger by other common measures such as tax cuts relative to GDP or long‑term revenue impact. Because the claim makes an unqualified, all‑encompassing assertion, it is misleading.

claim: There were no American flags at the first Democratic presidential debate.
rationale: The claim is ambiguous about which "first Democratic presidential debate" is meant, and when taken to mean the opening debate of the 2020 Democratic primary (June 2019) it is false. Televised U.S. presidential debates routinely include American flags in the stage or venue, and available broadcast photos and footage of that opening debate show at least one U.S. flag present. Given the lack of a clear time reference and the normal presence of flags at such events, the blanket claim that there were no American flags is incorrect.

claim: "Here's the fact: The No. 1 source of income into Mexico are Mexicans working here and sending the money back."
rationale: This is false as stated. While remittances from Mexicans working abroad (notably in the U.S.) are a large and growing source of foreign currency for Mexico, the largest national sources of income are exports (manufactured goods and oil) and foreign investment, which total far more than remittances. Remittances are important for many households and regions but are not the number-one source of income for the country as a whole.

claim: "Here, we have Thanksgiving, we have Christmas, we have the 4th of July. Every year in Iran, they celebrate Death to America day."
rationale: This claim is misleading. Iran does have annual state-organized events (notably Quds Day and the November 4 anniversary of the 1979 embassy takeover) where anti‑American slogans such as “Death to America” are sometimes chanted, but there is no formal national holiday called “Death to America Day” equivalent to Thanksgiving/Christmas/Independence Day nor is it a universal celebration by the population.

claim: "39% of All California Students are illegals."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that 39% of all California students are undocumented. U.S. Census/ACS estimates and state education data indicate the undocumented share of California’s total population is under 10%, and the portion of K–12 or college students who are undocumented is a much smaller fraction, far below 39%. The claim appears to conflate or misstate categories and lacks supporting data.

claim: Says Patrick Morrisey undertook "efforts to put educators in jail."
rationale: The claim overstates the record. While West Virginia Attorney General Patrick Morrisey publicly said public-employee strikes were illegal and supported enforcement measures during the 2018 teachers’ walkout (and warned of possible penalties), there is no public record that he pursued or carried out criminal prosecutions to put educators in jail. The available evidence shows rhetoric and legal warnings rather than actual efforts to incarcerate teachers.

claim: "Debt has almost doubled in Austin under Gov. Perry."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and unsupported: there is no clear evidence that the City of Austin’s debt 'almost doubled' specifically during Rick Perry’s years as governor. Governors do not set municipal budgets, and available public reporting that examined debt increases under Perry concerned state-level debt, not Austin city indebtedness. Without a precise timeframe and debt measure, the statement is misleading and not substantiated.

claim: "We have counties where there have been one arrest under the SAFE Act. It indicates there's not a whole lot of interest in enforcing this in our upstate counties."
rationale: The claim mixes an unverifiable specific factual assertion (that some counties had exactly one SAFE Act arrest) with an interpretive conclusion about enforcement interest. Without named counties, dates, or comprehensive arrest/prosecution data, the factual part can't be confirmed and the inference is not justified—low arrest counts can reflect low incidence, differing charging practices, or reporting definitions rather than lack of enforcement. Therefore the overall claim is not supported as stated.

claim: Says Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker doesn't make his calendar public -- "he's on our dime and we don't know where he is."
rationale: The claim that Gov. Scott Walker “doesn't make his calendar public” is inaccurate. During his tenure the governor’s office routinely released official schedules, travel logs and event listings, and his administration responded to public records requests for calendar entries, even if not every internal detail was published in real time. Saying taxpayers had no access to his whereabouts overstates the situation.

claim: "Hidden in the CARES Act was an obscure $135 billion tax break for 43,000 millionaires."
rationale: This is misleading. The CARES Act did change tax rules (notably allowing net operating loss carrybacks and other business-related changes) that analysts estimated could reduce revenue on the order of roughly $100–150 billion over several years, but that is an aggregate projection—not a discrete, obscure $135 billion tax break narrowly targeted at 43,000 millionaires. The provisions benefited corporations, pass-through businesses and a range of taxpayers, and the counts and dollar totals cited depend on modeling assumptions and definitions of “millionaire.”

claim: Says the New York bike path assault "was the ninth vehicle assault used by ISIS."
rationale: This specific numeric claim is not supported by authoritative counts. While ISIS has claimed or inspired multiple vehicle-ramming attacks, media and government reporting did not establish the New York bike path attack as definitively the "ninth" such ISIS attack — counts vary depending on which incidents are included and whether ISIS actually directed them. Because the tally depends on inconsistent inclusion criteria, the precise ordinal "ninth" is unreliable.

claim: Democrats plan to keep student loan interest rates low  "by raising taxes on small businesses, very small businesses … the kinds of small businesses that give jobs to graduates."
rationale: There is no broad Democratic plan or platform to specifically keep student loan interest rates low by raising taxes on small or very small businesses. Democratic tax proposals historically target corporations, high-income individuals, or wealthy households rather than imposing broad new taxes on small employers; claims that Democrats plan to fund student-loan interest relief by taxing the kinds of small businesses that hire graduates are a partisan mischaracterization or lack evidence. The statement appears to conflate general calls for revenue with a targeted small-business tax policy that Democrats have not advanced.

claim: "We’ve been able to create about 60,000 net new jobs" in Virginia since February.
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it omits the year and source for the baseline and end dates; official job counts are published monthly by the Virginia Employment Commission and BLS and vary by survey and seasonal adjustment. Without a specific timeframe and source (payroll vs household survey), the 60,000 figure is unsubstantiated and thus treated as false for lack of verifiable evidence.

claim: The Central Falls fire department is "one of the lowest, if not the lowest, paid fire departments in the state and entire region."
rationale: I cannot confirm the absolute claim that Central Falls is among or at the very bottom of firefighter pay in the state and entire region. Municipal firefighter pay rankings require current, comprehensive salary and total-compensation data (base pay, overtime, benefits) across jurisdictions; without that data the statement is unverified and overgeneralizes. While Central Falls has been reported to have relatively low municipal pay historically, that does not prove it is the lowest in the state/region.

claim: Georgia has had the nation’s busiest Court of Appeals for a decade or more.
rationale: Publicly reported caseload statistics and contemporary news coverage have repeatedly identified the Georgia Court of Appeals as the busiest intermediate appellate court in the United States for more than a decade, with consistently high filings and dispositions relative to other state appellate courts. That characterization has been used in multiple annual caseload comparisons.,

claim: "Since 1995, the top 400 wealthiest families have seen their incomes go up 400 percent and their tax rates go down 40 percent."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and not reliably supported by public data as stated. Analyses of the Forbes 400 and tax records show very large gains for the richest households since the mid‑1990s and declines in some measures of effective federal tax rates, but the exact figures (“incomes up 400 percent” and “tax rates down 40 percent”) depend heavily on definitions, time windows, and whether changes are measured in percent versus percentage points and are not a definitive, universally accepted statistic. Fact‑checking organizations have found the broad trend (wealthy gains and lower taxes) but flagged this precise formulation as misleading without context and sourcing.

claim: Says he "will protect your guaranteed benefits" in Medicare while "Mitt Romney would take away Medicare as guaranteed benefits."
rationale: Romney's 2012 plan proposed replacing traditional Medicare for future beneficiaries with a premium‑support (voucher‑style) system rather than a defined, guaranteed benefit. While Romney pledged not to change benefits for current retirees or those near retirement, his policy would remove Medicare's guaranteed‑benefit structure for future enrollees, so the claim that he would end guaranteed benefits is substantially accurate.

claim: Says Chris Christie was "behind" in the polls against Jon Corzine during the 2009 governor's race.
rationale: Multiple public polls in mid- to late-2009 showed Jon Corzine ahead of Chris Christie at various points in the gubernatorial campaign, though Christie closed the gap and overtook Corzine by the fall and ultimately won the election. So saying Christie was "behind" in the polls during the 2009 race is accurate for portions of the campaign but not true for the entire period.

claim: Says Betsy DeVos is the "most unpopular person in our government."
rationale: The statement is a subjective opinion rather than an objectively verifiable fact. While Betsy DeVos registered very low approval ratings and significant controversy during her tenure as Education Secretary, there is no objective, time-invariant measure showing she was unequivocally "the most unpopular person in our government" across all officials and time periods. Thus the claim cannot be confirmed as a factual assertion.

claim: Under the new health care law, the elderly will be denied care when they have "passed the age limit for treatment."
rationale: There is no provision in the U.S. Affordable Care Act or related federal reforms that institutes a blanket "age limit for treatment" which causes the elderly to be denied care. The ACA expanded coverage, banned lifetime caps, and did not create government panels that automatically refuse care to people past a certain age; claims about "age limits" echo debunked "death panel" rhetoric. While cost-effectiveness discussions and advisory bodies exist, they do not authorize automatic denials based solely on age.

claim: Says a "Clorox bottle claimed it could kill (the 2019 coronavirus)... before it was developed."
rationale: This is false. Clorox labels that say they kill 'coronavirus' have historically referred to the coronavirus family or to endemic human coronaviruses (common cold strains) tested in the lab, not specifically to the novel SARS‑CoV‑2 identified in late 2019; manufacturers and regulators clarified and updated claims about SARS‑CoV‑2 in 2020. The claim misinterprets the generic use of 'coronavirus' on product labeling as a prediction about a specific future virus.

claim: "New York, for all of their complaining, Gov. Cuomo's complaining, has only had a 1.5% decrease in revenue" due to the coronavirus pandemic.
rationale: This is incorrect — New York experienced revenue declines and multi‑billion dollar budget shortfalls in 2020–2021 due to the COVID‑19 pandemic, far larger than a 1.5% drop. Although later federal relief and accounting measures mitigated some losses, initial year‑over‑year tax receipts and projected gaps were several percent (and in dollar terms billions), not a mere 1.5%.

claim: "Amazon accepts Dogecoin."
rationale: Amazon does not directly accept Dogecoin as a payment method on its website or in its checkout. Reports of Dogecoin acceptance stem from rumors or from third‑party services that let people buy Amazon gift cards with crypto, not from an official Amazon payment integration.

claim: Says the Austin City Council "may give $4 million a year to subsidize a race track."
rationale: I could not find authoritative evidence that the Austin City Council has approved or officially proposed an ongoing $4 million per year payment specifically to subsidize a race track. Public records and reporting more commonly describe one-time incentives, tax rebates, or different funding amounts for events or facilities, so the claim as stated is not supported. It may conflate proposals, other jurisdictions, or different sums/timing.

claim: Dave Aronberg's career legal experience is "less than two years as Asst. AG/private attorney."
rationale: This claim is incorrect. Public biographical information shows Dave Aronberg held multiple years of legal positions (including service as an assistant/state prosecutor and work in private practice and as an Assistant Attorney General or in attorney general office roles) rather than only "less than two years." His legal career spans several years prior to and alongside his public service, so the characterization as under two years is misleading.

claim: "Dandelion root is able to kill 98% of cancer cells within 48 hours."
rationale: The claim overgeneralizes and misrepresents the evidence. While some laboratory (in vitro) studies have reported that certain dandelion root extracts can induce death in specific cancer cell lines within ~48 hours, those results are limited to controlled cell-culture conditions and specific concentrations and do not demonstrate that dandelion root kills 98% of cancer cells in humans. There are no robust clinical trials showing this effect in patients, so the blanket statement is false.

claim: Small businesses "create 70 percent of the jobs in America."
rationale: The statement as absolute is incorrect. Small businesses do not account for 70% of all jobs in the U.S.; they employ roughly half of the private‑sector workforce, though they do account for a large share of net new jobs in some periods. The 70% figure is a mischaracterization or a time- and definition‑dependent statistic often taken out of context.

claim: Says a video shows a "gay party in Italy few weeks before COVID-19."
rationale: The claim makes a specific assertion about the video's content, location and timing but provides no verifiable source or metadata. I cannot confirm the video's date or that it was filmed in Italy just weeks before COVID-19, and many similar clips were previously misattributed or reposted with false timestamps. Without original video files, geolocation or corroborating reporting, the claim is not supported and is treated as false.

claim: Says an NBC producer at the Olympics was caught on a hot mic saying "60% of people in this stadium will be dead within 10 days."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reputable news reporting that an NBC producer was caught on a hot mic saying “60% of people in this stadium will be dead within 10 days.” Major outlets and fact-checking organizations investigated similar viral clips and found them unverified or manipulated, and NBC has denied such an on-air remark. The claim appears to originate from social-media posts that misattribute or edit audio for sensational effect.

claim: Says that in Curry County, "if you make a 911 call you’re likely to wait for an hour for a response."
rationale: The claim is an unsupported generalization: emergency response times vary by county, call priority, location within the county, and time of day, and I’m not aware of authoritative data showing that most 911 callers in any Curry County routinely wait an hour. While rural areas and under-resourced jurisdictions can experience long delays for some calls, standard EMS/police dispatch targets are typically much shorter and available reporting does not substantiate a blanket “likely to wait an hour” statement for Curry County. Without a specific source, timeframe, and definition of “likely,” the claim overstates the situation.

claim: "Pfizer vaccine now completely worthless in Israel as >80% of all COVID-19 patients were previously vaccinated."
rationale: The claim is false because a high proportion of COVID-19 cases being vaccinated (in some Israeli datasets at certain times) does not mean the Pfizer vaccine is "completely worthless." Israel had very high vaccination coverage and later observed waning protection against infection and more vaccinated people among mild cases; however vaccines continued to provide substantial protection against hospitalization and death, and boosters restored much of the lost protection. The raw >80% figure, if reported, is likely from a period or subgroup and is misleading without denominators, timing, age, and booster-status.

claim: Says Sen. Tim Kaine "approves of and even applauds his son's participation in a known terrorist organization, #Antifa."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Sen. Tim Kaine has approved of or applauded his son's participation in “Antifa,” and Kaine has publicly condemned political violence. Reports identify Antifa as a decentralized protest movement rather than a formal, single organization, and no reliable sources show Kaine endorsing his son’s involvement in violent extremism.

claim: "In Florida felonies can be things like buying weed, tampering with an odometer or disturbing a lobster trap. So basically spring break."
rationale: The claim that those acts can be felonies in Florida is essentially correct: marijuana transactions involving amounts above statutory thresholds or with intent to sell are felonies, odometer tampering to defraud is a felony under Florida law, and knowingly damaging or interfering with commercial lobster/fishing gear can be prosecuted as a serious offense. Whether a particular incident is charged as a felony depends on quantity, intent, damage, and other circumstances, so not every instance (e.g., a small purchase of weed) would automatically be a felony.

claim: Says New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg says "we can only have three bullets" and "the NRA wants firearms with nukes on them."
rationale: There is no credible record or reputable reporting showing Mayor Michael Bloomberg made the quoted statements. The phrases are sensational and inconsistent with Bloomberg’s documented public remarks on gun control; they appear to be misattribution, satire, or a fabricated quote.

claim: Says James Langevin voted to spend "$3 billion for a jet engine no one wants."
rationale: There is no clear record that Rep. James Langevin cast a discrete, named vote to spend exactly "$3 billion for a jet engine no one wants." Members routinely vote for broad defense appropriations that include many line items, and the wording "no one wants" is subjective and not a factual description of a specific congressional authorization. Without a specific bill, engine program, or roll‑call, the claim is misleading.

claim: "When a bill is sent to the governor’s office, there is no option for changing it. You sign it or you don’t sign it. While there was lots of conversation, there was really no opportunity for any sort of amending."
rationale: The claim is overly broad and therefore incorrect: while a governor (or the president) typically can sign, veto, or allow a bill to become law without signature, many executives also have tools to modify bills (for example line-item vetoes for appropriation items or amendatory/conditional veto powers in some states). Additionally, legislatures can respond to vetoes or conditional vetoes by amending and repassing bills or overriding vetoes. Thus there is sometimes a formal or practical opportunity to alter a bill after it reaches the governor, depending on jurisdiction.

claim: "The Nevada Gaming Commission did not find Trump ‘trustworthy’ enough for a gaming license."
rationale: The Nevada Gaming Control Board recommended denying former President Trump a gaming license, finding concerns about his honesty, integrity and suitability; the Nevada Gaming Commission subsequently voted to deny his application. Both bodies cited his conduct and legal issues as reasons that he did not meet the character standards required for licensure, which is commonly summarized as being not sufficiently “trustworthy.”

claim: Each Georgia taxpayer would have to send $5,000 to the treasury to cover the state’s debt.
rationale: The claim is presented as an absolute fact but depends on which liabilities are counted (direct bonded debt vs. total obligations including pensions) and which population is counted as “taxpayers” (all residents, tax filers, or returns). Using commonly reported figures for Georgia’s outstanding state debt (tens of billions) and the millions of Georgia taxpayers, no single authoritative, up-to-date source supports the exact $5,000 per-taxpayer number as a definitive figure. Therefore the blanket statement is misleading and likely inaccurate without context or a date.

claim: If you ask Amazon’s Alexa about the origin of the coronavirus pandemic, it says "the government planned" it.
rationale: False. Multiple fact-checks and Amazon's statements showed viral clips claiming Alexa said the coronavirus was "planned by the government" were misleading or edited; Alexa does not have a single canned answer asserting a government-planned pandemic. Alexa pulls answers from internet sources and phrasing can produce problematic or conspiracy-laden snippets if those appear online, but that is not the same as Alexa itself claiming the government planned the pandemic.

claim: Says a deer became "riddled with tumors from eating plants sprayed with Monsanto’s Roundup."
rationale: The claim is an anecdote asserting causation without supporting evidence. Regulatory bodies and peer‑reviewed literature have not documented a confirmed case linking Roundup (glyphosate) exposure to tumors in a specific deer, and proving causation would require necropsy, toxicology and exposure data that are not provided. Without such evidence the assertion is unsupported.

claim: Social Security is a "Ponzi scheme."
rationale: Calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" is inaccurate: Social Security is a statutory, government-run social insurance program funded by payroll taxes with explicit legal entitlements and a trust fund invested in Treasury securities, not a secretive fraud designed to enrich operators. Although it uses current workers' taxes to pay current beneficiaries (a pay-as-you-go element) and faces long-term financing challenges, those features do not meet the defining characteristics of a Ponzi scheme such as deception, promises of high returns, and private operator fraud.

claim: "In the past year, Floridians, not government, created almost 135,000 new private sector jobs. We netted more than 120,000 total jobs in the first 11 months of 2011; the third most of any state in the nation."
rationale: I could not confirm the precise figures as stated. While Florida did gain jobs in 2011, the exact numbers and the attribution ("Floridians, not government" creating almost 135,000 private-sector jobs and netting more than 120,000 total jobs in the first 11 months of 2011) do not match readily verifiable BLS state employment series without additional clarification of definitions and time windows. The statement appears to conflate different series and lacks a clear, checkable timeframe.

claim: Suggests Amber Heard snorted cocaine while on the stand in court.
rationale: There is no credible, contemporaneous reporting or verified video evidence from the Depp–Heard trial showing anyone explicitly suggesting Amber Heard snorted cocaine while she was on the witness stand. While attorneys and media discussed past substance use and there were social‑media rumors about her comportment, that does not amount to a documented claim that someone alleged she snorted cocaine during testimony. Given the absence of reliable sources making that specific allegation, the claim is not supported.

claim: Says more Republicans than Democrats voted for the Wall Street bailouts.
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization and not reliably true. Votes on the 2008–2009 financial rescue measures (e.g., EESA/TARP) were bipartisan and the party-level counts differed by chamber and by specific roll call — some key Senate votes had majorities from both parties, and House votes split differently — so you cannot truthfully say that more Republicans than Democrats overall voted for 'the bailouts' without specifying which vote. Because the statement lacks that context and is contradicted by the mixed roll-call patterns, it is false as a blanket claim.

claim: About 800 people refused to get a drug screening because they are "out there on drugs."
rationale: The claim provides a specific count without any context (time, place, or source) and I could not corroborate a verified report stating that "about 800" people refused drug screening for being "out there on drugs." Numeric allegations require named authorities or documented reporting; absent that, the statement is unverified and likely misleading. Because the claim lacks sourcing and context, it cannot be treated as factual.

claim: "Joe Biden just confirmed that he is running for president in 2020 and it has America applauding!"
rationale: The claim mixes a factual element with misleading timing and an overgeneralization. Joe Biden announced his 2020 presidential campaign on April 25, 2019 (so he did run in 2020), but saying he 'just confirmed' that he is running for 2020 is time-misleading and the assertion that 'it has America applauding' is an exaggerated, subjective generalization — reactions were mixed. As presented, the statement is therefore false.

claim: Arnold Schwarzenegger slept on the ground in front of a bronze statue of himself because he had been turned away from a hotel.
rationale: This specific story is not supported by reliable reports and is implausible on its face: bronze statues of Schwarzenegger were erected after he became famous, so sleeping in front of his own statue because a hotel turned him away would require the hotel to refuse him when he was already a celebrated figure—an unlikely scenario that lacks corroboration. Schwarzenegger has told truthful anecdotes about hardship early in his career (e.g., sleeping in his car or living modestly), but there are no verifiable sources confirming the claim as stated. Therefore the precise claim is assessed as false or a conflation of unrelated anecdotes.

claim: Says "John James supported Betsy DeVos’ agenda to cut public school funding and put it into wealthy private schools instead."
rationale: John James has publicly supported school-choice policies (vouchers, tax-credit scholarships, and expanded charter options) that align with Betsy DeVos’s agenda and that critics say divert public education dollars to private schools. While James framed these policies as increasing parental choice and opportunity, the practical effect of such policies is widely reported to reduce funding for traditional public schools and can benefit private-school attendees. The claim’s characterization that funds go to “wealthy” private schools is more interpretive and depends on specifics of program design and recipients.

claim: Says Clint Eastwood is dead.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Clint Eastwood has died; as of the last widely available updates (through mid‑2024) he was alive and the death of a major public figure would be broadly reported by reputable news outlets. Absent any credible, recent reporting, the claim that he is dead is incorrect.

claim: Because of union rules, cooks helpers moved into DMV jobs they were not trained for
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated as written and presented as a universal cause-effect rule. While unions often enforce seniority, bumping and reassignments, they generally do not and cannot legally place unqualified workers into positions that require specific civil-service qualifications or licensing such as many DMV roles. Without jurisdiction, union name, or evidence of a specific instance, the blanket causal statement is unsupported.

claim: A person’s immune system "tanks" after their second COVID-19 vaccine dose.
rationale: Clinical trial and real-world data show COVID-19 vaccines — including the second dose in a primary mRNA series — boost antibody levels and strengthen adaptive immunity rather than causing a collapse of the immune system. Typical post-vaccine effects (fatigue, fever) are short-lived signs of immune activation; occasional transient changes in some blood cell counts have been reported but do not represent sustained immune suppression. The claim that the immune system “tanks” after the second dose is a misunderstanding or misrepresentation of these temporary responses.

claim: "We have more coal reserves in the United States than they have oil reserves in Saudi Arabia."
rationale: Measured on commonly used metrics (recoverable coal in the U.S. vs proven crude oil in Saudi Arabia) the U.S. has substantially more total energy in its coal reserves than the energy contained in Saudi Arabia’s oil reserves. U.S. recoverable coal is on the order of a few hundred billion tons while Saudi proven oil is a few hundred billion barrels; when converted to common energy units the coal exceeds the oil by a significant margin.

claim: Says "Morgan Carroll opposed requiring convicted sex offenders to register their online profiles, making it harder to track online sex offenders and child predators."
rationale: I find no clear, corroborated evidence that Morgan Carroll broadly opposed a requirement that convicted sex offenders register 'online profiles.' Politicians sometimes vote against or critique specific bills on constitutional, privacy, or drafting grounds without opposing the underlying goal of tracking offenders; the claim appears to conflate or misstate that nuance and adds an unsupported causal assertion that her stance 'made it harder' to track offenders.

claim: "Biden’s Air Force One is not the same as Trump’s Air Force One," which indicates Biden is not the real president.
rationale: The statement is false because the phrase “Air Force One” is a call sign used for any Air Force aircraft when the president is aboard; different administrations may use different specific airframes, tail numbers, or liveries, but that does not bear on who is president. Presidential legitimacy is determined by election results and inauguration procedures, not which particular aircraft is used.

claim: "The current (agriculture) commissioner allowed tainted beef to be sent to school cafeterias."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated as written because it names no specific agriculture commissioner, jurisdiction, time, or evidence. I am not aware of credible reports or official findings that any current agriculture commissioner knowingly authorized sending tainted beef to school cafeterias, and such actions would normally trigger inspections, recalls, and news coverage. Without specific, verifiable facts this allegation cannot be supported.

claim: "Speaker Gingrich for 20 years supported a federal individual mandate" for health insurance.
rationale: Newt Gingrich publicly endorsed the idea of an individual requirement to obtain health insurance in conservative reform proposals beginning in the early 1990s and repeatedly described himself as having supported such a mandate for about two decades. Although he later opposed the specific ObamaCare mandate, historical policy proposals and his own statements show long-standing support for an individual mandate concept at the federal policy level.

claim: "We’ve been down this road before—blanket protectionism is a big part of why America had a Great Depression."
rationale: Enacting high tariffs like the 1930 Smoot–Hawley Act and the resulting retaliatory barriers sharply reduced international trade and are widely judged by economic historians to have worsened and prolonged the early 1930s contraction. While protectionism was not the sole cause (bank failures, monetary policy, and debt/deflation dynamics were also central), most scholars treat tariffs as a significant exacerbating factor in the Great Depression.

claim: After Fahrenheit 9/11 came out, "Bush's approval rating never was better, it only got worse."
rationale: The claim asserts Bush's approval monotonically declined after Fahrenheit 9/11's June 2004 release. Polls show approval fluctuated after June 2004 (including a post‑election uptick around November 2004) rather than a continuous one‑directional fall; later years did see larger declines, but the trajectory was not strictly "only worse" from the film's release onward. The statement also implies a direct causal link to the film, which is not supported by the poll record alone.

claim: The DeWine campaign is "receiving money from so many more people. (Cordray's) money is coming almost exclusively from the party, labor unions, and special counsel that he has given business to."
rationale: This is an overstatement. Public campaign‑finance reports and news coverage from the Ohio governor's race show both campaigns received a mix of funding: Cordray did receive transfers and support from the Democratic Party and labor groups, but he also raised substantial individual donations and outside contributions. Likewise, DeWine’s receipts included party and PAC support as well as individual donors, so it is incorrect to say Cordray’s money came "almost exclusively" from party, unions, and vendors or that DeWine’s funds came from "so many more people" without qualification.

claim: The Orlando shooter used "a weapon of war."
rationale: The Orlando (Pulse nightclub, 2016) shooter used commercially sold semi‑automatic firearms — an AR‑style rifle and a handgun — not military‑exclusive automatic weapons. Law enforcement and media reports described the weapons as civilian semi‑automatic models, so calling them a literal “weapon of war” is inaccurate; the phrase is a rhetorical characterization rather than a technical description.

claim: In Wisconsin, Foxconn has "4,000 jobs, people making $53,000 a year."
rationale: Those figures are not an accurate statement of actual, current Wisconsin employment. The $53,000 figure was the average annual wage Foxconn cited in its original 2017 proposal and the 4,000 number does not match real, persistent Foxconn headcounts (the project was scaled back and permanent employment has been far lower, with many jobs temporary or subcontracted).

claim: President Obama has "the worst ratings of any president at the end of his first year."
rationale: False. Modern approval polling shows President Obama’s approval at roughly around 50% at the end of his first year, which is not the lowest on record; several presidents in the modern (Gallup-era) polling period recorded lower first-year job‑approval ratings. The claim ignores the distinction between presidents before reliable national polling and the specific poll/timing used for comparison.

claim: Between 2000 and 2006,  "health insurance company profits quadrupled."
rationale: The statement is too broad and not supported by available industry data: while U.S. private health insurers saw substantial profit growth in the early 2000s, aggregate profits did not uniformly quadruple between 2000 and 2006 across the industry. Whether profits appear to have increased by that magnitude depends on which firms are counted, whether one uses net income vs. pre-tax income, and whether one isolates particular years or one-time gains.

claim: "The Parole Board operates with Mark Herring’s advice and consent."
rationale: The constitutional phrase “advice and consent” refers to a legislative confirmation role (e.g., a state senate), not the attorney general. Mark Herring served as Virginia’s attorney general and did not have authority to give advice-and-consent for Parole Board appointments; those appointments are made by the governor and normally confirmed by the state senate. Thus the claim is incorrect.

claim: Says in the governor’s proposed budget "the use of that, what is called one-shots, is a 500 percent increase over the last Corzine budget."
rationale: I cannot verify the claim that the governor’s proposed budget raised “one-shots” by 500% over the last Corzine budget. Public budget documents and contemporary reporting distinguish and quantify nonrecurring revenues (one‑shots), and a fivefold increase would require precise line‑item comparisons that are not supported by widely reported figures. The statement appears to conflate categories and lacks the necessary specification of which revenues and which years are being compared.

claim: Georgia ranks 49th for women serving in elected state and federal offices.
rationale: The statement is presented as an absolute but omits the year and the exact metric (state legislature only, combined state and federal offices, or inclusion of statewide executive offices). Rankings for women’s representation vary by source and year; authoritative trackers (e.g., Center for American Women and Politics) do not consistently place Georgia at 49th across common measures, and Georgia’s rank has shifted over time. Without a specific year and metric the claim is misleading and likely inaccurate.

claim: Gov. Kitzhaber oversaw creation of the Oregon driver card law "behind closed doors without allowing any input from citizens who represent the public interest."
rationale: The Oregon driver card was created through the regular legislative process and signed by Gov. Kitzhaber after bills were debated in the legislature, which included committee hearings and opportunities for public testimony and stakeholder input. While some critics argued outreach was imperfect, the claim that it was developed entirely "behind closed doors without allowing any input from citizens" contradicts the recorded public legislative process and rulemaking avenues that were available.

claim: Republicans "created a trillion dollar prescription drug entitlement program without paying for it."
rationale: Republicans did sponsor and pass the 2003 law creating Medicare Part D, a federal prescription drug benefit, but characterizing it as an un‑paid 'trillion dollar' entitlement is misleading. CBO and other budget analysts estimated the program's initial 10‑year net cost in the hundreds of billions and the law included some offsets; whether cumulative or long‑run costs exceed $1 trillion depends on timeframe and assumptions. Therefore the blanket claim that Republicans created a trillion‑dollar entitlement without paying for it is not accurate as stated.

claim: Says "the mandate is 71 times that a child’s body will be injected with a disease" for immunizations.
rationale: The claim is false. Routine childhood vaccines do not 'inject a disease' into a child 71 times; vaccines are generally inactivated, subunit/toxoid, mRNA, or use attenuated organisms that rarely cause disease in healthy recipients, and there is no credible evidence for a ‘71×’ multiplier. The phrase appears to be a misstatement or misinterpretation of data rather than a factual description of vaccine effects.

claim: "Republicans want to restore #gunrights to felons"
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization. While many Republican lawmakers and officials have supported measures to restore firearm rights for some people with felony convictions (often conditionally, after sentence completion, expungement, or pardon), the party is not uniformly in favor—positions vary by individual, chamber, and state. Saying ‘Republicans want’ as a blanket statement is therefore inaccurate.

claim: Says New Jersey has "the highest unemployment rate in the region" and "stagnant job growth."
rationale: The statement is too general and not supported as an enduring fact: state unemployment rates and job growth vary by time period and by which neighboring states are included. New Jersey has not consistently had the highest unemployment in its region, and it has recorded periods of job growth as well as slower growth, so the blanket claim of "highest unemployment" and "stagnant job growth" is misleading without a specific timeframe and definition of the region.

claim: "Schools that are consistently implementing COVID-19 mitigation strategies remain among the safest places for our students."
rationale: Multiple public-health studies and guidance from agencies have found that schools using layered COVID-19 mitigation measures (masking, ventilation, testing, cohorting, vaccination) have substantially reduced in-school transmission and are generally among lower-risk settings for students compared with many community settings. The claim is contingent on consistent, proper implementation and can vary with community transmission levels and circulating variants.

claim: "There's only four senators senior to me ... there's still 44 older than me."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it lacks who is speaking and when. "Senior" can mean Senate seniority (tenure) while "older" refers to age, and confirming the exact counts (4 more senior, 44 older) requires the speaker's identity and date; without that context the numeric claim cannot be checked. Therefore I treat it as false/unsubstantiated.

claim: Georgia is the second-fastest growing state for international tourists.
rationale: The claim is unsupported as stated because it gives no year, metric (arrivals, spending), or whether it means the U.S. state Georgia or the country Georgia. Rankings for fastest-growing tourist destinations fluctuate by year and data source, and there is no consistent, widely cited evidence that either Georgia (U.S. state) or Georgia (country) is universally 'the second-fastest growing' for international tourists. Without a specified timeframe and metric, the statement is misleading and cannot be verified.

claim: With voting by mail, "you get thousands and thousands of people sitting in somebody's living room, signing ballots all over the place."
rationale: The statement alleges a widespread, routine practice of thousands of people signing ballots in private homes, but evidence shows only isolated instances of illegal ballot collection or tampering, not a systemic phenomenon. Most jurisdictions use safeguards (signature verification, chain-of-custody rules, drop boxes, criminal penalties) and post-election audits/studies find mail-ballot fraud to be extremely rare, so the broad claim is misleading.

claim: "This Is Real: Biden Waves To An Empty Field."
rationale: The claim that Biden was waving to an empty field is misleading/false: multiple fact-checks and event footage show people and supporters were present out of the camera’s frame, and Biden’s wave appears directed toward those off-screen. A single frame can make a scene look empty, but fuller video/context demonstrates he was not greeting an empty field.

claim: Says Vice President Kamala Harris called the unvaccinated "dirty Trump people."
rationale: There is no credible record, transcript, or reputable news report showing Vice President Kamala Harris used the phrase "dirty Trump people" to describe the unvaccinated. The quotation appears to be a fabricated or misattributed claim circulated on social media; Harris has urged vaccination and criticized misinformation but has not been documented using that insult.

claim: Says that Olive Garden is "funding" President Trump's 2020 re-election campaign.
rationale: U.S. law prohibits corporations from directly contributing to federal candidates, and there is no credible evidence that Olive Garden as a company directly funded President Trump’s 2020 campaign. Any political giving by the parent company (Darden) would occur through a political action committee or individual employee donations, which are distinct from direct corporate funding. Thus the claim that Olive Garden is "funding" Trump’s 2020 re-election is false as stated.

claim: Republicans "went out of the way to praise (Eric) Holder's nomination. ... Not a single Republican senator opposed Eric Holder's nomination."
rationale: The claim is incorrect. The Senate confirmed Eric Holder as Attorney General by a 75–21 vote in February 2009, and the opposition consisted entirely of Republican senators (21 Republicans voted against), so it is false that not a single Republican opposed him. While some Republicans praised aspects of his qualifications during hearings, praise was not unanimous and many Republicans opposed the nomination.

claim: Says Jeb Bush tweeted "Ok boomer" at Donald Trump.
rationale: There is no record on Jeb Bush’s verified Twitter account of him tweeting “Ok boomer” at Donald Trump; the viral screenshot claiming this has been debunked. Public archives and contemporary fact-checking found the image was fabricated or misattributed rather than an authentic tweet from Bush.

claim: "Private prison systems are calculating how many new beds (they will need) based on the ... number of third graders."
rationale: There is no documented evidence that private prison companies literally set future bed requirements by counting current third graders. While private prison operators and researchers use demographic and criminal-justice trends to forecast demand, and some studies link poor early-grade reading to higher long-term incarceration risk, the claim as stated — that bed planning is directly based on third-grade counts — is unsupported and misleading.

claim: The "stand your ground" law caused the shooting death of Trayvon Martin.
rationale: Trayvon Martin was shot and killed by George Zimmerman during an encounter in 2012; the immediate cause was Zimmerman's actions, not a statute. Florida's "stand your ground" law is a legal defense removing a duty to retreat and was the subject of public debate in the case, but there is no clear evidence the law directly caused Zimmerman to shoot or was applied to justify the killing at the time. Saying the law 'caused' the shooting asserts a direct causal link that is not supported by available facts.

claim: "I’m proud to say that under my administration, as you just heard, we will be building the first new heavy icebreakers the United States has seen in over 40 years."
rationale: The United States’ last new heavy polar icebreakers (USCGC Polar Star and Polar Sea) were built and commissioned in the mid-to-late 1970s, and no new heavy icebreakers have been completed since. In recent years the Coast Guard’s Polar Security Cutter program has been funded and contracts/keel-lay activities begun to build new heavy icebreakers, so saying the administration will be building the first new heavy icebreakers in over 40 years is accurate.

claim: The CDC said it "made a mistake" and reduced its count of Florida COVID-19 cases from 90,000 to 11,000.
rationale: There is no evidence the CDC publicly said it 'made a mistake' and cut Florida’s total COVID-19 case count from 90,000 to 11,000. The CDC has issued corrections to specific surveillance datasets and clarified methodology (e.g., deduplication and reclassification) that produced smaller adjustments, but not a wholesale reduction of that magnitude. The claim misstates both the agency’s wording and the scale of any correction.

claim: "27 U.S. Air Force pilots resign over COVID-19 vaccination mandate."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence from Department of Defense or major news outlets confirming that exactly 27 U.S. Air Force pilots resigned specifically over the COVID-19 vaccine mandate. Reporting around vaccine refusals noted small numbers of separations and administrative actions across services, but numbers and personnel types (pilots vs other airmen, active duty vs National Guard) were inconsistent and not corroborated as “27 pilots” resigning. Claims stating that precise figure appear to come from unverified or misleading sources rather than official counts.

claim: "Historically," Senate ratification of arms control treaties "has been bipartisan."
rationale: This claim overgeneralizes. While several major arms control agreements (e.g., INF, New START, NPT) drew bipartisan Senate support, there are prominent exceptions: the SALT II treaty was never sent for ratification after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty was rejected by the Senate in 1999 with substantial partisan opposition. Thus ratification has not been uniformly bipartisan historically.

claim: "$3 billion over the next five years will be taken out of our public schools and be put into vouchers."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and unverified: it claims a specific $3 billion reallocation over five years but does not identify which law, jurisdiction, or proposal would enact it. Voucher programs and budget impacts vary widely by state and would require specific legislative appropriation, and there is no known, universal plan currently mandating a $3 billion transfer from public schools to vouchers nationwide. Without a named bill or jurisdiction the precise claim cannot be confirmed.

claim: "If the FAA is worried about what the 5G deployment will do to the planes, what do you think it will do to our bodies?"
rationale: This claim is misleading. The FAA's concerns about 5G deployment were about potential interference with aircraft radio altimeters and avionics, not evidence that 5G causes harm to human bodies. Major health agencies and standard-setting bodies (e.g., WHO, FCC, ICNIRP) state that radiofrequency emissions from 5G at regulated exposure limits have not been shown to cause adverse health effects, though limited uncertainties remain.

claim: In 2011, "the average annual compensation for a teacher in the Milwaukee Public Schools system will exceed $100,000."
rationale: This claim is not supported by known salary data: in 2011 the typical MPS teacher base salary was roughly in the mid‑$40k to mid‑$50k range and even when employer benefits are added, total annual compensation would still be well under $100,000. An average above $100,000 would be implausible given state and national teacher pay levels at that time and MPS payroll distributions.

claim: "Reporters rehearse questions with White House press (secretary)."
rationale: As a general claim this is false: White House press secretaries answer questions from reporters and do not normally 'rehearse' reporters’ questions with them in advance. Journalistic norms and briefing procedures emphasize independent questioning, though the press office does hold background briefings, provide topic previews, or coordinate logistics with pool reporters. Those specific exceptions do not support the blanket assertion that reporters rehearse questions with the press secretary.

claim: Says science shows the physiological effects of wearing masks include hypoxemia, hypercapnia, shortness of breath, toxicity and increased muscle tension.
rationale: High-quality research and public-health guidance show that routine use of surgical and cloth masks does not cause hypoxemia, clinically significant hypercapnia, or systemic toxicity in healthy people. While some individuals report subjective shortness of breath or discomfort and tight-fitting respirators increase breathing resistance, measured oxygen saturation and carbon dioxide levels remain in normal ranges for most users; claims of generalized 'toxicity' or widespread physiologic harms are unsupported.

claim: Says a mall Santa beat up a child molester.
rationale: The claim is presented with no specifics (who, when, where) and I find no reliable corroboration; stories of a 'mall Santa' attacking an alleged child molester frequently circulate as unverified viral anecdotes. Without credible news reports, police records, or named sources to confirm the incident, the claim should be treated as false.

claim: "Hillary Clinton surged the trade deficit with China 40% as Secretary of State, costing Americans millions of jobs."
rationale: The claim mixes a roughly true arithmetic change in the goods deficit with a false causal attribution and an unsupported jobs figure. While the U.S. goods deficit with China rose in the years after the 2009 trough (an increase on the order of tens of percent by 2013), U.S. trade policy and tariffs are set by multiple agencies and Congress, and the Secretary of State does not control bilateral trade balances. The assertion that Clinton ‘cost Americans millions of jobs’ by causing a 40% surge is not supported by evidence tying that change specifically to her actions; job impacts attributed to trade with China are multi-year, multi-administration effects tied to many factors including globalization, technology, and policy across administrations.

claim: Most voters prefer zombies to the current U.S. Congress.
rationale: The claim asserts a majority of voters prefer zombies to the current U.S. Congress, but there is no consistent, reputable evidence showing over 50% hold that view. Some tongue-in-cheek or niche polls have found sizable minorities or pluralities expressing preference for 'zombies' over Congress, but those results depend heavily on wording and sample and do not demonstrate that most voters overall prefer zombies. Without a broad, well-conducted poll showing a majority, the claim is not supported.

claim: "Biden impeachment in progress."
rationale: House Republicans announced and carried out an impeachment inquiry into President Biden (announced in September 2023) and related committee investigations were ongoing as of mid-2024, so an impeachment process (investigatory stage) was in progress. However, the House had not adopted articles of impeachment or completed a full impeachment vote by that time, so there was not a completed impeachment action.

claim: "More than 90 percent of the gains have gone to the top 1 percent."
